CHAPTERS.title: Applied Anatomy: Introduction and Uterine Artery

questions.q: A person has a 46,XX karyotype. How many Barr bodies would typically be seen on a buccal smear?
options: Barr bodies are not seen in females
questions.why: Barr body count equals the number of X chromosomes minus one. 46,XX (2 X chromosomes) gives 1 Barr body; 46,XY (1 X chromosome) gives 0.

questions.q: Which structure is the female homologue of the male bulbourethral (Cowper's) gland?
questions.why: Bartholin's glands (greater vestibular glands) are homologous to the bulbourethral glands. Skene's/paraurethral glands are the homologue of the prostate.

questions.q: The labia majora are embryologically homologous to which male structure?
questions.why: The labia majora and scrotum both develop from the labioscrotal swellings — the same embryological origin.

questions.q: In a newborn with ambiguous genitalia, what is considered the single best method to determine genetic sex?
questions.why: Assessing external genitalia is the most common first step but is unreliable in ambiguous genitalia. Karyotyping is the definitive, best method.

questions.q: The fallopian tubes, uterus, cervix, and upper vagina all develop from which embryological duct?
questions.why: The paramesonephric (Müllerian) ducts give rise to the fallopian tubes, uterus, cervix, and upper vagina in a genetic female.

questions.q: Which organ has a surface lined by a single layer of cuboidal epithelium, whose most common tumour type is an epithelial cell tumour?
questions.why: The ovarian surface epithelium is a single layer of cuboidal cells; epithelial cell tumours are the most common ovarian tumour type arising from it.

questions.q: The fallopian tube is lined by ciliated columnar epithelium. Its most common cancer is:
questions.why: Tubal adenocarcinoma is the most common cancer of the fallopian tube, consistent with its columnar epithelial lining.

questions.q: In the cervix, the exocervix (stratified squamous epithelium) most commonly gives rise to squamous cell carcinoma — the overall most common cervical cancer — while the endocervix (columnar epithelium) more typically gives rise to:
questions.why: Endocervical columnar epithelium gives rise to adenocarcinoma, while the exocervix’s squamous epithelium gives rise to squamous cell carcinoma, the overall most common cervical cancer type.

questions.q: In the Bartholin gland, the gland itself (cuboidal epithelium) most commonly develops which cancer?
questions.why: The Bartholin gland proper is cuboidal and most commonly gives rise to adenocarcinoma; its duct (transitional epithelium) gives rise to transitional cell carcinoma, and its opening (squamous epithelium) to squamous cell carcinoma.

questions.q: The fallopian tube, uterus, cervix, and upper vagina all share which embryological origin?
questions.why: These structures all arise from the paramesonephric (Mullerian) duct, of mesodermal origin.

questions.q: Unlike the rest of the vagina, the lower vagina and Bartholin’s gland both develop from the urogenital sinus, making their embryological origin:
options: Identical to the ovary’s genital-ridge origin
questions.why: The lower vagina forms from the sinovaginal bulbs of the urogenital sinus (endodermal), unlike the upper vagina, uterus, cervix, and tubes, which are mesodermal (Mullerian).

questions.q: Roughly what fraction of uterine blood supply comes via the ovarian artery anastomosis, versus the uterine artery itself?
questions.why: About 80% of uterine blood supply is via the uterine artery, with roughly 20% via the anastomotic branch from the ovarian artery.

questions.q: The right ovarian vein drains directly into which vessel, unlike the left?
questions.why: The right ovarian vein drains directly into the IVC, while the left ovarian vein drains into the left renal vein first — an asymmetry relevant to imaging and vein thrombosis workups.

questions.q: Which node group is NOT a primary drainage site for the cervix?
questions.why: Cervical lymphatics drain chiefly to the hypogastric, obturator, parametrial, and external iliac nodes — not primarily to the superficial inguinal nodes, which matters for staging cervical cancer spread.

questions.q: Lymphatics from the uterine cornu can travel alongside which structure to reach the superficial inguinal nodes — the same route implicated in round ligament pain?
questions.why: Cornual lymphatics can accompany the round ligament through the inguinal canal to the superficial inguinal nodes, distinct from fundal drainage, which runs mainly to the paraaortic nodes via the ovarian vessels.

questions.q: By the 'upper two-thirds vs lower one-third' rule, the lower third of the vagina mainly drains to which nodes?
questions.why: The upper two-thirds of the vagina drains like the cervix (hypogastric/obturator/external iliac groups); the lower third drains like the vulva, to the superficial inguinal nodes.

questions.q: The uterine artery is a direct branch of which vessel?
options: Anterior division of the internal iliac artery
Posterior division of the internal iliac artery
questions.why: The uterine artery branches from the anterior division of the internal iliac (hypogastric) artery, typically alongside the superior vesical, vaginal, and middle rectal arteries.

questions.q: The uterine artery crosses the ureter at roughly what distance from the cervix?
questions.why: It crosses about 2 cm lateral to the supravaginal cervix, at the base of the broad ligament — the single most important surgical landmark in gynaecologic anatomy.

questions.q: "Water under the bridge" describes the relationship between the uterine artery and which structure?
questions.why: The ureter ("water") runs beneath the uterine artery ("bridge"). This crossing is the classic point of ureteric injury during hysterectomy.

questions.q: A surgeon is clamping the uterine pedicle during an abdominal hysterectomy. Which structure is at greatest risk at exactly this step?
questions.why: The ureter runs just beneath the uterine artery at the level of the internal os, so clamps placed too close to the cervix risk kinking or transecting it.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the classic "points of danger" for the ureter during pelvic surgery?
options: Pelvic brim, crossing the iliac vessels
Base of broad ligament, beneath the uterine artery
Near the lateral vaginal fornix, close to the cervix
At the umbilical port site in laparoscopy
questions.why: The three classic danger points are the pelvic brim, the base of the broad ligament under the uterine artery, and near the lateral fornix/vaginal vault. The umbilicus is not one of them.

questions.q: The ascending branch of the uterine artery anastomoses with which vessel near the uterine cornu?
questions.why: This anastomosis gives the uterus a dual blood supply (internal iliac + aortic, via the ovarian artery) — one reason uterine artery embolisation for fibroids can leave residual perfusion.

questions.q: The descending (cervicovaginal) branch of the uterine artery mainly supplies:
questions.why: The descending branch supplies the cervix and upper vagina, while the ascending branch runs up along the body of the uterus toward the cornu.

questions.q: Radial arteries in the myometrium give rise to basal arteries and which other paired vessels, shed with the functional endometrial layer each cycle?
questions.why: Spiral arteries supply the functional layer and undergo vasospasm before menstruation, causing shedding. Failed trophoblastic remodelling of spiral arteries is also central to pre-eclampsia.

questions.q: After bilateral uterine artery ligation for postpartum haemorrhage, bleeding can sometimes persist because of collateral flow from which vessel?
questions.why: Because the ovarian artery anastomoses with the uterine artery near the cornu, its collateral flow can maintain some perfusion even after the uterine vessels are tied off.

questions.q: The ovary's primary arterial supply comes from:
options: The ovarian artery, a direct branch of the aorta
questions.why: The ovarian artery arises directly from the abdominal aorta (just below the renal arteries) and descends via the infundibulopelvic ligament — a separate origin from the uterine artery.

questions.q: The angle of anteflexion, normally about 120°, is measured between:
options: Cervix and the body of the uterus
questions.why: Anteflexion is the angle between the cervix and the body (corpus) of the uterus, normally around 120°.

questions.q: The angle of anteversion, normally about 90°, is measured between:
questions.why: Anteversion is the angle between the cervix and the vagina, normally around 90°.

questions.q: On a per-vaginal exam of an anteverted uterus, which part is MOST easily palpated?
options: Posterior lip of the cervix only
questions.why: In the more common anteverted position (about 80% of women), the fundus is easily felt and the cervix is comparatively difficult to palpate.

questions.q: In a retroverted uterus, the fundus points toward the sacral promontory and is difficult to palpate on PV exam. Instead, which part is easily felt?
questions.why: In a retroverted uterus, the cervix (with its posterior lip prominent) is easily felt, while the fundus is difficult to palpate — the reverse of the anteverted pattern.

questions.q: The round ligament attaches the uterine cornu to which structure?
options: The anterior one-third of the labia majora
questions.why: The round ligament runs from the uterine cornu, through the inguinal canal, to attach at the anterior one-third of the labia majora.

questions.q: The round ligament's blood supply comes from Sampson's artery, which is itself a branch of:
questions.why: Sampson's artery, supplying the round ligament, is a branch of the uterine artery.

questions.q: The uterine artery arises from the ANTERIOR division of the internal iliac artery. What does the POSTERIOR division chiefly supply instead?
options: Muscles of the lower limb (gluteal region)
questions.why: The posterior division of the internal iliac artery mainly supplies the gluteal/lower-limb musculature, unlike the anterior division, which supplies pelvic viscera including the uterus via the uterine artery.

questions.q: In the surgical devascularisation ladder for intractable postpartum haemorrhage, after the uterine artery, which vessel is ligated next if bleeding continues?
questions.why: The step-wise ladder for uncontrolled PPH escalates from uterine artery ligation, to ovarian artery ligation, to anterior division of the internal iliac artery if bleeding persists.

questions.q: Why does uterine artery embolisation for fibroids typically leave vaginal blood supply intact?
options: The vagina has no significant blood supply
The uterine artery supplies the vagina only in childhood
Embolisation always spares the descending cervical branch
The vagina is supplied by the vaginal artery, not the uterine artery
questions.why: The vagina’s blood supply comes chiefly from the vaginal artery rather than the uterine artery, so uterine artery embolisation generally spares it.

questions.q: Which ligament is the chief mechanical support of the uterus and carries the uterine vessels at its base?
questions.why: The cardinal (transverse cervical) ligament runs from the cervix and lateral vaginal fornix to the pelvic sidewall and is the main uterine support; it carries the uterine vessels at its base.

questions.q: Which ligament is the embryological remnant of the gubernaculum and runs through the inguinal canal to the labium majus?
questions.why: The round ligament corresponds developmentally to the gubernaculum testis — why it can stretch painfully in pregnancy ("round ligament pain"), and why canal-of-Nuck cysts occur along its course.

questions.q: Which ligament gives the main posterior support to the cervix and upper vagina, and is plicated in McCall culdoplasty?
questions.why: The uterosacral ligaments run from the cervix to the sacrum and are key posterior supports, surgically reinforced in vault-prolapse procedures like McCall culdoplasty.

questions.q: The broad ligament is best described as:
options: A double fold of peritoneum draping the uterus, tubes and related structures
A dense fibromuscular band with no peritoneal covering
A ligament exclusive to the ovary
questions.why: It's a peritoneal fold, not a true fibrous ligament — within its two layers run the uterine vessels, round ligament, ovarian ligament, and fallopian tube.

sections.name: Complete Coverage: Homologous Organs & Sex Determination

questions.q: The male internal genitalia — seminal vesicle, epididymis, ejaculatory duct, and vas deferens — are remembered by which mnemonic?
questions.why: SEED: Seminal vesicle, Epididymis, Ejaculatory duct, Vas Deferens — the male internal genitalia homologous to the female fallopian tube, uterus, cervix, and vagina.

questions.q: The labia minora are the female homologue of which male structure?
questions.why: The labia minora and penile urethra share the same embryological origin (urogenital folds).

questions.q: The clitoris is the female homologue of which male structure?
questions.why: The clitoris and penis are homologous structures, both developing from the genital tubercle.

questions.q: The paraurethral (Skene) glands in females are homologous to which male structure?
questions.why: Skene's (paraurethral) glands are the female homologue of the prostate gland.

questions.q: Assessment of external genitalia, the most common method of sex determination, has which key drawback?
options: It cannot be performed before birth
It is not applicable/reliable in cases of ambiguous genitalia
It is more expensive than karyotyping
questions.why: External genitalia assessment is the most common method but is unreliable when genitalia are ambiguous, making karyotyping the best method in such cases.

questions.q: On karyotyping for sex determination, presence of a Y chromosome indicates a male, while its absence indicates:
options: An intersex state in all cases
Cannot be determined from karyotype alone
questions.why: Presence of the Y chromosome determines a male karyotype; its absence indicates a female karyotype.

units.title: Blood, Nerve & Lymphatic Supply: Ovary & Fallopian Tube

questions.q: The ovarian artery, the main arterial supply of the ovary, is a branch of the abdominal aorta arising at which vertebral level?
questions.why: The ovarian artery branches from the abdominal aorta at the L2 vertebral level.

questions.q: The ovary receives its nerve supply (T10, T11) via the ovarian plexus, which also supplies the broad ligament and:
questions.why: The ovarian plexus (T10, T11) supplies the ovary, the lateral fallopian tube, and the broad ligament.

questions.q: The ovary’s lymphatic drainage is to which lymph nodes, reflecting its embryological origin high in the abdomen?
questions.why: The ovary drains to the paraaortic lymph nodes, consistent with its high abdominal embryological origin.

questions.q: The fallopian tube’s arterial supply is split, with the lateral one-third supplied by the ovarian artery and the medial two-thirds supplied by:
questions.why: The medial two-thirds of the fallopian tube is supplied by the uterine artery, and the lateral one-third by the ovarian artery.

questions.q: The applied clinical relevance of the fallopian tube’s nerve supply (T11, T12, L1) is pain in a ruptured ectopic pregnancy, occurring due to:
questions.why: Pain in a ruptured ectopic pregnancy arises from stretching of the fallopian tube, transmitted via its T11, T12, L1 nerve supply.

questions.q: The fallopian tube’s lymphatic drainage is mainly to the paraaortic lymph nodes, but its intramural part (along with the round ligament) can also drain to:
questions.why: The intramural part of the fallopian tube, travelling with the round ligament, can drain to the superficial inguinal lymph nodes.

units.title: Blood, Nerve & Lymphatic Supply: Uterus, Cervix & Vagina

questions.q: The uterus receives its nerve supply (T10–L1) via a named plexus called the:
questions.why: The uterus is supplied by T10–L1 via the Frankenhauser ganglion, also known as the uterovaginal plexus.

questions.q: In the lymphatic drainage of the uterus, the body of the uterus drains to the external and internal iliac lymph nodes, while the fundus drains to:
questions.why: The fundus of the uterus drains to the paraaortic lymph nodes, while the body drains to the external and internal iliac nodes.

questions.q: The cervix's arterial supply is from the descending cervical artery, which is itself a branch of the:
questions.why: The descending cervical artery, supplying the cervix, is a branch of the uterine artery.

questions.q: The cervix receives its nerve supply from which spinal segments?
questions.why: The cervix is innervated by S2–S4.

questions.q: The cervix's lymphatic drainage follows the mnemonic HOPE; this stands for hypogastric, obturator, paracervical, and:
questions.why: HOPE: Hypogastric, Obturator, Paracervical, External iliac lymph nodes — the primary cervical drainage sites.

questions.q: The vagina’s arterial supply, the vaginal artery, is a branch of which vessel?
questions.why: The vaginal artery, supplying the vagina, is a branch of the internal pudendal artery.

questions.q: The vagina’s nerve supply differs by region: the upper vagina is supplied by S2–S4, while the lower vagina is supplied by:
questions.why: The lower vagina is supplied by the pudendal nerve, while the upper vagina is supplied by S2–S4.

questions.q: Following the "upper two-thirds vs lower one-third" rule, the upper two-thirds of the vagina drains to the HOPE lymph node group, which lies in the pelvis, whereas the lower one-third drains to nodes reflecting its:
options: Direct drainage to deep inguinal nodes only
questions.why: The lower one-third of the vagina, developing from the urogenital sinus, drains like external genitalia — to the superficial inguinal nodes — while the upper two-thirds drains internally to the HOPE nodes.

questions.q: The vulva (pudendum) is primarily supplied by the internal pudendal artery, except for the mons pubis, which is supplied by the:
questions.why: The mons pubis is supplied by the external pudendal artery, while the rest of the vulva is supplied by the internal pudendal artery.

questions.q: The vulva’s nerve supply includes the pudendal nerve throughout, plus the ilioinguinal and genitofemoral nerves supplying the:
questions.why: The ilioinguinal and genitofemoral nerves supply the anterior-superior part of the vulva.

questions.q: The posterior-inferior part of the vulva is additionally supplied by the pudendal nerve and:
options: The posterior cutaneous nerve of the thigh
questions.why: The posterior-inferior vulva is supplied by the posterior cutaneous nerve of the thigh, in addition to the pudendal nerve.

questions.q: In the vulva’s lymphatic drainage, the glans of the clitoris drains to a distinct node, part of the deep inguinal group, known as the lymph node of Cloquet, also called the:
questions.why: The glans clitoris drains to the lymph node of Cloquet/Rosenmuller, part of the deep inguinal lymph node group.

questions.q: Besides the glans, the body and crura of the clitoris drain via the superficial inguinal nodes onward to the:
questions.why: The body and crura of the clitoris drain to superficial inguinal nodes, which then continue to the deep inguinal nodes.

questions.q: The vulva is also known by which alternative anatomical term?
questions.why: The vulva, the external genitalia of females, is also known as the pudendum.

units.title: Lining Epithelium, Cancers & Embryological Derivatives (Full Table)

questions.q: The uterine cavity is lined by ciliated columnar epithelium, but a key clinical note is that:
options: Cilia are present only after menopause
Cilia are lost at the onset of menstruation
Cilia regenerate every day regardless of cycle phase
questions.why: The uterus is lined by ciliated columnar epithelium, but cilia are lost at the onset of menstruation.

questions.q: The most common cancer of the uterus (endometrium) is:
questions.why: Endometrial carcinoma (adenocarcinoma) is the most common uterine cancer, arising from the columnar glandular epithelium.

questions.q: The endocervix is lined by columnar epithelium, whose most common cancer is:
questions.why: The endocervix (columnar epithelium) most commonly gives rise to adenocarcinoma, while the exocervix (squamous epithelium) gives rise to squamous cell carcinoma.

questions.q: The vagina is lined by non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium, whose most common cancer is:
questions.why: The vagina’s non-keratinized stratified squamous lining most commonly gives rise to squamous cell carcinoma.

questions.q: The hymen is lined by which epithelium, and what is its most common cancer?
options: Non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium; squamous cell carcinoma
questions.why: The hymen, like the vagina, is lined by non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium and most commonly develops squamous cell carcinoma.

questions.q: In the Bartholin gland, the duct is lined by transitional epithelium, whose most common cancer is:
questions.why: The Bartholin gland duct (transitional epithelium) most commonly develops transitional cell carcinoma, distinct from the gland itself (adenocarcinoma).

questions.q: The opening of the Bartholin gland is lined by squamous epithelium, whose most common cancer is:
questions.why: The opening of the Bartholin gland (squamous epithelium) most commonly develops squamous cell carcinoma.

questions.q: Embryologically, the ovary develops from the:
questions.why: The ovary develops from the genital ridge, distinct from the Mullerian-duct origin of the tube/uterus/cervix/upper vagina.

questions.q: The fallopian tube, uterus, cervix, and upper vagina (all of Mullerian/paramesonephric origin) are classified as having which germ layer origin?
questions.why: Mullerian duct-derived structures (tube, uterus, cervix, upper vagina) are of mesodermal origin, while the lower vagina and Bartholin’s gland (from the urogenital sinus) are of endodermal origin.

questions.q: On per speculum examination, the exocervix normally appears pink, while the endocervix (visible at the external os) appears:
questions.why: On per speculum examination, the exocervix appears pink while the endocervix appears red, visible around the external os.

sections.name: Complete Coverage: Uterine Position & Artery Details

units.title: Anteversion/Retroversion, Round Ligament & Uterine Artery (Full Detail)

questions.q: Approximately what proportion of women have an anteverted uterus (fundus pointing towards the pubic symphysis)?
questions.why: About 80% of women have an anteverted uterus; the remaining 20% have a retroverted uterus (fundus towards the sacral promontory).

questions.q: On PV examination of a retroverted uterus, which part of the cervix is more easily felt?
questions.why: In a retroverted uterus, the posterior lip of the cervix is more easily felt on PV exam; in an anteverted uterus, the anterior lip is more easily felt.

questions.q: The clinical significance of the normal angles of anteflexion and anteversion includes mechanical support of the uterus and:
questions.why: The normal uterine angles help prevent prolapse and provide mechanical support to the uterus.

questions.q: Besides being an embryological remnant of the gubernaculum, the round ligament's functional role is to provide:
options: The primary/chief mechanical support of the uterus
Indirect/secondary support, keeping the uterus anteverted
questions.why: The round ligament provides indirect (secondary) support, helping keep the uterus in its anteverted position — the cardinal ligament remains the chief mechanical support.

questions.q: Besides the uterus, fallopian tube, round ligament, and cervix, which additional structure is supplied by branches of the uterine artery?
questions.why: The uterine artery also supplies the ureter, in addition to the uterus, fallopian tube (medial 2/3), round ligament (Sampson’s artery), and cervix.

questions.q: The branches of the uterine artery, moving from outside the myometrium towards the endometrium, follow the mnemonic UARBS: Uterine → Arcuate → Radial → Basal → Spiral. Which of these lies immediately deep to the radial artery?
options: Basal artery (which then gives the spiral artery)
questions.why: Following UARBS from outside to inside: Uterine → Arcuate → Radial → Basal → Spiral artery, with the basal artery lying just deep to the radial artery.

questions.q: To minimize the risk of ureteric injury during hysterectomy at the site of "water under the bridge," the surgical principle is to:
options: Apply the clamp as far from the uterus as possible
Apply the clamp as close to the uterus as possible
Avoid clamping the uterine artery altogether
Ligate the ureter first for identification
questions.why: To avoid ureteric injury at the "water under the bridge" site, the clamp on the uterine artery should be applied as close to the uterus as possible.

CHAPTERS.title: Applied Anatomy: Fallopian Tubes, Ovary and Uterus

questions.q: Which part of the fallopian tube is the narrowest, lying within the uterine wall itself?
questions.why: The interstitial (intramural) part runs through the uterine wall and is the narrowest segment, acting as an anatomical sphincter.

questions.q: The isthmus of the fallopian tube is the preferred site for which procedure?
questions.why: The isthmus, the second-narrowest and most fibromuscular part, is the standard site for laparoscopic tubal ligation.

questions.q: The ampulla is the most common site for which two clinically important events?
questions.why: The ampulla is the widest, longest part with the most mucosal folds — the usual site of fertilization, and consequently the most common site of ectopic pregnancy.

questions.q: Genital tuberculosis most commonly affects which part of the tube, and can cause which complication?
questions.why: Genital TB most commonly involves the ampulla and can lead to bilateral cornual block, a recognised cause of infertility.

questions.q: What is the investigation of choice to assess fallopian tube patency?
questions.why: HSG (hysterosalpingography) is the standard investigation of choice for assessing tubal patency.

questions.q: The term 'adnexa' refers to:
options: The ovary and fallopian tube together
The broad and round ligaments together
questions.why: 'Adnexa' collectively refers to the ovary and fallopian tube on a given side.

questions.q: 'Peg cells' are a normal histological finding in the lining of the:
questions.why: Peg cells are a recognised cell type in the ciliated columnar lining of the fallopian tube.

questions.q: Gonococcal infection of the fallopian tube classically leads to:
questions.why: Gonococcal salpingitis classically causes fimbrial block, in contrast to genital tuberculosis, which more often affects the ampulla and can cause bilateral cornual block.

questions.q: Hysteroscopic tubal sterilisation (e.g. the Essure method) targets which part of the fallopian tube, in contrast to the isthmus used for laparoscopic ligation?
questions.why: Hysteroscopic sterilisation methods like Essure work at the interstitial (intramural) part of the tube, approached from inside the uterine cavity, unlike laparoscopic ligation which targets the isthmus.

questions.q: An ovarian volume of 10 cc or more is classically associated with which condition?
questions.why: Normal ovarian volume is about 6–7 cc; a volume of 10 cc or more is a classic supportive criterion for PCOS.

questions.q: During intrauterine life the ovary descends into the pelvis with the help of which structure, which later splits into two ligaments?
options: Gubernaculum, into the ovarian and round ligaments
Mesonephric duct, into the round and broad ligaments
Paramesonephric duct, into the ovarian and infundibulopelvic ligaments
Urogenital ridge, into the broad and cardinal ligaments
questions.why: The ovary is an abdominal organ in early development and descends via the gubernaculum, which the uterus later divides into the ovarian ligament (above) and round ligament (below).

questions.q: The infundibulopelvic (suspensory) ligament of the ovary is deliberately preserved during which procedure?
questions.why: It carries the ovarian vessels and nerves, so it is preserved whenever the ovary is left in place during hysterectomy.

questions.q: A large ovarian mass causing pain along the medial thigh is most likely compressing which nerve?
questions.why: The obturator nerve lies lateral to the ovary; a large ovarian mass pressing on it classically causes pain radiating along the medial thigh.

questions.q: Posteriorly, the ovary is related to which two structures?
questions.why: The ureter and internal iliac artery lie posterior to the ovary — a relationship relevant to injury risk during oophorectomy.

questions.q: The ovary normally lies in which fossa on the lateral pelvic wall?
questions.why: The ovary normally occupies the ovarian fossa of Waldeyer on the lateral pelvic wall.

questions.q: Superiorly and anteriorly, the ovary is related to which vessel?
questions.why: The external iliac artery lies superior/anterior to the ovary.

questions.q: Medially, the ovary is related to the:
questions.why: The ovarian ligament lies medial to the ovary, connecting it to the uterine cornu.

questions.q: The mesovarium is the part of which structure that attaches to the ovary?
questions.why: The mesovarium is the fold of broad ligament that attaches to and suspends the ovary.

questions.q: The broad ligament can be divided into three parts by proximity to nearby structures. Which part lies closest to the fallopian tube?
questions.why: The mesosalpinx is the part of the broad ligament closest to and enclosing the fallopian tube.

questions.q: Which part of the broad ligament lies closest to the uterus itself?
questions.why: The mesometrium is the largest part of the broad ligament, closest to and surrounding the uterus.

questions.q: The surface of the ovary is covered by a single layer of cuboidal epithelium, beneath which lies a fibrous capsule called the:
options: Basement membrane only, with no capsule
questions.why: The tunica albuginea is the fibrous capsule lying just beneath the surface (germinal) epithelium of the ovary.

questions.q: Which follicle stage has a single layer of flattened follicular cells around the primary oocyte?
questions.why: The primordial follicle is the earliest stage: a primary oocyte surrounded by a single layer of flattened cells.

questions.q: A fluid-filled antral cavity first appears at which stage of follicular development?
questions.why: The antral (tertiary) follicle is defined by the appearance of a fluid-filled cavity (the antrum), absent in earlier stages.

questions.q: From outermost to innermost, which is the correct order of layers around the oocyte in a Graafian follicle?
options: Granulosa cells, theca interna, theca externa
Theca interna, theca externa, granulosa cells
Theca externa, theca interna, granulosa cells
Granulosa cells, theca externa, theca interna
questions.why: From outside in: theca externa, then theca interna, then the granulosa cell layer surrounding the antrum and oocyte.

questions.q: Cumulus oophorus (discus proligerus) refers to:
options: The fluid-filled cavity of the follicle
A synonym for the corpus luteum
The outermost fibrous layer of the follicle
Granulosa cells projecting into the antral cavity around the oocyte
questions.why: The cumulus oophorus is the mound of granulosa cells that projects into the antrum, separating the oocyte from the antral fluid.

questions.q: Hilar cells in the ovarian medulla are histologically homologous to which testicular cell type, relevant to a rare hormone-secreting tumour?
questions.why: Hilar cells are homologous to testicular Leydig cells; a hilar cell tumour is a rare, androgen-secreting, masculinising ovarian tumour.

questions.q: A primary follicle is distinguished from a primordial follicle by having:
options: Theca externa and interna layers already formed
A single layer of cuboidal (granulosa) cells around the oocyte, instead of flattened cells
questions.why: The primary follicle has a single layer of cuboidal granulosa cells, replacing the flattened cells of the primordial follicle; multiple layers mark the secondary follicle stage.

questions.q: Within the ovary, hilar cells and blood vessels are found chiefly in the:
questions.why: The ovarian medulla contains the main blood vessels and hilar cells, while the cortex contains follicles at various stages.

questions.q: Why does the uterus grow from roughly 60–80 g (non-pregnant) to about 1000 g at term?
questions.why: The pregnant uterus grows mainly through hypertrophy (enlargement of existing smooth muscle fibres) rather than hyperplasia (new fibre formation).

questions.q: The cervix-to-corpus ratio is about 2:1 (cervix larger than the corpus) at which life stage?
questions.why: Before puberty the cervix is proportionally larger than the corpus (about 2:1); this reverses to roughly 1:3–1:4 by reproductive age.

questions.q: At menopause, the cervix:corpus ratio returns toward roughly 1:1, mainly because of:
questions.why: Postmenopausal atrophy affects the corpus more than the cervix, bringing the ratio back toward the prepubertal 1:1–2:1 range.

questions.q: Moving anterior to posterior, which is the correct order of structures attached at the uterine cornu?
options: Round ligament, fallopian tube, ovarian ligament
Fallopian tube, round ligament, ovarian ligament
Ovarian ligament, fallopian tube, round ligament
Round ligament, ovarian ligament, fallopian tube
questions.why: Anterior to posterior at the cornu: round ligament, then fallopian tube, then ovarian ligament.

questions.q: The uterine isthmus lies between which two landmarks, and what does it become during pregnancy?
options: The internal os and external os; the cervical canal
The anatomical and histological internal os; the lower uterine segment
The fundus and body; the placental bed
The cornu and isthmus; the round ligament
questions.why: The isthmus, between the anatomical and histological internal os, stretches during pregnancy to form the lower uterine segment (LUS).

questions.q: Which two endometrial sublayers together form the 'functional layer' shed during menstruation?
questions.why: The zona compacta and zona spongiosa together form the functional layer, which is shed each cycle; the zona basalis remains and regenerates it.

questions.q: Endometrial thickness is typically greatest during which phase of the cycle?
questions.why: Endometrial thickness peaks in the secretory phase (roughly 7–16 mm), exceeding even the late proliferative phase.

questions.q: The myometrium's middle muscle layer is sometimes called the 'living ligature' because it:
options: Contracts around blood vessels to control bleeding after delivery
Physically stitches the uterine incision closed
Anchors the uterus to the sacrum
questions.why: The interlacing middle layer of myometrium contracts after delivery to compress the blood vessels running through it, limiting postpartum bleeding.

questions.q: The pouch of Douglas (rectouterine pouch) is the peritoneal reflection between the uterus and which structure?
questions.why: The pouch of Douglas is the posterior peritoneal reflection between the uterus/upper vagina and the rectum — the most dependent part of the peritoneal cavity.

questions.q: Culdocentesis (needle aspiration via the posterior vaginal fornix into the pouch of Douglas) classically helps diagnose:
questions.why: Aspirating non-clotting blood from the pouch of Douglas via culdocentesis supports a diagnosis of ruptured ectopic pregnancy with hemoperitoneum.

questions.q: The uterovesical fold is the peritoneal reflection from the bladder onto the uterus, located at the level of the:
questions.why: The uterovesical fold reflects from the bladder onto the uterus at the level of the isthmus, forming the surgical landmark used to enter the vesicouterine space (the "bladder flap") during Caesarean section.

sections.name: Complete Coverage: Fallopian Tube, Ovary & Uterus Details

questions.q: The total length of the fallopian tube is approximately:
questions.why: The fallopian tube is approximately 10 cm long.

questions.q: The interstitium of the fallopian tube, containing circular muscle fibres, acts as the tube’s:
questions.why: The interstitium has circular muscle fibres and acts as an anatomical sphincter.

questions.q: The isthmus, in contrast, acts as a physiological sphincter, meaning:
options: It has no muscular component at all
The product of conception moves from the wide ampulla into the narrow isthmus
questions.why: The isthmus is a physiological sphincter because the conceptus must move from the wide ampulla into the narrower isthmus.

questions.q: The ampulla, the widest and longest part of the tube, is also characterized by having:
options: The fewest mucosal folds of any segment
The most muscular wall of any segment
questions.why: The ampulla has the maximum mucosal folds (plicae) of any part of the fallopian tube.

questions.q: Comparing tubal sterilization approaches: laparoscopic tubal ligation is performed at the isthmus, whereas hysteroscopic sterilization (e.g. Essure) targets the:
questions.why: Laparoscopic ligation targets the isthmus, while hysteroscopic methods like Essure target the interstitium (intramural part).

questions.q: The normal dimensions of the ovary are approximately:
questions.why: The ovary normally measures approximately 3 × 2 × 1 cm.

questions.q: The normal volume of the ovary is:
questions.why: The normal ovarian volume is 6–7 cc (≥ 10 cc raises suspicion for PCOS).

questions.q: During intrauterine life the ovary descends into the pelvis with the help of the gubernaculum; further descent is then prevented by the:
questions.why: The uterus prevents further descent of the ovary, unlike in males where the testis continues to descend into the scrotum.

questions.q: The infundibulopelvic (suspensory) ligament of the ovary, preserved during hysterectomy without oophorectomy, characteristically contains:
questions.why: The infundibulopelvic ligament contains the ovarian vessels and nerves, connecting the ovary to the lateral pelvic wall.

questions.q: Laterally, the ovary is related to the obturator nerve and which other structure?
questions.why: Laterally, the ovary is related to both the obturator nerve and the infundibulopelvic ligament.

questions.q: A rare hilar cell tumor of the ovary, arising from cells homologous to testicular interstitial (Leydig) cells, is notable for:
options: Secreting androgens and causing a masculinizing tumor
Secreting estrogen and causing precocious puberty
Being the most common ovarian tumor overall
questions.why: Hilar cell tumors are rare, secrete androgens, and cause a masculinizing tumor picture.

questions.q: A secondary follicle is distinguished from a primary follicle by having:
options: Theca externa and interna layers only
Multiple layers of granulosa cells (versus a single layer)
questions.why: The secondary follicle has multiple layers of granulosa cells, compared to the single layer of cuboidal granulosa cells in a primary follicle.

questions.q: A mature Graafian follicle typically reaches a size of:
questions.why: The Graafian (mature) follicle typically measures 18–20 mm, and is considered mature at ≥ 17 mm.

questions.q: The fluid-filled cavity within a Graafian follicle is known as the antral cavity or:
questions.why: The fluid within the antral cavity of a Graafian follicle is called liquor folliculi.

questions.q: The normal shape of the uterus is described as:
questions.why: The uterus is classically described as pear-shaped.

questions.q: The normal size of the uterus is approximately:
questions.why: The uterus normally measures about 3 × 2 × 1 inches.

questions.q: Progesterone, acting as a smooth muscle relaxant on the uterus, has the applied clinical use of:
questions.why: Progesterone’s smooth-muscle-relaxant effect on the uterus is used clinically to help prevent preterm labour.

questions.q: The uterine cavity is best described as a:
options: Large fluid-filled space at all times
Potential cavity, with anterior and posterior walls opposed to each other
Cavity identical in shape to the peritoneal cavity
questions.why: The uterine cavity is a potential cavity, with its anterior and posterior walls normally opposed to each other.

questions.q: The volume of the uterine cavity increases dramatically in pregnancy, from about 10 mL (non-pregnant) to approximately:
questions.why: The uterine cavity volume increases from about 10 mL non-pregnant to approximately 5 L in pregnancy.

questions.q: The shape of the uterine cavity differs by imaging plane: it appears triangular in the coronal plane and:
questions.why: The uterine cavity is triangular on coronal section and slit-like on sagittal section.

questions.q: The investigation of choice to directly visualize the inside of the uterine cavity is:
questions.why: Hysteroscopy is the investigation of choice to directly look inside the uterine cavity.

questions.q: At the uterine cornu, moving from superior to inferior, the fallopian tube attaches above, while the round ligament and ovarian ligament attach:
options: Below it, at roughly the same level as each other
questions.why: Superior to inferior at the cornu: the fallopian tube is superior, with the round ligament and ovarian ligament below it at a similar level.

questions.q: A cervical fibroid is technically classified as:
options: Not a true fibroid at all
questions.why: Cervical fibroids are classified as extrauterine fibroids.

questions.q: The most common cause of failure of female sterilization (tubal ligation) is:
options: Use of an incorrect suture material
questions.why: The most common cause of sterilization failure is identification of the wrong structure during the procedure.

questions.q: The cervix:corpus ratio at puberty is approximately:
questions.why: At puberty, the cervix:corpus ratio is about 1:2 (corpus now larger than cervix).

questions.q: The cervix:corpus ratio during the reproductive age group is approximately:
questions.why: During the reproductive years, the cervix:corpus ratio is about 1:3 or 1:4.

questions.q: The histological internal os of the uterus is defined as the point where:
options: Columnar uterine lining is replaced by cervical lining
The peritoneum reflects onto the bladder
The fallopian tube joins the uterus
questions.why: The histological internal os marks where the columnar uterine lining is replaced by cervical-type lining, distinct from the anatomical internal os.

questions.q: The length of the uterine isthmus in the non-pregnant state is approximately:
questions.why: The non-pregnant isthmus is approximately 0.5 cm in length.

questions.q: During labour, the lower uterine segment (formed from the isthmus) reaches approximately 10 cm in length, comprising 5 cm of isthmus plus:
options: 5 cm of cervix, due to effacement
questions.why: At labour, the lower uterine segment is about 10 cm: 5 cm isthmus plus 5 cm of cervix incorporated due to effacement.

questions.q: The body (corpus) of the uterus is composed of three layers: endometrium, myometrium, and:
questions.why: The corpus has three layers: endometrium (innermost), myometrium (muscular), and serosa (outermost).

questions.q: Of the three endometrial sublayers, the zona basalis is notable because it:
options: Is shed first during every cycle
Is not shed during menstruation and regenerates the functional layer
Forms the bulk of the shed functional layer
questions.why: The zona basalis remains after menstruation and regenerates the functional layer (zona compacta + zona spongiosa) each cycle.

questions.q: Endometrial thickness immediately after menstruation is typically:
questions.why: Immediately after menstruation, endometrial thickness is at its thinnest, around 1–2 mm.

questions.q: Endometrial thickness in the early proliferative phase is typically:
questions.why: In the early proliferative phase, endometrial thickness is typically 5–7 mm.

questions.q: Endometrial thickness in the late proliferative (preovulatory) phase can reach up to:
questions.why: In the late proliferative/preovulatory phase, endometrial thickness can reach up to 11 mm.

questions.q: Endometrial thickness in the secretory phase typically ranges from:
questions.why: In the secretory phase, endometrial thickness typically ranges from 7–16 mm — the thickest phase of the cycle.

questions.q: In postmenopausal females, normal endometrial thickness is typically:
questions.why: In postmenopausal females, normal endometrial thickness is < 4 mm.

questions.q: The female urethra is closely related anatomically to the:
questions.why: The female urethra is closely related to the anterior vaginal wall.

questions.q: The endocervix is lined by which epithelium, and typically appears which colour on speculum exam?
questions.why: The endocervix (supravaginal part) is lined by columnar epithelium and appears red on speculum, while the exocervix (portio vaginalis) is stratified squamous and appears pink.

questions.q: Cervical ectropion (eversion) refers to:
options: Red columnar epithelium visible outside the external os
questions.why: Ectropion is eversion of the red endocervical (columnar) epithelium beyond the external os; it is physiological and does not require biopsy.

questions.q: Physiological cervical ectropion is most commonly seen in:
questions.why: High oestrogen states, especially pregnancy, are the most common physiological cause of ectropion, which can present with post-coital bleeding.

questions.q: The cervical transformation zone is the area between the:
options: Original and the new squamocolumnar junction
questions.why: At puberty, oestrogen and Doderlein bacilli drive squamous metaplasia, forming a new SCJ; the dynamic zone between the original and new SCJ is the transformation zone.

questions.q: Most squamous cell carcinomas of the cervix arise at which site?
options: Endocervical canal, deep to the SCJ
questions.why: The transformation zone (more than the SCJ itself) is the most common site for cervical squamous cell carcinoma; adenocarcinoma tends to arise from the endocervix.

questions.q: The cervix is composed mainly of which tissue, with only about 10–15% smooth muscle fibres?
questions.why: The cervix is predominantly collagen/connective tissue, with a comparatively small (10–15%) smooth muscle component.

questions.q: Cervical effacement during labour occurs due to breakdown of collagen and:
options: Increased water content of the cervical tissue
questions.why: Effacement results from collagen breakdown together with increased water content of the cervical connective tissue, softening and thinning the cervix.

questions.q: On examination, a pinpoint external os is typical of a nulliparous cervix, while a transverse, slit-like os is typical of a:
questions.why: Childbirth changes the external os from the nulliparous pinpoint shape to a transverse, slit-like multiparous shape.

questions.q: The descending cervical artery, a branch of the uterine artery, runs prominently at which clock positions?
questions.why: The descending cervical artery is prominent at the 3 and 9 o’clock positions of the cervix.

questions.q: A paracervical block is deliberately avoided at the 3 and 9 o’clock positions because:
options: The descending cervical artery runs there, risking intravascular injection
Those are the safest injection sites
questions.why: Injecting at 3 and 9 o’clock risks hitting the descending cervical artery; the block is instead given at 2, 4, 8, and 10 o’clock.

questions.q: Which nodal involvement in cervical cancer is considered evidence of distant metastasis (Stage 4B) rather than routine pelvic spread?
questions.why: The cervix normally drains to hypogastric, obturator, paracervical, and external iliac nodes. Superficial inguinal node involvement falls outside this pathway and signals distant metastasis (Stage 4B).

questions.q: Sensory innervation of the cervix is chiefly via which ganglion/plexus?
questions.why: The Frankenhauser (uterovaginal) plexus, fed by S2–S4, carries sensory fibres from the cervix.

questions.q: Peritoneum covers which surface of the cervix?
questions.why: Only the posterior surface of the cervix carries a peritoneal covering; the anterior surface does not.

questions.q: The vaginal artery is homologous to which artery in males?
questions.why: The vaginal artery, a branch of the internal iliac artery supplying the vagina and bladder base, is homologous to the inferior vesical artery in males.

questions.q: Which vaginal wall is longer, and by roughly how much?
questions.why: The posterior vaginal wall is longer than the anterior wall by about 2 cm.

questions.q: Rugae — transverse folds of the vaginal wall — are considered:
options: The most specific gross feature of the vagina
questions.why: Rugae are the most specific identifying feature of the vagina on inspection.

questions.q: Of the four vaginal fornices, which is the deepest?
questions.why: The posterior fornix is the deepest of the four fornices, and the usual entry point for culdocentesis.

questions.q: Laterally, the vagina is related to all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.why: The bladder is an ANTERIOR relation of the vagina. The cardinal ligament, ureter, and Bartholin gland are lateral relations.

questions.q: The vaginal axis makes an angle of approximately 90° with the cervix. What is this angle called?
questions.why: The vaginal axis meets the cervix at the angle of anteversion, normally about 90°.

questions.q: The vaginal axis makes an angle with the horizontal of approximately:
questions.why: The vaginal canal runs at roughly 45° to the horizontal in the standing position.

questions.q: The vaginal epithelium is classically described as:
options: Non-keratinised stratified squamous, with no glands
questions.why: The vagina is lined by non-keratinised stratified squamous epithelium and, notably, has no glands of its own.

questions.q: Since the vagina itself has no glands, vaginal discharge normally originates mainly from:
options: Cervical and endometrial gland secretions (plus Bartholin gland during intercourse)
questions.why: Physiological vaginal discharge is mainly cervical and endometrial gland secretion, with a Bartholin gland contribution during intercourse.

questions.q: Doderlein bacilli convert vaginal glycogen (built up under oestrogen’s influence) into:
questions.why: Doderlein bacilli (lactobacilli) metabolise glycogen into lactic acid, keeping the vagina acidic.

questions.q: Vaginal pH is typically most acidic during which state?
questions.why: Pregnancy drives vaginal pH to its most acidic (about 3.5–4), reflecting increased Doderlein bacilli activity; menstruation and menopause instead shift pH alkaline.

questions.q: On vaginal cytology, superficial cells with pyknotic nuclei predominate when which hormone is dominant?
questions.why: Oestrogen-dominant states show pink, eosinophilic superficial cells with pyknotic nuclei; progesterone favours intermediate cells, and a low-hormone state favours parabasal cells.

questions.q: Immediately after birth, vaginal pH is slightly acidic due to the influence of:
questions.why: Residual maternal oestrogen keeps the newborn’s vaginal pH slightly acidic for the first couple of weeks of life.

questions.q: Between about 2 weeks of age and puberty, vaginal pH becomes alkaline (6–8), mainly because:
options: The vaginal epithelium is absent at this age
Cervical secretions predominate, with Doderlein bacilli not yet established
questions.why: Once maternal oestrogen wanes, Doderlein bacilli have not yet colonised the vagina, so cervical secretions predominate and pH is alkaline until puberty.

questions.q: During menstruation, vaginal pH shifts alkaline (6–8) mainly because:
questions.why: Menstrual blood is alkaline, temporarily shifting vaginal pH alkaline during menstruation.

questions.q: At menopause, vaginal pH becomes alkaline again (6–8), reflecting:
options: Decreased Doderlein bacilli, from lower oestrogen and glycogen
questions.why: Falling oestrogen after menopause reduces glycogen deposition, so Doderlein bacilli decline and pH becomes alkaline again.

questions.q: For vaginal cytology (the hormonal maturation index), the sample is best taken from:
options: The upper one-third of the lateral vaginal wall
questions.why: The upper one-third of the lateral vaginal wall is the most hormonally sensitive site and the standard sampling location for the maturation index.

questions.q: The endocervix is also known as the:
questions.why: The endocervix, close to the uterus, is also called the supravaginal part of the cervix.

questions.q: The exocervix (the part of the cervix inside the vagina) is also known as the:
questions.why: The exocervix is also called the portio vaginalis, as it lies within the vagina.

questions.q: Cervical ectropion classically presents clinically with:
questions.why: Cervical ectropion (with exposed red columnar epithelium) classically presents with post-coital bleeding.

questions.q: In physiological cervical ectropion (as seen in pregnancy), biopsy is:
options: Required only if bleeding is absent
questions.why: Physiological ectropion does not require biopsy, as it is a normal hormonally-driven finding.

questions.q: The squamo-columnar junction (SCJ) is defined as the point where:
options: The cervix opens into the vagina
The cervix connects to the uterus
The uterine artery crosses the ureter
Columnar epithelium (endocervix) changes into squamous epithelium (exocervix)
questions.why: The SCJ is where columnar epithelium of the endocervix transitions into the squamous epithelium of the exocervix.

questions.q: Originally (pre-puberty), the SCJ is located at the external os; at puberty, a new SCJ forms due to the effects of estrogen and:
questions.why: At puberty, estrogen and Doderlein's bacteria drive formation of a new SCJ, distinct from its original pre-pubertal location at the external os.

questions.q: The most common type of cervical cancer overall is:
questions.why: Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) is the most common type of cervical cancer.

questions.q: While SCC of the cervix most commonly arises at the transformation zone, adenocarcinoma of the cervix most commonly arises at the:
questions.why: Adenocarcinoma, arising from columnar epithelium, most commonly arises at the endocervix.

questions.q: The external os is defined as the point where:
options: The cervix opens into the vagina
The cervix connects to the uterus
The fallopian tube enters the uterus
questions.why: The external os is the point where the cervix opens into the vagina.

questions.q: The internal os is defined as the point where:
options: The cervix connects to the uterus
The cervix opens into the vagina
questions.why: The internal os is the point where the cervix connects to the uterus.

units.title: Cervical Lymphatics, Nerve Supply & Paracervical Block

questions.q: In the HOPE mnemonic for cervical lymphatic drainage, the hypogastric lymph nodes are also known as:
questions.why: Hypogastric lymph nodes are also known as internal iliac lymph nodes.

questions.q: The nerve supply of the cervix arises from which spinal segments?
questions.why: The cervix is innervated by S2–S4.

questions.q: A paracervical block is safely given at the 2 and 4 o’clock, and 8 and 10 o’clock positions, specifically to avoid the descending cervical artery, found at:
questions.why: The descending cervical artery lies at 3 and 9 o’clock, so paracervical block is given at 2, 4, 8, and 10 o’clock instead to avoid it.

units.title: Vaginal Blood Supply, Lymphatics & General Description

questions.q: The vaginal artery, supplying the vagina, is a branch of which vessel?
questions.why: The vaginal artery is a branch of the internal iliac artery.

questions.q: Besides the vagina itself, the vaginal artery also supplies the:
questions.why: The vaginal artery supplies both the vagina and the base of the bladder.

questions.q: Following the vagina's own lymphatic drainage pattern, the upper part drains to the HOPE lymph node group, while the lower part drains to:
questions.why: The upper vagina drains to the HOPE nodes, while the lower vagina drains to superficial inguinal nodes.

questions.q: The vagina is best described anatomically as a:
options: Fibromuscular hollow tube connecting the cervix to the vulva (introitus)
Purely epithelial structure with no muscular wall
questions.why: The vagina is a fibromuscular hollow tube, connected to the cervix at one end and opening at the vulva (introitus) at the other.

questions.q: The peritoneum covers the vagina only over the upper one-third of which wall, forming the pouch of Douglas?
questions.why: Peritoneal covering of the vagina is present only over the upper one-third of the posterior wall, forming the pouch of Douglas.

questions.q: Anteriorly, the vagina is related to the bladder and:
questions.why: Anteriorly, the vagina is related to the bladder and urethra.

questions.q: Posteriorly, the vagina is related to the pouch of Douglas, the ampulla of the rectum, and the:
questions.why: Posteriorly, the vagina is related to the pouch of Douglas, ampulla of rectum, and the perineal body.

questions.q: Among the muscular lateral relations of the vagina are the levator ani, bulbospongiosus, and:
questions.why: The lateral muscular relations of the vagina include levator ani, pubovaginalis, and bulbospongiosus.

sections.name: Complete Coverage: Vaginal Histology, pH & Cytology

units.title: Doderlein Bacilli, pH Stages & Discharge Sources

questions.q: At puberty, vaginal pH becomes acidic (around 4–5), primarily due to the appearance of:
questions.why: Vaginal pH becomes acidic at puberty due to the appearance of Doderlein's bacilli, which convert glycogen to lactic acid.

questions.q: Doderlein's bacilli, responsible for the acidic vaginal pH of reproductive life, characteristically:
options: Are present from birth throughout life
Appear at puberty and disappear at menopause
questions.why: Doderlein's bacilli appear at puberty (driven by estrogen and glycogen) and disappear at menopause.

questions.q: Since the vagina has no glands of its own, vaginal discharge is derived mainly from cervical discharge, with additional contributions from endometrial gland discharge and:
questions.why: Vaginal discharge also includes contributions from endometrial gland discharge, and Bartholin gland discharge specifically during intercourse.

questions.q: On vaginal cytology, intermediate cells (blue/basophilic, with a small nucleus) predominate when which hormone is dominant?
questions.why: Intermediate cells predominate when progesterone is the dominant hormone.

questions.q: Parabasal cells on vaginal cytology (blue/basophilic with a hazy outline and big nuclei) are seen when:
options: No hormone predominates (e.g., low estrogen and progesterone states)
Both estrogen and progesterone are markedly elevated
questions.why: Parabasal cells appear when no hormone predominates, such as in hypoestrogenic states.

questions.q: Which artery lies POSTERIOR to the ureter, dividing into anterior and posterior divisions just after the ureter crosses it?
questions.why: The common iliac artery lies posterior to the ureter and divides into internal and external iliac arteries just after the ureter crosses it at the pelvic brim.

questions.q: The distance between the median sacral artery and the ureter — a landmark for the ureter's entry into the pelvis — is approximately:
questions.why: This 3 cm landmark helps identify where the ureter enters the pelvis at the bifurcation of the common iliac artery.

questions.q: Among the three classic danger points for ureteric injury in hysterectomy, which is the SINGLE most common?
options: Pelvic brim, crossing the iliac vessels
'Water under the bridge' — the uterine artery crossing
At the internal os, near the cervix
questions.why: The uterine artery crossing (‘water under the bridge’, about 2 cm lateral to the internal os) is the most common site of ureteric injury; the pelvic brim is the second most common.

questions.q: The best intraoperative way to positively identify the ureter during pelvic surgery is to:
options: Look for a white, glistening tube
questions.why: Watching for peristalsis is the most reliable way to positively identify the ureter intraoperatively.

questions.q: Laterally, the external iliac artery is related to which two structures?
options: Obturator nerve and internal iliac vein
questions.why: The iliopsoas muscle and genitofemoral nerve lie lateral to the external iliac artery.

questions.q: Which two arteries lie ANTERIOR to the ureter as it courses through the pelvis?
options: Common iliac and internal iliac arteries
Internal iliac and superior vesical arteries
questions.why: The ovarian artery (a direct aortic branch) and the uterine artery (from the anterior division of the internal iliac) both lie anterior to the ureter; the common and internal iliac arteries lie posterior to it.

questions.q: Ranking the three classic areas of ureteric susceptibility in hysterectomy: 'water under the bridge' is most common and the pelvic brim is second most common. What is the third, remaining site?
options: At the internal os, near the cervix
At the pelvic sidewall near the sciatic notch
questions.why: The third classic danger point is at the internal os, near the cervix — alongside the pelvic brim (2nd most common) and the uterine artery crossing / ‘water under the bridge’ (most common).

questions.q: 'Parametrium' refers to:
options: The peritoneum covering the uterine fundus
All the connective tissue and ligaments surrounding the uterus, between the uterus and the lateral pelvic wall
questions.why: Parametrium is the collective term for the connective tissue and ligaments (including the cardinal ligament, carrying the uterine artery and ureter) between the uterus/cervix and the lateral pelvic wall — the tissue whose extent of removal defines the Piver-Rutledge hysterectomy types.

questions.q: In a Type 1 (simple/total abdominal) hysterectomy, the uterine artery is clamped:
options: At its origin from the internal iliac artery
At the level of the internal os
At the site where the ureteric branch is given off
questions.why: Type 1 hysterectomy clamps the uterine artery at the level of the internal os, without removing the parametrium.

questions.q: Which type of hysterectomy removes the COMPLETE cardinal and uterosacral ligaments along with the upper two-thirds of the vagina?
questions.why: Type 3 (radical) hysterectomy removes the complete cardinal and uterosacral ligaments and the upper two-thirds of the vagina, clamping the uterine artery at its origin.

questions.q: Wertheim's (Type 2) hysterectomy carries which distinction?
options: Highest risk of ureteric injury among the three types
questions.why: Type 2 (Wertheim's/modified radical) hysterectomy carries the highest per-procedure risk of ureteric injury of the three types.

questions.q: Although Wertheim’s hysterectomy carries the highest per-procedure risk of ureteric injury, which type is the most common OVERALL cause of ureteric injury, simply because it is performed so much more often?
questions.why: Type 1 (simple) hysterectomy is both the most commonly performed hysterectomy and, consequently, the most common overall cause of ureteric injury.

questions.q: In Type 2 and Type 3 hysterectomy, which structures are additionally removed compared with Type 1, besides the uterus and cervix?
questions.why: Types 2 and 3 both remove the fallopian tubes and ovaries along with the uterus and cervix, in addition to parametrial tissue, vaginal cuff, and lymph nodes.

questions.q: Comparing all three Piver-Rutledge types, which is the ONLY one in which pelvic lymph nodes are NOT removed?
options: None — all three remove lymph nodes
questions.why: Type 1 (simple) hysterectomy does not remove pelvic lymph nodes; both Type 2 and Type 3 do.

questions.q: In Type 2 (Wertheim's) hysterectomy, how much of the vagina is removed, compared with Type 3?
options: Upper one-third (vs. upper two-thirds in Type 3)
None of the vagina is removed
questions.why: Type 2 removes the upper one-third of the vagina, while Type 3 (radical) removes the upper two-thirds — alongside a correspondingly larger parametrial and ligament resection.

questions.q: A supracervical (subtotal) hysterectomy involves removal of:
options: Only the uterus, with the cervix retained
questions.why: Supracervical (subtotal) hysterectomy removes only the uterus; the cervix is retained.

questions.q: Supracervical hysterectomy is particularly indicated in the setting of:
questions.why: Supracervical hysterectomy, being quicker with less dissection, is a recognised option in the setting of postpartum haemorrhage.

questions.q: 'Panhysterectomy' specifically refers to:
options: Radical hysterectomy with lymph node dissection
Total abdominal hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy (TAH+BSO)
questions.why: Panhysterectomy = TAH + BSO: total abdominal hysterectomy plus removal of both fallopian tubes and ovaries.

questions.q: In a straightforward Type 1 (simple) hysterectomy, are the ovaries routinely removed?
options: No — they are only removed if there is a specific added indication, such as increased ovarian cancer risk
Yes, but only the left ovary
questions.why: Simple hysterectomy does not routinely remove the ovaries; BSO is added only for a specific indication, converting it to a panhysterectomy (TAH+BSO).

questions.q: Compared with abdominal hysterectomy, vaginal hysterectomy allows a shorter return to normal activity, but is generally limited to a uterine size up to about:
questions.why: Vaginal hysterectomy is generally feasible for a uterus up to about 16–18 weeks in size; abdominal hysterectomy can accommodate any size.

questions.q: A recognised disadvantage of laparoscopic hysterectomy, relative to open abdominal surgery, is:
options: Difficulty judging the extent of thermal injury, and lack of haptic feedback
Inability to remove any uterine size
questions.why: Laparoscopic hysterectomy has a shorter recovery and smaller incisions, but carries the specific disadvantages of hard-to-judge thermal spread and no haptic feedback.

questions.q: Which of these is an advantage specific to robotic hysterectomy?
options: 3-D visualisation with scaled, more precise instrument movement
Lower overall cost than laparoscopic surgery
questions.why: Robotic surgery offers 3-D views, motion scaling, and more precise movement with 7 degrees of freedom — traded off against high cost and no haptic feedback.

questions.q: During an ABDOMINAL hysterectomy, which ligament/pedicle is clamped FIRST, working superior to inferior?
options: Round ligament, fallopian tube, and ovarian ligament pedicle
questions.why: The abdominal approach clamps superior to inferior: round ligament/tube/ovarian pedicle first, then the uterine artery, then the cardinal ligament, then the uterosacral ligament.

questions.q: During a VAGINAL hysterectomy the clamping order is essentially reversed. Which structure is clamped FIRST, working inferior to superior?
questions.why: Vaginal hysterectomy clamps inferior to superior, starting with the uterosacral ligament, then the cardinal ligament, then the uterine artery, then the round ligament/tube/ovarian pedicle last.

questions.q: Type 1 hysterectomy, also known as simple/total abdominal hysterectomy (TAH), is notable for being:
options: The most commonly performed hysterectomy overall, mainly for benign lesions
The type with the highest per-procedure ureteric injury risk
questions.why: Type 1 (simple/TAH) is the most commonly performed hysterectomy overall, typically for benign lesions.

questions.q: In Type 2 (Wertheim’s/modified radical) hysterectomy, the parametrium removed is specifically described as:
options: The complete cardinal and uterosacral ligaments
The medial half of the cardinal and uterosacral ligaments
Only the uterosacral ligament, sparing the cardinal ligament
questions.why: Type 2 hysterectomy removes the medial half of the cardinal ligament (CL) and uterosacral ligament (USL), compared to complete removal in Type 3.

questions.q: In Type 2 (Wertheim’s) hysterectomy, the uterine artery is clamped at:
options: The site where the ureteric branch is given off
The level of the internal os
Its origin from the internal iliac artery
The level of the external os
questions.why: Type 2 hysterectomy clamps the uterine artery at the site where the ureteric branch is given off, an intermediate level compared to Type 1 (internal os) and Type 3 (origin).

questions.q: In the standard order of clamping during abdominal hysterectomy, the round ligament, fallopian tube, and ovarian ligament pedicle are clamped first; however, if oophorectomy is also indicated, this first step is modified to instead clamp at the:
questions.why: If oophorectomy is indicated, the first clamp is placed at the infundibulopelvic ligament instead of the round ligament/tube/ovarian ligament pedicle, to also secure the ovarian vessels.

questions.q: A disadvantage of robotic hysterectomy, beyond lack of haptic feedback and high cost, is that the bulky device:
options: Limits the movements of surgical assistants
Increases the risk of thermal bowel injury specifically
Requires a larger abdominal incision than open surgery
questions.why: The bulky robotic device can limit the movements of surgical assistants around the patient.

questions.q: Fossa navicularis is the depression located between which two structures?
questions.why: Fossa navicularis is the shallow depression between the introitus and the fourchette.

questions.q: The labia minora differ from the labia majora in that they contain:
options: Sebaceous glands only, with no hair, sweat, or apocrine glands
questions.why: Unlike the labia majora (which has hair, sweat, sebaceous, and apocrine glands plus fat), the labia minora contain only sebaceous glands and no hair follicles.

questions.q: The round ligament attaches to which part of the labia majora?
options: It does not attach to the labia majora
questions.why: The round ligament terminates at the anterior one-third of the labia majora, after passing through the inguinal canal.

questions.q: The clitoris is best described as:
options: A remnant of the mesonephric duct
Highly vascular erectile tissue, 1.5–2 cm long
questions.why: The clitoris is highly vascular erectile tissue, normally about 1.5 to 2 cm in length.

questions.q: Hart's line marks the junction between:
options: Keratinized (lateral) and non-keratinized (medial) epithelium of the labia minora
questions.why: Hart's line divides the labia minora into a medial non-keratinized zone and a lateral keratinized zone.

questions.q: The most common site for vulval cancer is:
questions.why: The labia majora is the most common site for vulval cancer, more often than the area near Hart’s line.

questions.q: The vestibule's boundaries are anterior = clitoris, posterior = fourchette, and lateral =
questions.why: The labia minora form the lateral boundaries of the vestibule.

questions.q: In the vestibule, the paraurethral (Skene's) gland ducts open on either side of which structure?
questions.why: Of the vestibule's six openings, the paraurethral (Skene's) ducts open on either side of the urethral opening.

questions.q: The Bartholin duct openings in the vestibule are located:
options: On either side of the urethra
On either side of, and posterior to, the introitus
questions.why: The Bartholin duct openings sit posterolateral to the introitus, at roughly the 4 and 8 o’clock positions.

questions.q: A hymen with multiple small sieve-like openings is called:
questions.why: A cribriform hymen has multiple small, sieve-like openings, distinct from the single opening (annular), the split opening (septate), or the frilly edge (fimbriated) variants.

questions.q: An imperforate hymen presents at puberty with which classic problem?
options: Cyclical pain without menstrual outflow, as blood cannot exit
questions.why: With no outflow tract, an imperforate hymen causes cyclical pain from trapped menstrual blood (haematocolpos), without visible bleeding.

questions.q: Pubarche (development of pubic hair) occurs due to androgen exposure and corresponds to which Tanner stage?
questions.why: Pubarche corresponds to Tanner stage 3 of pubic hair development.

questions.q: Hidradenoma of the vulva is a tumour of which structure, typically located on the labia majora?
questions.why: Hidradenoma is a tumour arising from vulval sweat glands, characteristically on the labia majora.

questions.q: Clitoromegaly is defined as clitoral length of:
questions.why: Clitoromegaly is defined as a clitoral length of 4 cm or more.

questions.q: Clitoromegaly noted AT BIRTH is most often due to:
questions.why: Clitoromegaly present at birth reflects intrauterine androgen exposure, whereas clitoromegaly appearing at puberty reflects excessive androgens at that later stage.

questions.q: A cyst located adjacent to the urethra is most likely a:
questions.why: A paraurethral (Skene’s) gland cyst characteristically sits adjacent to the urethra.

questions.q: A cyst found on the lateral wall of the vagina is characteristic of:
questions.why: Gartner’s cysts arise on the lateral vaginal wall, from remnants of the mesonephric (Wolffian) duct.

questions.q: A Bartholin's cyst is located:
options: Between the labia minora and majora, in the vestibule, outside the introitus
questions.why: A Bartholin’s cyst forms between the labia minora and majora, within the vestibule, outside the introitus, at the site of the blocked gland/duct.

questions.q: Gartner's cyst is a remnant of which embryological structure?
questions.why: Gartner’s duct cysts are remnants of the mesonephric (Wolffian) duct, which normally regresses in females.

questions.q: The Bartholin gland is also known as the:
questions.why: The Bartholin gland is also called the greater vestibular gland.

questions.q: The Bartholin gland duct normally opens at which clock positions in the vestibule?
questions.why: The Bartholin duct openings sit at the 4 and 8 o’clock positions in the vestibule, outside the introitus.

questions.q: The Bartholin gland's normal function is to:
options: Produce acidic secretions for vaginal defence
questions.why: The Bartholin gland produces alkaline secretions during intercourse, aiding lubrication.

questions.q: An asymptomatic Bartholin's cyst under 3 cm is best managed by:
options: Incision and drainage with Word catheter
questions.why: Small (<3 cm), asymptomatic Bartholin’s cysts are managed conservatively; larger asymptomatic cysts (>3 cm) warrant incision and drainage with Word catheter placement.

questions.q: For a symptomatic Bartholin's cyst, incision and drainage is followed by insertion of a Word catheter mainly to:
options: Prevent recurrence by allowing epithelialisation of a new tract
questions.why: The Word catheter is left in place for several weeks to allow a new epithelialised tract to form, reducing the chance of recurrence after drainage.

questions.q: A recurrent Bartholin's cyst in a woman aged 40 or older (or postmenopausal) should be managed by:
options: Excision of the cyst with biopsy
questions.why: In women 40 or older, recurrent Bartholin’s cysts are excised with biopsy to rule out Bartholin gland cancer; marsupialisation is preferred for recurrence under age 40.

questions.q: Which of these is an indication for biopsy of an enlarged Bartholin gland?
options: A postmenopausal woman with an enlarged Bartholin gland
A cyst that resolves with conservative management
questions.why: An enlarged Bartholin gland in a postmenopausal woman is a specific indication for biopsy, alongside a solid mass, a fixed cyst lining, or recurrence at age 40+.

questions.q: The most common histological type of Bartholin gland cancer is:
questions.why: Adenocarcinoma is the most common histological type of Bartholin gland cancer, typically occurring in postmenopausal women.

units.title: Vulval Landmarks & Hymen Types: Missed Details

questions.q: The fourchette is defined as the point where:
questions.why: The fourchette is the point where the labia minora meet posteriorly.

questions.q: The posterior commissure is defined as the point where:
options: The mons pubis meets the clitoris
questions.why: The posterior commissure is the point where the labia majora meet posteriorly (distinct from the fourchette, which is where the labia minora meet).

questions.q: The normal (non-enlarged) length of the clitoris is approximately:
questions.why: The normal clitoris measures approximately 1.5–2 cm in length.

questions.q: The clitoris is enclosed by the prepuce above and the ___ below.
questions.why: The clitoris is enclosed by the prepuce above and the frenulum below.

questions.q: The mons pubis is best described as:
options: The area between the labia minora
The junction of keratinized and non-keratinized epithelium
The hair-bearing area above the pubic symphysis
questions.why: The mons pubis is the hair-bearing area located above the pubic symphysis.

questions.q: After labia majora, the second most common site for vulval cancer is:
questions.why: Labia majora is the most common site for vulval cancer, followed by the area along Hart's line.

questions.q: A hymen with a dividing band of tissue splitting the vaginal opening into two is called:
questions.why: A septate hymen has a septum dividing the vaginal opening into two openings.

questions.q: A hymen with a frilly, fringed edge is termed:
questions.why: A fimbriated hymen has a frilly/fringed edge and is a normal anatomical variant.

units.title: Bartholin Gland Anatomy, Cyst, Abscess & Cancer

questions.q: The Bartholin gland is located at the junction of the anterior two-thirds and posterior one-third of the labia, within the:
questions.why: The Bartholin gland lies at the junction of the anterior 2/3 and posterior 1/3 of the labia, within the superficial perineal pouch.

questions.q: A normal (non-enlarged) Bartholin gland is:
options: Easily palpable as a firm nodule
questions.why: A normal Bartholin gland is not palpable on examination.

questions.q: The Bartholin gland ducts run in which direction before opening into the vestibule?
questions.why: The Bartholin gland ducts course medially and forward before opening in the vestibule.

questions.q: A Bartholin’s cyst classically presents as:
options: A rapidly growing painful mass with fever
An intermittent, painless, unilateral mass that enlarges during intercourse
questions.why: Bartholin’s cyst classically presents as an intermittent painless unilateral mass, which enlarges during intercourse and may cause dyspareunia.

questions.q: For a recurrent Bartholin’s cyst in a woman under age 40, the preferred management is:
options: Excision of the cyst with biopsy
questions.why: In women under 40, recurrent Bartholin’s cysts are managed with marsupialisation; excision with biopsy is reserved for age ≥ 40 or postmenopausal women.

questions.q: Unlike the painless Bartholin’s cyst, a Bartholin abscess presents with pain, induration, and:
questions.why: A Bartholin abscess presents with pain, induration, and a warm, tender swelling — distinguishing it from the painless cyst.

questions.q: The management of a Bartholin abscess is:
options: Conservative management alone, regardless of size
Incision and drainage with insertion of a Word catheter
