questions.why: A Bartholin abscess is managed with incision and drainage, followed by insertion of a Word catheter to prevent recurrence.

questions.q: Besides recurrence at age ≥ 40 and being postmenopausal, other indications for biopsy of an enlarged Bartholin gland include a solid mass and:
options: Cyst lining fixed to surrounding structures
A cyst under 1 cm in size
questions.why: Fixation of the cyst lining to surrounding structures, along with a solid mass, are indications for biopsy.

questions.q: Bartholin gland cancer typically occurs in which age group?
questions.why: Bartholin gland cancer typically occurs in postmenopausal females.

questions.q: The diagnostic criteria used for Bartholin gland cancer are known as the:
questions.why: The Honan criteria are used for diagnosing Bartholin gland cancer.

questions.q: The most common presenting symptom of Bartholin gland cancer is:
questions.why: A vulval mass is the most common presenting symptom of Bartholin gland cancer.

questions.q: The normal lymphatic drainage pathway of the vulva proceeds:
options: Deep inguinal → superficial inguinal → pelvic nodes
Pelvic → superficial inguinal → deep inguinal nodes
Superficial inguinal → deep inguinal → pelvic (external iliac) nodes
Directly from vulva to pelvic nodes in all cases
questions.why: Vulval lymphatics normally drain superficial inguinal → deep inguinal → pelvic (external iliac) nodes in sequence.

questions.q: The sentinel lymph node in vulval cancer is defined as:
options: The first lymph node to receive drainage from the tumour
A node found only on frozen section
questions.why: The sentinel node is simply the first node in the drainage pathway to receive lymphatic flow (and potential metastasis) from the tumour.

questions.q: Which dye/tracer combination is used for sentinel lymph node biopsy in vulval cancer?
questions.why: Isosulphan blue dye and/or radiolabelled technetium-99 are used to identify the sentinel node in vulval cancer.

questions.q: Clitoral lymphatics characteristically bypass the superficial inguinal nodes and drain directly to:
options: The lymph node of Cloquet (a femoral node)
questions.why: Clitoral lymphatics can bypass the superficial inguinal nodes, draining directly to the lymph node of Cloquet.

questions.q: A vulval tumour arising less than 2 cm from the midline (e.g. clitoris, fourchette, perineum) requires which lymph node dissection strategy, since its lymphatics cross to the opposite side?
options: Pelvic dissection only, sparing the groin
questions.why: Midline structures (<2 cm from midline) have crossing lymphatics, so bilateral inguinofemoral dissection is required.

questions.q: A tumour of the labia majora, more than 2 cm from the midline, has lymphatics that:
options: Always cross to the opposite side
Do not cross the midline, so unilateral dissection may be appropriate
Drain only to the pelvic nodes
questions.why: Lateral structures (>2 cm from midline, e.g. labia majora) have lymphatics that do not cross the midline, so unilateral dissection may suffice.

questions.q: Vulval cancer accounts for roughly what proportion of gynaecological cancers, with a mean age at diagnosis of about 65?
questions.why: Vulval cancer makes up about 3–4% of gynaecological cancers, most common between ages 50–70 (mean 65).

questions.q: The most common histological type of vulval cancer is:
questions.why: Squamous cell carcinoma is by far the most common histological type of vulval cancer.

questions.q: The second most common histological type of vulval cancer, after squamous cell carcinoma, is:
questions.why: Melanoma is the second most common vulval cancer type, ahead of adenocarcinoma.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT a recognised risk factor for vulval (squamous) cancer?
questions.why: Herpes simplex virus is specifically noted as NOT a risk factor for vulval cancer, unlike HPV, lichen sclerosis, and VIN.

questions.q: Condyloma acuminata (HPV-related genital warts) is a risk factor for vulval cancer, unlike:
questions.why: Condyloma lata (a manifestation of secondary syphilis) is NOT a risk factor, in contrast to condyloma acuminata, which is HPV-related and IS a risk factor.

questions.q: The most common presenting symptom of vulval cancer is:
questions.why: Pruritus (itching) is the most common presenting symptom of vulval cancer, ahead of a mass/ulcer or pain.

questions.q: The keratinising type of vulval SCC (about 60% of cases) is typically seen in older women (65–70) and is associated with:
questions.why: Keratinising-type vulval SCC is linked to lichen sclerosis and differentiated VIN, is not HPV-driven, and is typically unifocal.

questions.q: The warty type of vulval SCC (about 40% of cases) is typically seen in slightly younger women (55–60) and is associated with:
questions.why: Warty-type vulval SCC is HPV-driven, arising from undifferentiated VIN, and is typically multifocal.

questions.q: Which subtype of vulval SCC is characteristically multifocal, versus the other, which is typically unifocal?
questions.why: The warty (HPV-driven) type is typically multifocal, while the keratinising type is typically unifocal.

questions.q: In FIGO staging of vulval cancer, Stage I disease (tumour restricted to the vulva) is subdivided based on which two features?
options: Size (≤2 cm) and depth of invasion (≤1 mm)
questions.why: Stage IA is ≤2 cm AND ≤1 mm depth of invasion; Stage IB is >2 cm OR >1 mm depth — a biopsy is required to assess this depth.

questions.q: Stage III vulval cancer is defined by:
options: Tumour confined to the vulva alone
questions.why: Stage III vulval cancer is defined by inguinofemoral lymph node involvement.

questions.q: Which of these findings would classify vulval cancer as Stage IV?
options: Tumour size 3 cm with clear margins
Isolated inguinofemoral node involvement without fixation
Depth of invasion of 1.5 mm alone
questions.why: Stage IV includes fixed/ulcerated groin nodes, pelvic node involvement, upper 2/3 vaginal/urethral/rectal involvement, or distant metastasis.

questions.q: When a vulval growth is clearly visible, biopsy is best obtained using:
options: Excisional biopsy of the entire lesion only
questions.why: A visible growth is sampled with Key's forceps or a wedge biopsy.

questions.q: When no discrete growth is visible, but an area of vulva appears hypo/hyperpigmented or atrophied, the next step is:
questions.why: A vulvoscopy-directed biopsy is used to evaluate abnormal-appearing vulval skin when no discrete growth is visible.

questions.q: Stage IA vulval cancer (≤2 cm, depth ≤1 mm) is managed by:
options: Wide local excision with a 2 cm tumour-free margin
questions.why: Stage IA disease is managed with wide local excision and a 2 cm tumour-free margin, without routine lymph node dissection.

questions.q: Stage III and Stage IV vulval cancer are generally managed with:
questions.why: Advanced (Stage III–IV) vulval cancer is generally managed with chemoradiation.

questions.q: After radical vulval surgery, a large raw area combined with lymphoedema leads to prolonged immobility, raising the risk of:
questions.why: Prolonged post-operative immobility from a large raw area and lymphoedema increases the risk of deep vein thrombosis.

questions.q: When groin lymph nodes are PALPABLE and found positive for vulval cancer on frozen section, the recommended management is:
options: No dissection, proceed straight to chemoradiation
questions.why: Palpable nodes positive on frozen section are managed with bilateral inguinofemoral lymph node dissection.

questions.q: If palpable groin nodes are negative for vulval cancer on frozen section, they should be managed:
options: With observation alone, no further workup
questions.why: Palpable nodes that prove negative on frozen section are then managed following the same algorithm as non-palpable nodes.

questions.q: For NON-palpable groin nodes, Stage IA disease WITHOUT lymphovascular space invasion (LVSI) requires:
options: No lymph node dissection at all
questions.why: Stage IA disease without LVSI carries minimal nodal risk, so no lymph node dissection is required.

questions.q: For non-palpable nodes in any stage OTHER than IA, the recommended step is:
options: Bilateral dissection only if nodes are enlarged
Ipsilateral inguinofemoral lymph node dissection or sentinel node biopsy
questions.why: Beyond Stage IA, non-palpable nodes are evaluated with ipsilateral inguinofemoral dissection or sentinel node biopsy.

questions.q: If ipsilateral node dissection/biopsy is positive on frozen section, the next step is:
options: Contralateral inguinofemoral lymph node dissection (bilateral overall)
Switch directly to chemoradiation without further surgery
questions.why: A positive ipsilateral result prompts contralateral inguinofemoral dissection too, making the procedure bilateral overall.

questions.q: Unilateral-only groin dissection (when ipsilateral nodes are negative) is appropriate only if ALL of the following are met EXCEPT:
options: Tumour at least 2 cm from the midline
No local extension of the tumour
questions.why: The three conditions for unilateral-only dissection are: tumour <2 cm, ≥2 cm from midline, and no local extension. LVSI is not one of the listed conditions.

questions.q: The key histological difference between VIN and invasive vulval cancer is:
options: In VIN, the overlying (basement) membrane remains intact; in invasive cancer, it is broken with dysplastic cell spread
Invasive cancer never shows HPV changes
questions.why: VIN keeps an intact basement membrane; invasive cancer is defined by its breach, allowing dysplastic cells to spread beyond it.

questions.q: VIN 3 is characterised by dysplasia involving:
options: Only the lower third of the epithelium
The entire thickness of the epithelium, but without lymphatic or vascular invasion
questions.why: VIN 3 involves the full thickness of the epithelium (compare VIN 1: lower third; VIN 2: two-thirds) but by definition has no lymphatic or vascular invasion.

questions.q: VIN in YOUNGER women is typically:
options: Unrelated to HPV and usually progressive
More likely to progress to invasive cancer than VIN in older women
questions.why: VIN in younger women is HPV-related, and about 90% regresses spontaneously.

questions.q: VIN in OLDER women is typically:
options: Not HPV-related, associated with lichen sclerosis, and more likely to progress to invasive cancer
Identical in behaviour to VIN in younger women
questions.why: VIN in older women is generally not HPV-related, is linked to lichen sclerosis, and carries a higher risk of progression to invasive cancer.

questions.q: Within gynaecological cancers, sentinel lymph node biopsy is most established for vulval cancer, followed by:
questions.why: Vulval cancer has the most established role for SLN biopsy in gynaecology, with cervical cancer next, and its use is now being explored across other gynaecological cancers too.

questions.q: Outside gynaecology, sentinel lymph node biopsy is also well established in the management of all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.why: SLN biopsy is well established in breast cancer, penile cancer, and malignant melanoma; testicular cancer is not part of this listed group.

units.title: Lymphatics, Epidemiology, Risk Factors & Staging: Missed Details

questions.q: In a small proportion of cases (about 0.5%), vulval lymphatics can bypass the inguinal nodes entirely and drain directly into the:
questions.why: In about 0.5% of cases, vulval lymphatics drain directly into the pelvic nodes, bypassing the inguinal chain.

questions.q: While clitoral lymphatics usually bypass the SILN and drain directly to the lymph node of Cloquet, they can rarely bypass both SILN and DILN to enter directly into the:
questions.why: Rarely, clitoral lymphatics bypass both SILN and DILN, entering directly into the pelvic nodes.

questions.q: When inguinofemoral lymph nodes are enlarged with clinical suspicion, dissection reveals metastasis in approximately what proportion of cases?
questions.why: Enlarged, clinically suspicious nodes are positive for metastasis in about 75% of cases on dissection.

questions.q: When inguinofemoral lymph nodes are NOT enlarged (no clinical suspicion), dissection still reveals micrometastasis in approximately what proportion of cases?
questions.why: Non-enlarged nodes without clinical suspicion are positive for micrometastasis in about 25% of cases, justifying the staging algorithm for non-palpable nodes.

questions.q: Comparing the two most common sites for vulval cancer, the ranking is:
options: Labia majora more common than labia minora
Labia minora more common than labia majora
Clitoris more common than labia majora
Perineum more common than labia majora
questions.why: The labia majora is more commonly affected than the labia minora in vulval cancer.

questions.q: Besides pruritus (the most common symptom), vulval cancer can also present with:
options: A lump, mass, or ulcer in the vulva
questions.why: Vulval cancer can present with a lump, mass, or ulcer, in addition to pruritus.

questions.q: Vulval cancer can also present with pain and urinary symptoms, occurring due to:
questions.why: Pain and urinary symptoms in vulval cancer occur due to urethral involvement.

questions.q: The predominant route of spread of vulval cancer is lymphatic, with a less common route being:
questions.why: Vulval cancer spreads mainly via lymphatics, with vascular spread being less common.

questions.q: Among HPV subtypes implicated in vulval cancer, which is more commonly associated than the other?
questions.why: HPV 16 is more commonly implicated in vulval cancer than HPV 18 (both also cause cervical cancer).

questions.q: Although not a general risk factor for vulval SCC, extramammary Paget’s disease of the vulva is specifically a risk factor for:
options: Squamous cell carcinoma of the vulva
questions.why: Extramammary Paget’s disease of the vulva is a specific risk factor for adenocarcinoma of the vulva, distinct from the general SCC risk factors.

questions.q: Stage II vulval cancer is defined by tumour spread to the lower one-third of the urethra, vagina, or:
questions.why: Stage II vulval cancer involves spread to the lower 1/3rd of the urethra, vagina, or anus (as opposed to Stage IV, which involves the upper 2/3rds or rectum).

questions.q: The most important prognostic marker in vulval cancer is:
questions.why: Lymph node involvement is the single most important prognostic marker in vulval cancer.

questions.q: VIN 1 is characterized by dysplasia involving:
options: The lower one-third of the epithelium
Only the basal layer, sparing the rest
questions.why: VIN 1 involves dysplasia of the lower one-third of the epithelium.

questions.q: VIN 2 is characterized by dysplasia involving:
options: The lower one-third of the epithelium
The entire epithelium, with no lymphovascular invasion
The entire epithelium, with lymphovascular invasion
questions.why: VIN 2 involves dysplasia of about two-thirds of the epithelium, an intermediate grade between VIN 1 (lower 1/3rd) and VIN 3 (entire epithelium).

CHAPTERS.title: Investigations in Gynaecology: Hysteroscopy and HSG

questions.q: Trans-abdominal sonography (TAS), unlike trans-vaginal sonography (TVS), requires:
questions.why: TAS requires a full bladder as an acoustic window; TVS does not.

questions.q: TVS uses a higher frequency than TAS (roughly 5–10 Hz vs 3–5 Hz). What is the trade-off of this higher frequency?
options: Better resolution but reduced depth of penetration
Worse resolution but greater depth of penetration
questions.why: Higher-frequency ultrasound gives better resolution but penetrates less deeply — fine for the closer transvaginal view, less suited to transabdominal imaging.

questions.q: TVS is indicated when the uterus is not palpable per abdomen; TAS is preferred when:
options: The uterus IS palpable per abdomen
questions.why: TAS is indicated when the uterus is palpable per abdomen; TVS is used when it is not.

questions.q: According to newer diagnostic criteria, polycystic ovarian morphology on ultrasound requires unruptured follicles numbering:
questions.why: The follicle-count threshold for PCOS morphology was raised from ≥18 (older criteria) to ≥20 per ovary in newer criteria.

questions.q: Ultrasound is the investigation of choice (IOC) for which two things?
questions.why: Ultrasound is the IOC for diagnosing fibroids and for measuring endometrial thickness.

questions.q: TVS is technically difficult in cases of vaginal narrowing, such as in:
options: A virgin patient or a postmenopausal patient
A pregnant patient in the second trimester
A patient with a retroverted uterus
questions.why: Vaginal narrowing in virgin or postmenopausal patients can make TVS difficult to perform.

questions.q: MRI is considered the best imaging modality for:
questions.why: MRI is the best investigation for soft tissue evaluation, and is non-invasive and safe in pregnancy.

questions.q: The junctional/transitional zone between the endometrium and myometrium, best seen on MRI, is normally:
questions.why: The normal transitional zone is under 8 mm thick on MRI.

questions.q: The ovaries are best visualised on which MRI sequence?
questions.why: Ovaries are best visualised on T2-weighted MRI sequences.

questions.q: In suspected adenomyosis, MRI supports the diagnosis when the transitional zone measures:
options: It cannot be assessed on MRI
questions.why: A transitional zone ≥12 mm on MRI supports a diagnosis of adenomyosis, reflecting endometrial growth into the myometrium.

questions.q: For Mullerian malformations, which imaging modality is considered the gold standard?
questions.why: MRI is the gold standard for characterising Mullerian malformations, though 3D USG and combined laparoscopy/hysteroscopy also have roles.

questions.q: PET scan is the investigation of choice (IOC) for assessing:
questions.why: PET scan is the IOC for detecting nodal metastasis in ovarian cancer.

questions.q: For Mullerian malformations, ultrasound serves as:
options: A co-incidental screening finding, with 3D USG as the investigation of choice among ultrasound modalities
An investigation that cannot detect these at all
questions.why: Mullerian malformations are often picked up incidentally on routine ultrasound; among ultrasound techniques, 3D USG is the IOC, though MRI remains the overall gold standard.

questions.q: MRI is used in endometrial carcinoma mainly to assess:
options: How much myometrium is invaded by tumour
questions.why: In endometrial carcinoma, MRI is used to assess the depth of myometrial invasion, important for staging.

questions.q: In cervical cancer, MRI is particularly useful for assessing:
questions.why: MRI is valuable in cervical cancer for assessing parametrial invasion — involvement of the ligamentous tissue surrounding the uterus — which affects staging and management.

questions.q: For assessing tubal patency, HSG serves as the investigation of choice, while which procedure is considered the gold standard?
questions.why: HSG is the IOC for tubal patency, while laparoscopic chromopertubation (direct visualisation of dye spill from the fimbrial ends) is the gold standard.

questions.q: Mullerian malformation may be picked up as an incidental finding during:
options: HSG performed for another indication, such as infertility workup
questions.why: Mullerian malformations are sometimes discovered incidentally on HSG done to investigate infertility or other concerns.

questions.q: When Mullerian malformation needs to be definitively characterised and other imaging is inconclusive, which combined procedure is used as a last resort?
questions.why: Combined laparoscopy and hysteroscopy, visualising both the exterior and interior of the uterus, is used as a last-resort definitive workup for Mullerian malformation.

questions.q: In SIS, saline is infused into the uterine cavity via which device?
questions.why: SIS distends the uterine cavity with saline delivered via a Foley's catheter, then is imaged by TVS.

questions.q: On ultrasound during SIS, infused saline appears:
questions.why: Saline appears black (anechoic) on ultrasound, making uterine pathology stand out clearly against it.

questions.q: SIS is particularly indicated for evaluating:
questions.why: SIS is indicated to evaluate suspected endometrial polyps and submucous fibroids.

questions.q: Compared with plain TVS alone, SIS offers:
options: Better assessment of the ovaries specifically
Better visualisation inside the uterine cavity, since pathology stands out against the black saline background
A way to assess tubal patency, which TVS cannot do
questions.why: SIS distends the cavity, giving superior visualisation of intracavitary pathology compared with TVS alone.

questions.q: The dye used for HSG is:
options: A water-soluble iodinated radio-opaque dye (e.g. Urografin)
questions.why: HSG uses a water-soluble iodinated radio-opaque dye such as Urografin, followed by serial X-rays.

questions.q: The cannula classically used to instil dye through the cervix during HSG is the:
questions.why: The Leech-Wilkinson cannula is the classic instrument used to instil dye during HSG.

questions.q: HSG is ideally performed during which phase of the cycle, and why?
options: Late luteal phase, to assess the corpus luteum
Any time, timing does not matter
The pre-ovulatory phase (day 7–10), to avoid disrupting an early pregnancy
questions.why: HSG is timed to the pre-ovulatory phase (D7–D10) since performing it later risks disrupting an early, unrecognised pregnancy.

questions.q: Which of these is an ABSOLUTE contraindication to HSG?
questions.why: Active pelvic infection (along with pregnancy and active genital TB) is a contraindication to HSG.

questions.q: Why is active genital tuberculosis a contraindication to HSG?
options: The dye can be neutralised by TB bacilli
Dye forced through the fimbrial end can disseminate the infection
questions.why: Pushing dye through the fimbrial end under pressure can disseminate active tuberculous infection, so HSG is avoided.

questions.q: On HSG, a filling defect with a smooth outline is more suggestive of:
questions.why: Polyps and fibroids classically produce smooth-outlined filling defects on HSG.

questions.q: Multiple filling defects with irregular margins, described as a 'moth-eaten' appearance on HSG, are characteristic of:
questions.why: Asherman's syndrome (intrauterine adhesions) produces multiple irregular, 'moth-eaten' filling defects on HSG.

questions.q: In a patient with genital tuberculosis presenting with infertility, HSG performed after a course of ATT is used mainly to:
questions.why: After anti-tubercular treatment, HSG is used to check whether tubal patency has been restored.

questions.q: A key limitation of HSG is that it:
options: Cannot be performed as an outpatient
Cannot visualise the exterior of the tubes and uterus
questions.why: HSG only shows the internal contour/patency of the cavity and tubes — it cannot visualise their exterior surfaces.

questions.q: A painful HSG procedure can cause cornual spasm, which on the film can be mistaken for:
questions.why: Pain-induced cornual spasm is a recognised artifact that can mimic a true cornual block on HSG.

questions.q: CO2 gas as a hysteroscopic distension medium is used only for:
questions.why: CO2 gas is suitable only for diagnostic hysteroscopy — it cannot be used for therapeutic procedures.

questions.q: Electrolyte-rich distension media (e.g. normal saline, Ringer's lactate) can be used only with which type of energy instrument?
questions.why: Electrolyte-rich media conduct electricity, so they can only be used with bipolar instruments (unipolar current would disperse through the fluid).

questions.q: Electrolyte-DEFICIENT media (e.g. glycine, sorbitol, mannitol) can be used with:
options: Only mechanical instruments, no energy source
questions.why: Being non-conductive, electrolyte-deficient media can be used with both unipolar and bipolar instruments, but can lead to uterine perforation and fluid-related complications.

questions.q: Fluid deficit during hysteroscopy is calculated as:
options: Total fluid used, regardless of outflow
Amount of fluid that comes out minus amount given
Amount of fluid given minus amount that comes out
A fixed value regardless of case
questions.why: Fluid deficit = fluid instilled minus fluid recovered, and is closely monitored to avoid fluid overload.

questions.q: The procedure should be stopped when fluid deficit reaches 1 litre with electrolyte-deficient media. What is the threshold with electrolyte-rich media?
options: There is no threshold with electrolyte-rich media
questions.why: The safety threshold is 1 L for electrolyte-deficient media, but higher, at 2.5 L, for electrolyte-rich media.

questions.q: Except for mannitol, electrolyte-deficient distension media are hypo-osmolar, which can lead to:
options: Hyponatremia, presenting with delirium and confusion
questions.why: Absorption of hypo-osmolar electrolyte-deficient media (all except mannitol) can cause dilutional hyponatremia, presenting with delirium and confusion.

questions.q: Normal intrauterine pressure during hysteroscopy is about 75–80 mmHg. What is the maximum safe pressure?
questions.why: Intrauterine pressure during hysteroscopy should not exceed 150 mmHg.

questions.q: Which of these is a contraindication to hysteroscopy, due to increased risk of fluid overload complications?
options: A history of one prior Caesarean section
questions.why: Cardiopulmonary disease raises the risk of fluid-overload complications (pulmonary embolism, congestive cardiac failure, pulmonary oedema) during hysteroscopy, alongside pregnancy, pelvic infection, and cervical cancer.

questions.q: Laparoscopy is considered the investigation of choice for which two conditions?
questions.why: Laparoscopy is the IOC for endometriosis and for chronic pelvic pain.

questions.q: Laparoscopy is the gold standard for diagnosing:
questions.why: Laparoscopy is the gold standard investigation for diagnosing PID, and laparoscopic chromopertubation is the gold standard for assessing tubal patency.

questions.q: When HSG shows a bilateral cornual block, combined laparoscopy and hysteroscopy is useful mainly to:
options: Treat the tubal block directly with a stent
Distinguish a true block from cornual spasm, by directly visualising both the exterior and interior
Replace the need for any further imaging
questions.why: Since a painful HSG can mimic a block via cornual spasm, combined laparoscopy and hysteroscopy directly visualises the exterior and interior to distinguish a true bilateral cornual block from this artifact.

questions.q: The standard patient position for hysteroscopy is:
questions.why: Hysteroscopy is performed with the patient in the lithotomy position.

questions.q: For DIAGNOSTIC hysteroscopy, pain relief is typically achieved with:
questions.why: Diagnostic hysteroscopy is usually done under a paracervical block with 1% xylocaine.

questions.q: THERAPEUTIC hysteroscopic procedures generally require:
options: A paracervical block alone, same as diagnostic
questions.why: Therapeutic hysteroscopy, being longer and more involved, generally requires general or regional anaesthesia rather than a paracervical block alone.

questions.q: Besides cardiopulmonary disease, which of these is also a contraindication to hysteroscopy?
options: A single ovarian cyst under 3 cm
Pregnancy, pelvic infection, or cervical cancer
A history of one uncomplicated vaginal delivery
questions.why: Pregnancy, active pelvic infection, and cervical cancer are all contraindications to hysteroscopy, alongside cardiopulmonary disease.

questions.q: During laparoscopy, orientation on the screen follows the convention that:
options: Left and right are always reversed, mirror-image
The patient’s left and right correspond to your own left and right
Only the surgeon’s perspective matters, not a fixed convention
Orientation changes depending on the entry port used
questions.why: By convention, the patient’s left and right on the laparoscopic view correspond to the viewer’s own left and right.

units.title: USG Role in Mullerian Malformation & Hysteroscopy Perforation Risk

questions.q: For Mullerian malformation, while MRI is the gold standard, ultrasound (specifically 3D USG) serves as the:
options: Investigation of choice for an initial/co-incidental assessment
Only modality that can diagnose it
questions.why: While MRI is the gold standard for Mullerian malformations, 3D USG serves as the investigation of choice, often picking it up as a co-incidental finding.

questions.q: Regardless of whether electrolyte-rich or electrolyte-deficient distension media is used, a shared risk during hysteroscopy is:
questions.why: Both electrolyte-rich and electrolyte-deficient distension media carry a risk of uterine perforation during hysteroscopy.

questions.q: The Wolffian duct is also known as the:
questions.why: The Wolffian duct is the mesonephric duct; the Mullerian duct is the paramesonephric duct.

questions.q: The Mullerian duct arises from invagination of coelomic epithelium; the Wolffian duct arises from:
questions.why: The Wolffian (mesonephric) duct arises from intermediate mesoderm.

questions.q: In intrauterine life, which duct develops FIRST and acts as a template for the other duct's formation?
questions.why: The Wolffian duct develops first and acts as a template guiding Mullerian duct formation.

questions.q: If the Wolffian duct fails to grow, what happens to the Mullerian duct?
options: It is also absent, since the Wolffian duct is its template
questions.why: Because the Mullerian duct forms using the Wolffian duct as a template, failure of Wolffian duct growth leads to absence of the Mullerian duct too.

questions.q: Mullerian duct anomalies are strongly associated with which other organ system’s anomalies, which should always be ruled out?
questions.why: Renal anomalies are strongly linked to Mullerian duct anomalies (both derive from nearby structures during development) and should always be screened for.

questions.q: The bilateral fold of coelomic epithelium carried by the Mullerian ducts goes on to form the:
questions.why: The peritoneal fold carried alongside the fusing Mullerian ducts forms the broad ligament.

questions.q: In females, the Mullerian duct forms the internal genital organs by which gestational week, while the Wolffian duct regresses shortly after?
questions.why: In females, the Mullerian duct forms internal genital organs by 9 weeks, and the Wolffian duct regresses to remnants by 10 weeks (the reverse occurs in males).

questions.q: All Wolffian duct remnants in the female are located in the:
questions.why: Epoophoron, paroophoron, and Gartner’s duct — all Wolffian duct remnants — are found within the broad ligament.

questions.q: The epoophoron is the ___ remnant of the mesonephric tubules, while the paroophoron is the ___ remnant.
questions.why: The epoophoron is the cranial remnant and the paroophoron the caudal remnant of the mesonephric tubules.

questions.q: Gartner's duct is a remnant of the:
questions.why: Gartner's duct is a remnant of the mesonephric (Wolffian) duct itself, distinct from the epoophoron/paroophoron (tubule remnants).

questions.q: Gartner's cyst characteristically presents as a swelling on the:
questions.why: Gartner's cyst arises along the antero-lateral wall of the vagina, following the course of the regressed Wolffian duct.

questions.q: Compared with a cystocele, a Gartner's cyst is distinguished by being:
options: Reducible, with a positive cough impulse
Non-reducible, with an absent cough impulse
questions.why: Unlike a cystocele (reducible, with cough impulse and preserved rugosities), a Gartner's cyst is non-reducible with no cough impulse.

questions.q: The absence of vaginal rugosities over a Gartner's cyst is explained by:
options: Stretching of the vaginal epithelium over the cyst
The cyst being lined by rugae itself
It is a normal finding, unrelated to the cyst
questions.why: The cyst stretches the overlying vaginal epithelium, effacing the normal rugal folds.

questions.q: How does a Gartner's cyst differ from a Bartholin's cyst in location?
options: Both occur at the same site
Bartholin’s cyst is on the vaginal wall; Gartner’s is at the introitus
Gartner's cyst is on the vaginal wall; Bartholin's cyst is outside the vestibule, between the labia
Gartner’s cyst only occurs in the cervix
questions.why: Gartner's cyst arises on the antero-lateral vaginal wall, while Bartholin's cyst arises outside the vestibule, between the labia minora and majora.

questions.q: An asymptomatic Gartner's cyst is managed by:
questions.why: Asymptomatic Gartner’s cysts require no intervention.

questions.q: A symptomatic Gartner's cyst (e.g. causing difficult intercourse) is managed by:
questions.why: Symptomatic Gartner’s cysts are managed by surgical removal.

sections.name: Formation of the Female Genital Tract

questions.q: Each of the two Mullerian ducts forms one lateral half of all of the following EXCEPT:
options: The fallopian tube of that side
The lower two-thirds of the vagina
The upper one-third of the vagina
questions.why: Each Mullerian duct forms one fallopian tube plus half of the uterus, cervix, and upper one-third of the vagina; the lower two-thirds of the vagina comes from the urogenital sinus, not the Mullerian ducts.

questions.q: The two Mullerian ducts initially lie lateral to the Wolffian ducts, then cross over them to:
options: Fuse with the urogenital sinus directly
questions.why: The Mullerian ducts cross the Wolffian ducts and meet each other in the midline, led initially by the left duct.

questions.q: Fusion of the two Mullerian ducts begins:
options: At the top (fundus) and proceeds downward
From the middle outward in both directions
questions.why: Mullerian duct fusion starts inferiorly and proceeds upward.

questions.q: After the Mullerian ducts fuse, a septum forms and then resolves. This septal resorption proceeds:
options: From below, upward, forming a single uterine cavity
questions.why: Like the fusion itself, resorption of the intervening septum proceeds from below upward, ultimately forming a single uterine cavity with a dome-shaped fundus.

questions.q: Complete fusion of the Mullerian ducts occurs by about ___ weeks, while the septum fully resolves by about ___ weeks of intrauterine life.
questions.why: Complete fusion occurs by 10 weeks IUL; the septum resolves and endometrium differentiates by about 18–20 weeks (the 5th month).

questions.q: Which of these structures develops independently of the Mullerian ducts and is therefore unaffected in Mullerian malformations?
options: The ovaries (from the genital ridge) and the lower one-third of the vagina (from the urogenital sinus)
questions.why: The ovaries (genital ridge origin) and the lower vagina (urogenital sinus origin) are not Mullerian-derived, so they are spared in Mullerian malformations.

questions.q: Class I Mullerian malformation (Mullerian agenesis) results in absence of the fallopian tubes, uterus, cervix, and upper vagina, while:
options: Ovaries and ovulation remain normal, since the ovaries are not Mullerian-derived
questions.why: Since the ovaries arise from the genital ridge (not the Mullerian ducts), ovarian function and ovulation are normal in Mullerian agenesis.

questions.q: Class II malformation (only one Mullerian duct present) results in a unicornuate uterus with:
options: Two fallopian tubes and a full-width uterus
One fallopian tube, and the uterus, cervix, and upper vagina each reduced to half
questions.why: A unicornuate uterus has a single fallopian tube, with the uterus, cervix, and upper vagina each present as only half their normal size.

questions.q: In a unicornuate uterus with a non-communicating rudimentary horn, which complication is most likely if that horn contains functioning endometrium?
options: Unilateral dysmenorrhoea, from obstructed menstrual flow
questions.why: A non-communicating rudimentary horn with functioning endometrium causes obstructed menstrual flow, presenting as unilateral dysmenorrhoea.

questions.q: A communicating rudimentary horn in a unicornuate uterus specifically raises the risk of:
questions.why: A communicating rudimentary horn allows sperm/embryo entry, raising the risk of pregnancy implanting within the rudimentary horn — a form of ectopic pregnancy.

questions.q: On HSG, a unicornuate uterus classically shows:
options: Bilateral dye spill with a normal-shaped cavity
Single-sided dye spill with a banana-shaped uterine cavity
questions.why: A unicornuate uterus shows single-sided spilling of dye (from the single fallopian tube) with a curved, banana-shaped cavity on HSG.

questions.q: Unicornuate uterus is the Mullerian anomaly MOST strongly associated with:
questions.why: Unicornuate uterus carries the strongest association with renal anomalies among the Mullerian malformations, and is also linked to ipsilateral renal agenesis.

units.title: Class III: Uterus Didelphys & Obstructed Hemivagina

questions.q: Uterus didelphys (Class III) results from:
options: Both Mullerian ducts present but failing to fuse, or fusing only at the vagina
Complete fusion with a persistent septum
questions.why: Uterus didelphys occurs when both Mullerian ducts develop but fail to fuse (or fuse only in the region of the vagina).

questions.q: Uterus didelphys typically presents with two complete uterine horns, two cervices, and:
options: Two vaginas, or occasionally a single vagina
A single fallopian tube shared between horns
questions.why: Uterus didelphys usually has two vaginas, though the vagina may occasionally be single.

questions.q: On HSG, uterus didelphys with two cervices requires:
options: A single cannula, as with a normal uterus
Two Leech-Wilkinson cannulae, one for each external os
questions.why: Because there are two separate external ossa, two Leech-Wilkinson cannulae are needed to perform HSG in uterus didelphys.

questions.q: A longitudinal vaginal septum can obstruct one hemivagina. If that side also has renal agenesis, the presentation classically includes:
options: Hematocolpos with dysmenorrhoea and a pelvic mass, plus ipsilateral renal agenesis
questions.why: Obstructed hemivagina with ipsilateral renal agenesis leads to hematocolpos on the obstructed side, presenting with dysmenorrhoea and a pelvic mass.

questions.q: Which complication is specifically listed as NOT seen with either unicornuate uterus or uterus didelphys?
questions.why: Transverse lie is specifically noted as a complication NOT seen with unicornuate uterus or uterus didelphys, unlike bicornuate and septate uterus.

questions.q: In a bicornuate uterus (Class IV), both Mullerian ducts are present but fusion fails above the level of the:
options: Cervix (only the cervix and vagina are fused)
Vagina alone, with the cervix also separate
questions.why: In bicornuate uterus, only the cervix and vagina are fused (single), while the uterine body remains as two separate horns.

questions.q: The single BEST feature to distinguish a bicornuate uterus from a septate uterus is:
options: The angle between the uterine horns on HSG
The distance between the horns on HSG
The internal cavity shape on HSG
The external fundal contour — divided (bicornuate) versus smooth (septate)
questions.why: The external fundal contour is the best differentiator: divided/notched in bicornuate uterus, smooth and normal in septate uterus — something HSG cannot show, since it only images the cavity.

questions.q: On HSG, the internal cavity shape of bicornuate and septate uteri:
options: Cannot be reliably differentiated from each other
questions.why: HSG cannot reliably differentiate bicornuate from septate uterus by cavity shape alone, since both show two separate horns internally; the external fundus (not seen on HSG) is the true distinguishing feature.

questions.q: On HSG, an obtuse angle (>105°) and wider distance (≥4 cm) between the two uterine horns is more typical of:
questions.why: Bicornuate uterus tends to show an obtuse inter-horn angle (>105°) and wider horn separation (≥4 cm), versus the acute angle (<75°) and narrower separation (<4 cm) of septate uterus.

questions.q: In a septate uterus (Class V), the fundus:
options: Is divided externally, like a bicornuate uterus
Is NOT divided — the uterus appears externally normal, with an internal septum only
Cannot be assessed by any method
questions.why: In septate uterus, fusion of the Mullerian ducts is complete and the fundus is not divided externally; only the septum (which failed to resolve) persists internally.

questions.q: Arcuate uterus (Class VI), the mildest Mullerian anomaly, is characterised by a fundus that is:
options: Not dome-shaped (flat-topped or mildly dimpled), with the best reproductive outcome of all anomalies
Associated with the worst reproductive outcome
questions.why: Arcuate uterus is the mildest anomaly, with a flat-topped or mildly dimpled fundus, and carries the best reproductive outcome of all the classes.

questions.q: Diethylstilbestrol (DES) was historically given to pregnant women for which indication?
questions.why: DES, a synthetic oestrogen, was historically given to women with a history of abortions, but proved teratogenic to the fetus.

questions.q: The most common structural defect caused by in-utero DES exposure in a female fetus is:
options: Vaginal adenosis (areas of vagina lined by columnar epithelium)
questions.why: Vaginal adenosis — columnar epithelium replacing normal squamous lining in patches of the vagina — is the most common DES-related defect.

questions.q: The most common cancer associated with in-utero DES exposure is:
options: Clear cell carcinoma of the vagina/cervix
Squamous cell carcinoma of the cervix
questions.why: Clear cell carcinoma of the vagina or cervix is the classic cancer risk associated with in-utero DES exposure.

questions.q: The MOST SPECIFIC uterine finding in DES-exposed women (though a hypoplastic uterus is more common overall) is:
questions.why: A T-shaped uterine cavity is the most specific (though not the most common) uterine finding associated with DES exposure; a hypoplastic uterus is the more common finding overall.

questions.q: Unlike most other Mullerian anomalies, DES-related anomalies in FEMALE offspring are notably NOT associated with:
questions.why: DES-exposed women have increased risks of breast cancer and premature menopause, and can develop cervical hoods/collars — but, unlike typical Mullerian fusion anomalies, are NOT particularly associated with renal anomalies.

questions.q: In MALE fetuses exposed to DES in-utero, recognised complications include cryptorchidism, testicular hypoplasia, hypospadias, microphallus, and:
questions.why: In male fetuses, DES exposure is linked to cryptorchidism, testicular hypoplasia, hypospadias, microphallus, and renal anomalies — note that renal anomalies ARE seen here, unlike in DES-exposed females.

questions.q: The most common Mullerian anomaly overall is:
questions.why: Septate uterus is the most common Mullerian anomaly, ahead of bicornuate uterus.

questions.q: The most common overall presentation of Mullerian anomalies is:
questions.why: Recurrent abortion is the most common presenting complaint across Mullerian anomalies.

questions.q: Comparing reproductive outcomes, which pairing correctly ranks best to worst?
options: Arcuate best (better than uterus didelphys), septate worst
questions.why: Arcuate uterus has the best reproductive outcome (better even than uterus didelphys), while septate uterus has the worst.

questions.q: The Mullerian anomaly most strongly associated with renal anomalies is:
questions.why: Unicornuate uterus carries the strongest association with renal anomalies (and with obstructed hemivagina) among Mullerian malformations.

questions.q: Increased risk of renal anomalies is seen with essentially all Mullerian malformations EXCEPT:
questions.why: Arcuate uterus, being the mildest anomaly, is the exception with no increased renal anomaly risk.

questions.q: Recurrent abortion due to Mullerian anomaly most commonly occurs during which trimester?
questions.why: Second-trimester loss is the most common timing for Mullerian-anomaly-related recurrent abortion.

questions.q: Which specific Mullerian anomaly is most associated with FIRST-trimester abortion (as opposed to the second-trimester pattern typical of most anomalies)?
questions.why: Septate uterus, with its poor vascularity septum, is specifically associated with first-trimester abortion, alongside being the anomaly most associated with recurrent abortion overall.

questions.q: Ectopic pregnancy as a complication of Mullerian anomaly is most associated with:
options: Unicornuate uterus (in a communicating rudimentary horn)
questions.why: Ectopic (rudimentary horn) pregnancy is most associated with unicornuate uterus.

questions.q: Preterm labour due to altered uterine shape is most associated with:
questions.why: Bicornuate uterus’s altered shape is particularly linked to preterm labour.

questions.q: Breech presentation is most commonly associated with which anomaly, ahead of septate and bicornuate uterus?
questions.why: Uterus didelphys is the most common anomaly associated with breech presentation, ahead of septate and bicornuate uterus; Mullerian malformations overall are the most common cause of recurrent breech.

questions.q: Transverse lie in a Mullerian anomaly is associated with septate and bicornuate uterus, but is specifically NOT seen in:
questions.why: Transverse lie is a recognised complication of septate and bicornuate uterus, but is specifically absent in unicornuate uterus and uterus didelphys.

questions.q: In Mullerian anomalies with outflow tract obstruction, the typical sequence of complications proceeds:
questions.why: Obstructed outflow leads first to hematometra (blood collection), which can then lead to endometriosis via retrograde menstruation.

questions.q: Unilateral dysmenorrhoea in a Mullerian anomaly is classically associated with:
options: Uterus didelphys with two patent vaginas
questions.why: Unilateral dysmenorrhoea points to an obstructed non-communicating horn, as seen in unicornuate uterus.

questions.q: Although infertility from Mullerian anomalies is relatively rare, the anomaly most associated with it is:
questions.why: Septate uterus is the anomaly most associated with infertility, though infertility overall is an uncommon presentation of Mullerian anomalies (often a co-incidental finding on HSG).

questions.q: On routine clinical examination, Mullerian anomalies are generally not detectable, EXCEPT:
options: Septate uterus, felt as a midline ridge
Arcuate uterus, felt as a flattened fundus
Uterus didelphys, where two vaginas may be found
Bicornuate uterus, felt as two separate cervices
questions.why: Clinical examination is generally unhelpful for Mullerian anomalies, except in uterus didelphys, where two vaginas may be found on exam.

questions.q: As a first (screening) investigation, Mullerian anomalies are often picked up as a co-incidental finding on TVS done for recurrent abortions, or on HSG done for:
questions.why: Mullerian anomalies are commonly co-incidental findings on TVS (done to work up recurrent abortion) or HSG (done to work up infertility).

questions.q: Ranking the investigation pathway for Mullerian anomalies from initial screening to definitive last-resort workup:
options: 3D USG (IOC) → MRI (gold standard) → combined laparoscopy and hysteroscopy (last resort)
questions.why: 3D USG is the investigation of choice, MRI is the gold standard for full characterisation, and combined laparoscopy plus hysteroscopy is reserved as a last resort to directly visualise the exterior and interior.

questions.q: Surgical correction of Mullerian anomalies (e.g. unification surgery for bicornuate uterus) is generally indicated for:
questions.why: Recurrent abortion is the main indication for surgical correction of a Mullerian anomaly such as bicornuate uterus.

questions.q: Unification surgery (metroplasty) for bicornuate uterus is known as Strassman metroplasty or:
questions.why: Strassman metroplasty and Tompkin's metroplasty are both unification procedures for bicornuate uterus (the same surgery can also be used for uterus didelphys).

questions.q: For a septate uterus, the modern surgical approach is:
questions.why: Septate uterus is treated by hysteroscopic resection of the septum; the older abdominal approach was Jones metroplasty.

questions.q: A recognised disadvantage of metroplasty is that it:
options: Improves fertility in all cases with no risks
Cannot be performed at all in modern practice
Requires delivery by Caesarean section and risks pelvic adhesions leading to infertility
Always requires removal of the ovaries
questions.why: After metroplasty, subsequent delivery must be by Caesarean section, and the procedure risks pelvic adhesion formation, which can itself cause infertility.

sections.name: Complete Coverage: Mullerian Anomaly & DES Details

questions.q: Besides unilateral dysmenorrhoea, ectopic pregnancy, and unilateral renal anomalies, unicornuate uterus can also be associated with:
questions.why: Unicornuate uterus can be associated with an ectopic ovary, in addition to unilateral dysmenorrhoea, ectopic pregnancy, and unilateral renal anomalies.

questions.q: While a T-shaped uterus is the most SPECIFIC uterine finding in DES exposure, the most COMMON uterine finding is:
questions.why: Hypoplastic uterus is the most common uterine finding in DES exposure, while T-shaped uterus is the most specific (though less common) finding.

questions.q: In-utero DES exposure can lead to cervical abnormalities described as:
questions.why: DES exposure can lead to cervical hoods/collars, in addition to vaginal adenosis and uterine anomalies.

questions.q: Long-term (chronic) outcomes of in-utero DES exposure in females include increased risk of clear cell carcinoma and premature menopause, as well as increased risk of:
questions.why: Chronic outcomes of DES exposure include an increased risk of breast cancer, along with clear cell carcinoma and premature menopause.

questions.q: Recurrent abortion, the most common obstetric complication of Mullerian anomalies, most commonly occurs during which trimester?
questions.why: Recurrent abortion in Mullerian anomalies most commonly occurs in the second trimester.

questions.q: Unlike the general pattern of second-trimester loss with Mullerian anomalies, first-trimester abortion is specifically associated with:
questions.why: Septate uterus is specifically associated with first-trimester abortion, unlike the general second-trimester pattern seen with other anomalies.

questions.q: Ectopic pregnancy, as an obstetric complication of Mullerian anomalies, is most strongly associated with:
questions.why: Ectopic pregnancy is most strongly associated with unicornuate uterus (particularly with a communicating rudimentary horn).

questions.q: Preterm labour, occurring due to the altered shape of the uterine cavity, is most strongly associated with:
questions.why: Preterm labour due to altered uterine shape is most strongly associated with bicornuate uterus.

questions.q: Women with Mullerian anomalies carry an increased risk of which mode of delivery?
questions.why: Mullerian anomalies carry an increased risk of Caesarean section delivery.

questions.q: Besides recurrent abortion, preterm labour, and IUGR, another obstetric complication associated with Mullerian anomalies is:
questions.why: Pregnancy-induced hypertension (PIH) is another recognised obstetric complication of Mullerian anomalies.

questions.q: Increased risk of renal anomalies is seen with Mullerian anomalies in general, with a notable exception in:
questions.why: All Mullerian anomalies carry an increased risk of renal anomalies, except arcuate uterus (the mildest form, with the best reproductive outcome).

questions.q: Although infertility is a rare gynaecological complication of Mullerian anomalies overall, when it does occur it is most commonly associated with:
questions.why: Septate uterus is the anomaly most commonly associated with infertility, though infertility overall is rare with Mullerian anomalies.

questions.q: Clinical (bimanual/speculum) examination is generally not useful for diagnosing Mullerian anomalies, with a notable exception in:
options: Arcuate uterus, which is always palpably distinct
Uterus didelphys, which may show two vaginas/two cervices on examination
Bicornuate uterus, which is diagnosed by palpation alone
Septate uterus, which shows a visibly split cervix
questions.why: Clinical examination is generally not useful for Mullerian anomalies, except in uterus didelphys, which can show two vaginas/cervices on examination.

CHAPTERS.title: Development of Vagina and Transverse Vaginal Septum

questions.q: The upper one-third of the vagina develops from the caudal fused part of the Mullerian duct, with which tissue origin?
questions.why: The Mullerian-derived upper vagina is mesodermal in origin, forming the fibromuscular wall.

questions.q: The lower two-thirds of the vagina develops from the sinovaginal bulb (from the urogenital sinus), with which tissue origin?
options: Mesenchymal only, with no epithelial contribution
questions.why: The sinovaginal bulb is endodermal in origin, forming the epithelium of the lower vagina.

questions.q: Where the upper and lower parts of the developing vagina meet, they initially form a:
questions.why: A transverse vaginal septum forms transiently where the upper (Mullerian) and lower (sinovaginal bulb) parts meet.

questions.q: The transverse septum formed during vaginal development normally dissolves by about:
questions.why: The transverse septum normally dissolves by 20 weeks IUL, giving a single canalised vaginal canal.

questions.q: Canalisation of the vagina is complete throughout its length EXCEPT at the:
options: Distal end, where the sinovaginal bulb meets the urogenital sinus proper (forming the hymen)
It is always complete with no exceptions
questions.why: The distal-most point, where the sinovaginal bulb tissue meets the urogenital sinus proper, remains as a membrane — the hymen — which has an opening for menstrual outflow.

questions.q: Both the hymen and the vagina share which epithelial lining?
questions.why: Both the hymen and vagina are lined by non-keratinised stratified squamous epithelium.

questions.q: Vaginal agenesis (complete absence of the vagina) is strongly associated with:
questions.why: Vaginal agenesis is a rare condition strongly associated with Mullerian agenesis.

questions.q: A key symptom pattern in vaginal agenesis is:
options: Painless amenorrhoea with no other symptoms
Cyclical abdominal pain WITHOUT visible menstruation (cryptomenorrhoea)
questions.why: Vaginal agenesis presents with hidden menstruation and cyclical pain from outflow obstruction, without visible external bleeding, and an absent vaginal opening on exam.

questions.q: A longitudinal vaginal septum (creating a hemivagina) is associated with:
questions.why: A longitudinal vaginal septum, creating a hemivagina, is associated with uterus didelphys.

questions.q: Transverse vaginal septum results from:
options: Complete absence of the sinovaginal bulb
Failure of resolution of the septum formed where upper and lower vagina meet
questions.why: Transverse vaginal septum is caused by failure of the normal septum (formed at the junction of the Mullerian- and sinovaginal-bulb-derived vagina) to resolve.

questions.q: Imperforate hymen and transverse vaginal septum share which common presenting complaint?
questions.why: Both imperforate hymen and TVS present with outflow tract obstruction (cryptomenorrhoea).

questions.q: The most common cause of cryptomenorrhoea (hidden menstruation) is:
questions.why: Imperforate hymen is the most common cause of cryptomenorrhoea, ahead of transverse vaginal septum and vaginal agenesis.

questions.q: A young woman presenting with primary amenorrhoea, cyclical pelvic pain, and urinary retention, but normal secondary sexual characteristics, should raise suspicion for:
options: An outflow tract obstruction such as imperforate hymen
questions.why: Normal secondary sexual characteristics with cyclical pain and primary amenorrhoea points to a purely anatomical outflow obstruction, not a hormonal or gonadal problem.

questions.q: In cryptomenorrhoea, retrograde menstruation through the tubes increases the risk of developing:
options: Endometriosis, which itself causes dysmenorrhoea (the most common symptom)
questions.why: Outflow obstruction promotes retrograde menstrual flow, raising the risk of endometriosis, whose most common symptom is dysmenorrhoea.

questions.q: Blood collecting in the vagina (from outflow obstruction) is called:
questions.why: Hematocolpos refers to blood collection within the vagina.

questions.q: Blood collecting within the fallopian tube, from severe or prolonged outflow obstruction, is called:
questions.why: Hematosalpinx refers to blood collection within the fallopian tube, the most proximal (and least common) site of collection in outflow obstruction.

questions.q: In cryptomenorrhoea, the karyotype, gonads (ovaries), breast development, and axillary/pubic hair are all normal, because:
options: The problem is purely anatomical (outflow obstruction), not hormonal or gonadal
The ovaries are also affected but compensate
questions.why: Cryptomenorrhoea from outflow obstruction is a purely structural problem; the 46,XX karyotype, ovaries, and secondary sexual characteristics are entirely normal.

questions.q: Besides primary amenorrhoea and cyclical pelvic pain, cryptomenorrhoea from outflow obstruction can also present with:
options: Urinary retention, from pressure on the bladder/urethra
questions.why: The distended, blood-filled vagina/uterus can press on the bladder and urethra, causing urinary retention alongside the classic cyclical pain and amenorrhoea.

questions.q: Comparing site of obstruction: imperforate hymen occurs at the introitus, while transverse vaginal septum most commonly occurs:
options: In the upper part of the vagina
questions.why: TVS most commonly occurs in the upper part of the vagina, well above the introitus.

questions.q: On local examination, imperforate hymen classically shows a tense, bulging (sometimes bluish) hymen, whereas TVS typically shows:
options: A hymen that is completely absent
No bulging, because the thick fibrous septum lies higher up
questions.why: With TVS, the hymen itself appears normal (no bulging) since the obstruction and thick fibrous septum lie further up the vaginal canal.

questions.q: A positive cough impulse at the introitus is expected with:
questions.why: Imperforate hymen shows a positive cough impulse at the introitus; TVS does not, since the obstruction is further up.

questions.q: Hematometra (blood collection in the uterus) is:
options: Less common with TVS than with imperforate hymen
More common with transverse vaginal septum than with imperforate hymen
questions.why: Hematometra is more common with TVS (less common with imperforate hymen), reflecting the septum’s more proximal location allowing collection to back up further.

questions.q: Urinary tract (renal) abnormalities are:
options: Usually NOT associated with imperforate hymen, but must be ruled out with TVS
questions.why: Urinary tract abnormalities are not typically linked to imperforate hymen, but TVS mandates renal imaging to rule them out.

questions.q: MRI is considered essential in TVS to determine site, thickness, and rule out renal abnormalities, whereas in imperforate hymen, MRI is:
questions.why: Imperforate hymen is usually a clinical diagnosis and does not require MRI, unlike TVS, where MRI is mandatory pre-operatively.

questions.q: Management of imperforate hymen is a cruciate incision, while management of transverse vaginal septum is:
questions.why: TVS requires surgical resection/excision of the septum, a more extensive procedure than the simple cruciate incision used for imperforate hymen.

questions.q: In cryptomenorrhoea from outflow obstruction, hormonal profile (FSH, LH, oestrogen) is:
options: Not needed, since these levels are normal
questions.why: Since the ovaries and hormonal axis are unaffected, hormonal profile testing is not needed in outflow-obstruction cryptomenorrhoea.

questions.q: The first investigation for a suspected outflow tract obstruction is:
options: USG pelvis, to confirm the uterus is present and assess for hematometra/hematocolpos
questions.why: USG pelvis is the first investigation, confirming uterine presence and assessing for hematometra/hematocolpos.

questions.q: MRI is the investigation of choice mainly to:
options: Differentiate between imperforate hymen and transverse vaginal septum
Replace ultrasound as the first-line test
questions.why: MRI’s main role here is to reliably differentiate imperforate hymen from TVS when the diagnosis is unclear.

questions.q: In the work-up of a suprapubic bulge, catheterising the bladder and finding the bulge decreases in size indicates the swelling was:
questions.why: If catheterisation reduces the bulge, the swelling was simply due to a full bladder.

questions.q: If a suprapubic bulge persists despite catheterisation, the next step is:
options: USG pelvis to look for hematometra, with MRI if still in doubt
Reassurance, as this is a normal finding
questions.why: A persistent bulge after catheterisation points to uterine swelling; USG pelvis is used to check for hematometra, with MRI reserved for cases still in doubt.

questions.q: On examination of suspected outflow tract obstruction, per vaginal examination is:
options: Contraindicated in a virgin patient; per rectal exam is used instead, which may reveal an anterior swelling
questions.why: PV exam is avoided in a virgin patient with suspected outflow obstruction; per rectal exam is used instead and may reveal an anterior swelling from the collected blood.

questions.q: Using the local examination algorithm for outflow obstruction: an ABSENT introitus points toward vaginal agenesis, while a PRESENT introitus with no visible opening points toward:
options: A normal finding requiring no further workup
questions.why: With the introitus present but no opening visible, imperforate hymen is the likely diagnosis; if a septum is felt through a present, open introitus, TVS is suspected instead.

sections.name: Complete Coverage: TVS Site & Hematocolpos Location

units.title: Missed Details: TVS Site & Hematocolpos Location

questions.q: The most common site for a transverse vaginal septum is the:
options: Lower part of the vagina, at the introitus
questions.why: A transverse vaginal septum most commonly occurs in the upper part of the vagina, unlike imperforate hymen which obstructs right at the introitus.

questions.q: The location of hematocolpos differs by condition: with imperforate hymen it collects in the lower vagina, while with transverse vaginal septum it collects in the:
questions.why: Hematocolpos collects in the lower vagina with imperforate hymen, but in the upper vagina with transverse vaginal septum, reflecting the different obstruction sites.

questions.q: At puberty, GnRH is released from the hypothalamus in which pattern?
options: A single large surge only at menarche
questions.why: GnRH is released in a pulsatile manner from the hypothalamus, driving the HPO axis.

questions.q: Which hormone is considered the initiator of the ovarian cycle?
questions.why: FSH, released from the anterior pituitary in response to GnRH, is the initiator of the ovarian cycle.

questions.q: The primary oocyte remains arrested in which stage until ovulation?
questions.why: Primary oocytes are arrested in the diplotene (dictyate) stage of prophase I from fetal life until ovulation.

questions.q: The earliest follicle stage, with a single layer of flat follicular cells, is the:
questions.why: The primordial follicle has a single layer of flat follicular cells around the oocyte.

questions.q: A follicle with a single layer of cuboidal cells around the oocyte is termed:
questions.why: The primary follicle is defined by a single layer of cuboidal cells replacing the flattened cells of the primordial stage.

questions.q: As the follicle differentiates into granulosa and theca cells, which receptors first appear?
questions.why: FSH receptors appear on granulosa cells as the follicle differentiates, enabling FSH-driven growth.

questions.q: Follicular growth up to the early pre-antral stage (about 70 days) is:
questions.why: Early follicular growth, up to the early pre-antral stage, proceeds independently of FSH.

questions.q: From the late pre-antral stage to the Graafian follicle (about 14 days), follicular growth becomes:
questions.why: From the late pre-antral stage onward, follicular growth becomes FSH-dependent, culminating in the Graafian follicle after about 14 days.

questions.q: The total time from primordial follicle to Graafian follicle is approximately:
questions.why: The full journey from primordial follicle to Graafian follicle takes about 84–85 days (70 FSH-independent + 14 FSH-dependent).

questions.q: Oestrogen, the main hormone product of granulosa cells, causes proliferation of the uterine endometrium. Giving unopposed oestrogen to a woman with an intact uterus raises the risk of:
questions.why: Unopposed oestrogen (without progesterone) in a woman with an intact uterus drives endometrial proliferation, raising the risk of hyperplasia and cancer — hence oestrogen is never given alone in this setting.

questions.q: Inhibin B, released by granulosa cells, provides negative feedback on FSH, causing atresia of all FSH-stimulated follicles EXCEPT:
options: Follicles in the contralateral ovary only
questions.why: As FSH falls under inhibin B’s negative feedback, only the dominant follicle (most FSH-sensitive) survives; the rest undergo atresia.

questions.q: A granulosa cell tumour is a feminising tumour (raised oestrogen) with which classic tumour marker?
questions.why: Inhibin B is the classic tumour marker for granulosa cell tumours; AMH is a newer marker.

questions.q: Anti-Mullerian hormone (AMH), the third hormone released by granulosa cells, is used clinically as a marker of:
questions.why: AMH, produced by pre-antral and small antral follicles from puberty onward and proportional to follicle number, is used as a test of ovarian reserve.

questions.q: The LH surge acts on LH receptors on the granulosa cells of the dominant follicle (receptors induced earlier by FSH) to cause:
options: Luteinisation of the granulosa cells, releasing progesterone
questions.why: LH luteinises the granulosa cells of the dominant follicle, which then release progesterone — the main hormone of the luteinised follicle.

questions.q: The LH surge also acts on theca cells, stimulating production of:
options: Androgens, later converted to oestrogen by granulosa-cell aromatase
questions.why: LH stimulates theca cells to produce androgens, which diffuse to granulosa cells for aromatisation into oestrogen.

questions.q: Regarding oestrogen subtypes, adipose tissue specifically releases:
questions.why: Adipose tissue specifically releases oestrone (E1), distinct from ovarian oestradiol (E2).

questions.q: Ovulation is brought about by the:
questions.why: Ovulation follows the combined FSH and LH surge but is specifically brought about by the LH surge.

questions.q: At ovulation, resumption of meiosis I converts the primary oocyte into a:
questions.why: Resumption of meiosis I at ovulation converts the primary oocyte into a secondary oocyte (plus the first polar body).

questions.q: The LH surge initiates an oestrogen-dominant phase, which is then maintained by combined oestrogen and progesterone as the luteinised granulosa cells become the:
questions.why: Luteinised granulosa cells form the corpus luteum, which maintains combined oestrogen and progesterone secretion.

questions.q: The corpus luteum is typically formed on which day of a standard 28-day cycle?
questions.why: The corpus luteum forms around day 14, right after ovulation.

questions.q: Growth and continued activity of the corpus luteum is maintained by:
questions.why: LH maintains the growth and secretory activity of the corpus luteum.

questions.q: The corpus luteum reaches maximum activity approximately how many days after ovulation?
questions.why: Corpus luteum activity peaks about 8 days after ovulation, around day 22 of a standard cycle.

questions.q: The typical lifespan of the (non-pregnancy) corpus luteum is:
questions.why: In the absence of pregnancy, the corpus luteum has a lifespan of about 12–16 days before degenerating.

questions.q: Besides progesterone and oestrogen, the corpus luteum also secretes which hormone that provides negative feedback on FSH?
questions.why: The corpus luteum secretes inhibin A, which negatively feeds back on FSH (distinct from inhibin B, secreted earlier by growing follicles).

questions.q: In high concentrations, progesterone provides negative feedback on LH, which eventually causes:
questions.why: High progesterone suppresses LH via negative feedback, and without adequate LH support, the corpus luteum degenerates.

questions.q: The first half of the menstrual cycle, dominated by oestrogen, is known as the follicular phase, also called the:
questions.why: The follicular phase is also known as the proliferative phase, named for its effect on the endometrium.

questions.q: Which phase of the cycle has a FIXED duration of about 14 days, regardless of total cycle length?
questions.why: The secretory (luteal) phase has a fixed 14-day duration; it is the follicular phase that varies in length between women.

questions.q: Because the luteal phase is fixed at 14 days, the day of ovulation in any cycle can be estimated as:
options: 14 days before the next expected menstruation
14 days after the last menstruation, always
Day 14 of every cycle regardless of length
It cannot be estimated without hormone testing
questions.why: Since the luteal phase is a constant 14 days, ovulation can be calculated as 14 days before the next expected period, regardless of overall cycle length.

questions.q: The oestrogen peak occurs how many hours before the LH peak?
questions.why: The oestrogen peak precedes the LH peak by about 14–24 hours, triggering the LH surge.

questions.q: The follicle size just before ovulation is typically:
questions.why: The mature (Graafian) follicle typically measures 18–20 mm (at least 17 mm) just before ovulation.

questions.q: Day 22 of a standard cycle corresponds to maximum corpus luteum size/activity and progesterone level, and is also notable for:
options: The point when all ovulation-confirming tests are done, with minimum FSH/LH
questions.why: Day 22 marks peak progesterone and corpus luteum activity, minimum FSH/LH, and is when ovulation-confirming tests (like serum progesterone) are performed.

questions.q: Mittelschmerz refers to:
options: Mid-cycle (ovulatory) pain experienced by some women
Pain from an ovarian cyst rupture unrelated to ovulation
questions.why: Mittelschmerz is mid-cycle, ovulatory pain experienced by some women.

questions.q: The pathophysiology of Mittelschmerz pain involves:
options: Rupture of the antral cavity at ovulation, with fluid collecting in the pouch of Douglas
questions.why: Rupture of the antral cavity at ovulation releases follicular fluid, which collects in the pouch of Douglas and irritates the peritoneum, causing pain.

questions.q: Fluid in the pouch of Douglas seen on ultrasound around mid-cycle is:
questions.why: Physiological fluid in the pouch of Douglas at mid-cycle is a normal finding associated with ovulation.

questions.q: If pregnancy occurs, the corpus luteum is maintained by hCG for approximately how long, protecting it from luteolysis?
questions.why: hCG from the developing pregnancy maintains the corpus luteum, protecting it from luteolysis for up to about 10 weeks.

questions.q: The corpus luteum of pregnancy contributes progesterone production (until the placenta takes over) and also secretes:
questions.why: The corpus luteum of pregnancy secretes relaxin in addition to progesterone.

questions.q: The superficial endometrial layer, shed during menstruation, is called the:
questions.why: The zona functionalis is the superficial layer shed each cycle during menstruation.

questions.q: The zona functionalis is supplied by which vessels, which are sensitive to hormonal changes?
questions.why: Spiral arteries supply the zona functionalis and are hormonally sensitive, constricting to trigger shedding.

questions.q: The zona basalis (deep layer) is NOT shed during menstruation and is supplied by:
options: Basal arteries, which are not hormonally sensitive
Spiral arteries, which are hormonally sensitive
No blood supply of its own
questions.why: The zona basalis is supplied by basal arteries, which are insensitive to hormonal changes, allowing this layer to persist and regenerate the functional layer.

questions.q: After menstruation, the zona basalis proliferates to:
questions.why: The zona basalis proliferates after menstruation to regenerate the zona functionalis for the next cycle.

questions.q: On ultrasound, the endometrium in the late proliferative/peri-ovulatory phase classically shows:
questions.why: The late proliferative/peri-ovulatory endometrium shows a characteristic trilaminar (triple-line) appearance on ultrasound.

questions.q: In the secretory phase, the endometrium on ultrasound appears:
options: Trilaminar, as in the late proliferative phase
Thick and echogenic, with posterior acoustic enhancement
questions.why: The secretory-phase endometrium appears thick and echogenic with posterior acoustic enhancement on ultrasound.

questions.q: In an anovulatory cycle, the absence of ovulation means there is no corpus luteum, and therefore no progesterone. This leads to:
options: Unopposed oestrogen driving endometrial proliferation, producing a weak endometrium that sheds irregularly
No change in bleeding pattern at all
questions.why: Without progesterone to oppose it, oestrogen drives ongoing endometrial proliferation; the resulting weak, overgrown endometrium sheds unpredictably.

questions.q: The classic bleeding pattern of anovulatory cycles — irregular, heavy, and painless — is known as:
questions.why: This pattern is termed oestrogen breakthrough bleeding.

questions.q: Dysmenorrhoea (from PGF2α-mediated uterine contractions) is characteristically seen only in:
questions.why: Dysmenorrhoea requires the progesterone withdrawal and prostaglandin release that follow corpus luteum regression — a process unique to ovulatory cycles.

questions.q: The combined oral contraceptive pill can help dysmenorrhoea partly because it:
questions.why: By suppressing ovulation (making cycles anovulatory), the OCP removes the progesterone-withdrawal/prostaglandin trigger for dysmenorrhoea.

questions.q: Primary dysmenorrhoea is defined as menstrual pain occurring:
options: Only with an underlying pelvic pathology
questions.why: Primary dysmenorrhoea, by definition, occurs with no underlying pelvic pathology.

questions.q: In the two-cell, two-gonadotropin theory, which gonadotropin primarily acts on THECA cells?
questions.why: LH acts on theca cells, stimulating androgen production.

questions.q: In the two-cell, two-gonadotropin theory, which gonadotropin primarily acts on GRANULOSA cells?
questions.why: FSH acts on granulosa cells, driving aromatase activity and oestrogen production.

questions.q: Granulosa cells possess aromatase but LACK which enzyme, meaning they cannot produce androgens on their own?
questions.why: Granulosa cells lack 17α-hydroxylase, so they cannot make androgens independently and rely on theca-derived androgens for oestrogen synthesis.

questions.q: Theca cells, stimulated by LH, produce androgens efficiently but LACK which enzyme needed to convert those androgens to oestrogen?
questions.why: Theca cells lack aromatase, so they cannot convert their own androgens into oestrogen.

questions.q: Because theca cells lack aromatase, the androgens they produce must:
options: Diffuse into neighbouring granulosa cells, which convert them to oestrogen
Remain in the theca cell permanently
questions.why: Theca-derived androgens diffuse into adjacent granulosa cells, where FSH-induced aromatase converts them to oestrogen.

questions.q: This division of labour — LH-driven theca cells making androgens, FSH-driven granulosa cells aromatising them to oestrogen — is known as:
questions.why: This cooperative hormone-producing arrangement between theca and granulosa cells is the two-cell, two-gonadotropin theory.

units.title: LH Surge Threshold, AMH, Progesterone & Steroidogenesis: Missed Details

questions.q: The LH surge is triggered when oestrogen reaches a sustained threshold of approximately:
questions.why: A sustained oestrogen level of ≥200 picogram for 48 hours triggers positive feedback, causing the LH surge.

questions.q: AMH concentration is directly proportional to:
questions.why: AMH concentration is proportional to the number of follicles (formed by pre-antral and small antral follicles from puberty onward), making it a marker of ovarian reserve.

questions.q: Besides inhibin B (the classic marker), a newer tumour marker for granulosa cell tumour is:
questions.why: AMH is a newer tumour marker for granulosa cell tumour, in addition to the classic marker inhibin B.

questions.q: Progesterone is present in small amounts even before ovulation, arising from:
questions.why: Small amounts of progesterone from luteinised granulosa cells are present even before ovulation, providing positive feedback on LH and FSH.

questions.q: The maximum progesterone level, reached around day 22 of a standard cycle, is approximately:
questions.why: Maximum progesterone level (around day 22, one week before menstruation) is approximately 15 ng/mL.

questions.q: On day 22 of the cycle, alongside maximum corpus luteum size and activity, FSH and LH levels are at their:
questions.why: Day 22 corresponds to minimum FSH and LH levels, alongside maximum corpus luteal activity and progesterone.

questions.q: From the beginning of the LH surge to its peak takes about 10–12 hours, while the LH surge overall (peak duration) lasts approximately:
questions.why: The LH surge lasts approximately 32–36 hours in total, though it takes only 10–12 hours to reach peak from its start.

questions.q: The first-line pharmacological management for primary dysmenorrhoea is:
questions.why: NSAIDs are the first-line management for primary dysmenorrhoea (targeting PGF2\u03b1-mediated pain); OCPs are used if NSAIDs are insufficient, by making the cycle anovulatory.

questions.q: In basic steroidogenesis, cholesterol is converted to pregnenolone via 17-alpha hydroxylase, and pregnenolone is then converted to androgen or progesterone via which enzyme?
questions.why: 3βHSD converts pregnenolone to androgen or progesterone in the basic steroidogenesis pathway.

questions.q: GnRH is chemically classified as a:
questions.why: GnRH is a decapeptide (10 amino acid) hormone.

questions.q: GnRH is secreted from which hypothalamic nucleus?
questions.why: GnRH is secreted from the arcuate nucleus of the hypothalamus, in a pulsatile manner.

questions.q: Continuous (non-pulsatile) GnRH secretion leads to:
options: Downregulation of GnRH receptors in the anterior pituitary
Sustained maximal LH and FSH release
