questions.why: Continuous, unlike pulsatile, GnRH exposure downregulates GnRH receptors on the anterior pituitary — the basis for continuous GnRH analogue therapy.

questions.q: A LOW GnRH pulse frequency (about once every 90 minutes) preferentially favours release of:
questions.why: Low-frequency GnRH pulses (about every 90 minutes) preferentially drive FSH release.

questions.q: A HIGH GnRH pulse frequency (about once every 60 minutes) preferentially favours release of:
questions.why: Higher-frequency GnRH pulses (about every 60 minutes) preferentially drive LH release.

questions.q: GnRH neurons originate in the olfactory epithelium during intrauterine life and migrate to the hypothalamus along with the olfactory nerve. Failure of this migration causes:
questions.why: Failed migration of GnRH neurons (alongside the olfactory nerve) from the olfactory epithelium to the hypothalamus causes Kallmann syndrome, explaining its associated anosmia.

questions.q: Kallmann syndrome is inherited as an X-linked recessive disorder (involving the KAL-1 gene) and is:
options: More common in males than females
More common in females than males
questions.why: Kallmann syndrome is more common in males than females, consistent with its X-linked recessive inheritance.

questions.q: GnRH analogues (e.g. leuprolide, goserelin, buserelin) are:
options: Given only as a single lifetime dose
Orally inactive, given as subcutaneous injections
questions.why: GnRH analogues are orally inactive and are given as subcutaneous injections, either continuously or in a pulsatile manner.

questions.q: Pulsatile GnRH administration stimulates the HPO axis, raising LH, FSH, and oestrogen; this pattern is used therapeutically for:
options: Delayed puberty, Kallmann syndrome, and anovulation
questions.why: Pulsatile GnRH is used to stimulate the HPO axis in delayed puberty, Kallmann syndrome, and for managing anovulation.

questions.q: Continuous GnRH administration initially causes a flare (transient HPO axis stimulation), followed by:
options: Immediate downregulation with no initial flare
Downregulation of the HPO axis, lowering LH and FSH
questions.why: Continuous GnRH causes an initial flare, then downregulates the HPO axis, ultimately lowering LH and FSH (and downstream oestrogen/androgen).

questions.q: Continuous GnRH therapy (creating a hypo-oestrogenic/hypo-androgenic state) is used for all of these hyperestrogenic or hormone-sensitive conditions EXCEPT:
questions.why: Continuous GnRH suppresses the axis and is used for hyperestrogenic/hormone-sensitive conditions (endometriosis, fibroids, ER+ breast cancer, hirsutism, precocious puberty, prostate cancer) — Kallmann syndrome, a hypogonadal state, instead needs pulsatile (stimulating) GnRH.

questions.q: Adverse effects of continuous GnRH therapy, from hypo-oestrogenism, include hot flashes, vaginal dryness, and:
questions.why: Continuous GnRH’s hypo-oestrogenic state produces menopause-like symptoms: hot flashes, vaginal dryness, and osteoporosis.

questions.q: To counter these hypo-oestrogenic side effects during prolonged (≥6 months) GnRH analogue therapy, which strategy is used?
questions.why: Low-dose oestrogen add-back therapy (e.g. using norethindrone, a progestogen with oestrogen-like action) mitigates hypo-oestrogenic side effects during prolonged GnRH analogue use.

questions.q: Compared with GnRH analogues, GnRH antagonists (e.g. elagolix, cetrorelix) have the advantage of being orally active and:
questions.why: GnRH antagonists are orally active and, unlike analogues, cause no initial flare — though they are more expensive.

questions.q: LH and FSH are structurally classified as:
questions.why: LH and FSH, released by the anterior pituitary, are glycoprotein hormones.

questions.q: LH, FSH, TSH, and hCG all share a common:
options: Single unified structure with no subunits
questions.why: LH, FSH, TSH, and hCG share an identical alpha subunit; each has its own distinct beta subunit conferring specificity.

questions.q: In females, FSH receptors are located on:
questions.why: FSH receptors in females are on granulosa cells (the male equivalent being Sertoli cells).

questions.q: In females, LH receptors are located on:
questions.why: LH receptors in females are on theca cells (the male equivalent being Leydig cells).

questions.q: FSH itself induces the appearance of LH receptors on which cells of the dominant follicle, preparing the follicle to respond to the LH surge?
questions.why: FSH induces LH receptors on the granulosa cells of the dominant follicle, priming it to respond when the LH surge occurs.

questions.q: One key function of FSH is the selection of a cohort of follicles:
questions.why: FSH drives the monthly selection of a cohort of growing follicles.

questions.q: Selection of the single DOMINANT follicle from this cohort typically occurs around:
questions.why: The dominant follicle is typically selected around day 8 of the cycle.

questions.q: Final release of the ovum at ovulation occurs through:
options: Breakdown of collagen in the follicular wall
questions.why: Collagen breakdown in the follicular wall (mediated by proteolytic enzymes under LH influence) allows final release of the ovum.

questions.q: LH is responsible for triggering ovulation and for:
options: Selecting the initial cohort of follicles
Growth and maintenance of the corpus luteum
questions.why: Beyond triggering ovulation, LH also drives growth and maintenance of the corpus luteum.

questions.q: Alongside FSH, LH also contributes to the:
options: Formation of the primordial follicle pool at birth
Regression of the corpus luteum only
Selection of the dominant follicle exclusively
Final growth and maturation of the follicle
questions.why: LH also contributes to the final growth and maturation stage of the follicle, alongside FSH.

questions.q: Normal FSH and LH levels are each typically:
questions.why: Normal FSH and LH levels are each below about 10 IU.

questions.q: At menopause, falling oestrogen removes negative feedback, resulting in:
questions.why: Loss of oestrogen’s negative feedback at menopause raises both LH and FSH.

questions.q: In pregnancy, high oestrogen and progesterone levels result in:
questions.why: High oestrogen and progesterone in pregnancy suppress LH and FSH via negative feedback.

questions.q: In PCOS, the classic gonadotropin pattern is:
options: FSH normal, LH raised (an increased LH:FSH ratio)
questions.why: PCOS classically shows normal FSH with raised LH, giving an increased LH:FSH ratio.

questions.q: In androgen insensitivity syndrome (46,XY), the gonadotropin pattern is similar to PCOS:
options: Both FSH and LH markedly raised
questions.why: Androgen insensitivity syndrome shares the normal-FSH, raised-LH pattern seen in PCOS.

questions.q: While oestrogen normally exerts negative feedback on LH and FSH, sustained oestrogen levels above approximately 200 pg/mL switch this to:
options: Positive feedback, triggering the LH surge
questions.why: Sustained oestrogen above roughly 200 pg/mL for about 48 hours switches feedback from negative to positive, triggering the LH surge.

questions.q: Human Menopausal Gonadotropin (HMG) is composed of:
questions.why: HMG is composed of equal parts, 75 IU LH and 75 IU FSH.

questions.q: HMG is sourced from:
questions.why: HMG is extracted from the urine of postmenopausal women, which is rich in gonadotropins due to loss of negative feedback.

questions.q: HMG is used to treat anovulation due to pituitary ablation, and also in:
questions.why: HMG is used both for anovulation from pituitary ablation and for controlled ovarian stimulation in IVF cycles.

questions.q: A recognised disadvantage of HMG therapy is a 5–15% risk of ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome, and a roughly 30% risk of:
questions.why: Because HMG stimulates multiple follicles, it carries a roughly 30% risk of multifetal pregnancy, alongside a 5–15% risk of ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome.

units.title: GnRH Half-Life & Kallmann Syndrome: Missed Details

questions.q: The half-life (T½) of natural GnRH is approximately:
questions.why: Natural GnRH has a very short half-life of approximately 2–4 minutes, necessitating pulsatile secretion.

questions.q: A key clinical feature that helps distinguish Kallmann syndrome from Turner syndrome is that Kallmann syndrome patients typically have:
questions.why: Unlike Turner syndrome, patients with Kallmann syndrome typically have normal height, alongside delayed puberty, infertility, and hyposmia/anosmia.

questions.q: The management of Kallmann syndrome is:
questions.why: Kallmann syndrome, being a hypogonadotropic state, is managed with pulsatile GnRH to stimulate the HPO axis.

questions.q: Natural estrogen is a C18 steroid; natural progesterone is a:
questions.why: Estrogen is a C18 steroid, while progesterone is a C21 steroid.

questions.q: The four natural estrogens are estrone, estradiol, estriol, and:
questions.why: The four natural estrogens are E1 (estrone), E2 (estradiol), E3 (estriol), and E4 (estetrol).

questions.q: The predominant estrogen in reproductive-age women is:
questions.why: Estradiol (E2) predominates in reproductive-age women and in pregnancy.

questions.q: The predominant estrogen in menopausal and in obese women is:
questions.why: Estrone (E1), produced peripherally in adipose tissue, predominates in menopausal and obese women.

questions.q: The normal E2:E1 ratio is about 2:1; in obese women, this ratio:
questions.why: In obese women, increased peripheral aromatisation reverses the normal E2:E1 ratio to about 1:2.

questions.q: The most specific estrogen in pregnancy, derived from fetal DHEA-S, is:
questions.why: Estriol (E3), derived from fetal adrenal DHEA-S, is the most pregnancy-specific estrogen.

questions.q: The most commonly used synthetic estrogen in combined oral contraceptive pills is:
questions.why: Ethinyl estradiol (EE) is the most commonly used synthetic estrogen in OCPs.

questions.q: The synthetic estrogen most commonly used in hormone replacement therapy (HRT) is:
questions.why: 17-β estradiol is the synthetic estrogen most commonly used in HRT.

questions.q: By potency, which of these synthetic estrogens is most potent?
questions.why: Potency ranking is EE > CEE > E2 > E1 > E3 > E4, making ethinyl estradiol the most potent.

questions.q: OCPs are classified by estrogen content; a 'low dose' pill contains:
questions.why: Low-dose pills contain <50 mcg estrogen; high-dose ≥ 50 mcg; very low-dose <20 mcg.

questions.q: First-generation progestins, such as norethindrone, have which distinguishing property?
options: Purely progestational, with zero androgenic effect
questions.why: First-generation progestins like norethindrone have both androgenic and oestrogenic activity.

questions.q: Which generation of progestins (e.g. desogestrel, norgestimate, gestodene) has the LEAST androgenic side effects among the numbered generations?
options: None; all generations are equally androgenic
questions.why: Third-generation progestins (desogestrel, norgestimate, gestodene) have the least androgenic side effects among the numbered generations; 4th-generation progestins (drospirenone, dienogest) are actually anti-androgenic.

questions.q: In the body, oestrogen synthesis proceeds from cholesterol through androgens via which enzyme?
questions.why: Aromatase converts androgens to oestrogens in the final step of oestrogen synthesis.

questions.q: Progesterone synthesis proceeds from cholesterol to pregnenolone, then to progesterone via which enzyme?
questions.why: 3β-HSD converts pregnenolone to progesterone.

questions.q: E2 (oestradiol) is mainly produced by granulosa cells (as in the two-cell, two-gonadotropin theory); E1 (oestrone) is mainly produced by:
options: Adipose tissue, converting androstenedione via aromatase
questions.why: Adipose tissue converts androstenedione to E1 (oestrone) via aromatase.

questions.q: Since obese women have more adipose tissue, they characteristically have:
questions.why: More adipose tissue means more peripheral aromatisation, raising E1 (oestrone) levels in obese women.

questions.q: Aromatase inhibitors, such as letrozole, are used therapeutically to:
options: Reduce oestrogen production, useful in hyperestrogenic conditions
Stimulate ovulation directly without affecting hormone levels
questions.why: By blocking aromatase, letrozole reduces oestrogen production, useful in hyperestrogenic conditions.

questions.q: In a non-pregnant woman, progesterone is mainly sourced from the corpus luteum, more specifically from:
options: Theca cells of the dominant follicle
questions.why: Luteinised granulosa cells (forming the corpus luteum) are the main progesterone source in a non-pregnant woman.

questions.q: Oestrogen receptors are located:
questions.why: Oestrogen receptors are intranuclear.

questions.q: Progesterone (and androgen) receptors are initially intracytoplasmic, but must move where to actually function?
options: They function in the cytoplasm without moving
questions.why: Progesterone and androgen receptors, though intracytoplasmic, must translocate into the nucleus to function.

questions.q: In the circulation, oestrogen is mostly protein-bound, chiefly to:
options: Sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG), more than albumin
questions.why: Oestrogen is mostly bound to SHBG (more than to albumin), with about 1% circulating free.

questions.q: Progesterone, in contrast, is mainly bound to albumin and corticosteroid-binding globulin (CBG), and notably:
options: Is bound mostly to SHBG, like oestrogen
Is NOT significantly bound to SHBG
Has no plasma protein binding at all
questions.why: Unlike oestrogen, progesterone is not significantly bound to SHBG; about 2% circulates free.

questions.q: The end metabolite of oestrogen is glucuronide; the end metabolite of progesterone is:
questions.why: Progesterone is metabolised to pregnanediol.

questions.q: Oestrogen's main action on the endometrium is:
questions.why: Oestrogen drives endometrial proliferation.

questions.q: Progesterone supports the endometrium and induces secretory changes, but continuous administration can also cause an 'autoproliferative' action leading to:
questions.why: Continuous progesterone can drive an autoproliferative action leading to endometrial hypertrophy.

questions.q: Because of this autoproliferative action supporting endometrial regrowth in a controlled way, progesterone (in appropriate regimens) serves as:
options: A risk factor for endometrial hyperplasia only
The drug of choice (DOC) for endometrial hyperplasia
A contraindication in all endometrial disease
questions.why: Progesterone (e.g. as continuous therapy) is the drug of choice for managing endometrial hyperplasia.

questions.q: On the myometrium, oestrogen supports growth of the non-pregnant uterus, while progesterone supports growth of:
options: Both the non-pregnant and the pregnant uterus
Neither; progesterone has no myometrial effect
Only the cervix, not the uterine body
questions.why: Progesterone supports myometrial growth in BOTH the non-pregnant and pregnant uterus, a broader role than oestrogen's.

questions.q: Fibroids (myometrial tumours) are classically described as being:
questions.why: Fibroids are dependent on both oestrogen and progesterone, not oestrogen alone.

questions.q: In Turner syndrome, non-functional streak ovaries lead to low oestrogen and progesterone, resulting in:
questions.why: Without adequate oestrogen/progesterone stimulation, the uterus in Turner syndrome remains infantile/hypoplastic.

questions.q: On endometrial biopsy, the proliferative phase (first half of the cycle) shows simple tubular glands and:
options: Pseudostratification (nuclei at different levels) and telescoping of glands
questions.why: The proliferative phase shows simple tubular glands, pseudostratification, and telescoping of glands.

questions.q: The first histological sign of ovulation on endometrial biopsy is:
questions.why: Subnuclear vacuoles are the first histological sign of ovulation on biopsy.

questions.q: Subnuclear vacuoles are typically seen on which days of the cycle?
questions.why: Subnuclear vacuoles classically appear on days 16–17 of the cycle.

questions.q: Subnuclear vacuoles are more prominent in which phase, relative to the ovulatory phase itself?
questions.why: Subnuclear vacuoles are more prominent in the early secretory phase than at ovulation itself.

questions.q: As the early secretory phase progresses, the endometrial glands show:
questions.why: Glands begin to coil as the early secretory phase progresses, preceding the more tortuous late-secretory appearance.

questions.q: In the late secretory phase, the classic 'corkscrew' or 'sawtooth' gland appearance (tortuous glands) is seen around day:
questions.why: Corkscrew/sawtooth tortuous glands appear around day 20 of the cycle.

questions.q: Stromal oedema on endometrial biopsy is characteristically seen around day:
questions.why: Stromal oedema is characteristically seen around day 22.

questions.q: Lymphocytic infiltration of the endometrium, signalling the approach of menstruation, is seen around day:
questions.why: Lymphocytic infiltration appears around day 26, just before menstruation begins.

questions.q: Endometrial biopsy as a test for ovulation is:
questions.why: Though histologically informative, endometrial biopsy is rarely used in current practice as an ovulation test.

questions.q: Recognised indications for endometrial biopsy include abnormal uterine bleeding and:
questions.why: Abnormal uterine bleeding (AUB) and suspected genital tuberculosis are recognised indications for endometrial biopsy.

questions.q: Under oestrogen's influence, cervical mucus becomes thin, profuse, and:
questions.why: Oestrogen makes cervical mucus thin, profuse, and watery, favourable for sperm penetration.

questions.q: Under progesterone's influence, cervical mucus becomes:
options: Thin and watery, as with oestrogen
questions.why: Progesterone makes cervical mucus thick, scanty, and viscous (non-stretchable/tacky).

questions.q: The Spinnbarkeit test assesses cervical mucus:
questions.why: The Spinnbarkeit test assesses the mucus's elasticity/stretchability, which is greatest under oestrogen dominance.

questions.q: A positive ferning pattern on cervical mucus microscopy, appearing by day 7 of the cycle, is due to:
questions.why: Increased sodium and chloride under oestrogen’s influence produce the ferning pattern by day 7.

questions.q: At menopause, falling oestrogen reduces cervical mucus, contributing to:
questions.why: Reduced cervical mucus at menopause contributes to senile vaginitis (vaginal dryness), managed with lubricants or local oestrogen.

questions.q: Levonorgestrel-releasing IUDs (e.g. Mirena) thicken cervical mucus, which is unfavourable for sperm penetration, and are associated with which additional benefit compared with copper IUDs?
options: A LOWER risk of pelvic inflammatory disease (PID)
questions.why: By thickening cervical mucus, LNG-IUDs like Mirena carry a lower PID risk, in contrast to copper IUDs, which raise PID risk.

questions.q: Oestrogen promotes ductal development and fat deposition in the breast; progesterone promotes:
questions.why: Progesterone promotes glandular (lobular) development of the breast.

questions.q: For contraception during lactation, combined OCPs are contraindicated, and the preferred option is:
options: No contraception is needed while breastfeeding
questions.why: Progesterone-only contraceptives are the drug of choice during lactation, since oestrogen reduces milk secretion.

questions.q: Oestrogen increases fallopian tube motility; progesterone decreases it. Failure of progesterone-only contraceptives, with reduced tubal motility, specifically raises the risk of:
questions.why: Reduced tubal motility from progesterone-only contraceptive failure raises the risk of ectopic pregnancy.

questions.q: A woman is found to have an ovarian tumour on ultrasound, with predominantly superficial cells on vaginal cytology (indicating high oestrogen). This picture suggests:
questions.why: An oestrogen-secreting ovarian tumour with predominant superficial cells on cytology points to a granulosa cell tumour.

questions.q: Vaginal cytology can be used as a test for ovulation when sampled around which day of the cycle?
questions.why: Vaginal cytology sampled around day 22 can serve as a test for ovulation.

questions.q: On breast tissue, unlike oestrogen and progesterone's effects on development, breast MILK SECRETION is:
options: Increased by oestrogen, unaffected by progesterone
Decreased by oestrogen; unaffected by progesterone
questions.why: Oestrogen decreases breast milk secretion, while progesterone has no effect on it.

questions.q: Regarding salt and water balance, oestrogen causes retention, while progesterone causes:
questions.why: Progesterone promotes salt and water excretion, opposite to oestrogen’s retention effect.

questions.q: Oestrogen increases bone mass and mineralisation and lowers serum calcium; in long bones, it also causes:
questions.why: Oestrogen causes epiphyseal closure in long bones.

questions.q: In precocious puberty, elevated oestrogen causes premature epiphyseal closure, resulting in:
questions.why: Premature epiphyseal closure from early oestrogen exposure results in short final stature.

questions.q: In menopause, falling oestrogen reduces bone mineral density, resulting in:
questions.why: Loss of oestrogen’s bone-protective effect at menopause leads to osteoporosis.

questions.q: Oestrogen increases clotting factors II, VII, VIII, and X, raising thrombosis risk with OCPs/HRT. This makes OCPs contraindicated in all of these EXCEPT:
questions.why: OCPs are contraindicated in VTE history, coronary artery disease, stroke, and smokers over 35 — not in well-controlled hypothyroidism.

questions.q: Because progesterone (unlike oestrogen) has no significant procoagulant effect, progesterone-only contraceptives:
options: Can be used in patients with a history of thrombosis
questions.why: Progesterone-only contraceptives, lacking oestrogen’s procoagulant effect, can be used even in patients with a thrombosis history.

questions.q: Progesterone raises basal body temperature (BBT) by approximately:
questions.why: Progesterone raises BBT by about 0.5°C after ovulation.

questions.q: Charting basal body temperature is used clinically as a:
options: Natural method of contraception and test for ovulation
questions.why: BBT charting is used both as a natural contraceptive method and as a test to confirm ovulation.

questions.q: Regarding LH, oestrogen levels below about 200 pg/mL exert negative feedback, while sustained levels at or above 200 pg/mL exert:
options: No effect on LH at all
Feedback only on FSH, not LH
questions.why: Sustained oestrogen ≥200 pg/mL switches feedback on LH from negative to positive, triggering the LH surge.

questions.q: Progesterone's feedback on FSH and LH is concentration-dependent: low concentrations give positive feedback, while high concentrations give:
options: A feedback effect only on prolactin
questions.why: Low progesterone concentrations feed back positively on FSH/LH; high concentrations feed back negatively.

questions.q: In hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, LH, FSH, oestrogen, and androgens are all low, reflecting a defect at the level of the:
questions.why: Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism reflects a hypothalamic/pituitary defect, with everything (LH, FSH, sex steroids) low.

questions.q: In hypergonadotropic hypogonadism, LH and FSH are HIGH while oestrogen/androgens are LOW, reflecting a defect at the level of the:
options: Gonads themselves, with loss of negative feedback on FSH/LH
questions.why: Hypergonadotropic hypogonadism reflects a gonadal defect; low sex steroids remove negative feedback, driving LH/FSH up.

questions.q: The vaginal maturation index counts the ratio of parabasal, intermediate, and superficial cells. A ratio dominated by superficial cells (e.g. 0:30:70 or 0:40:60) suggests:
questions.why: A superficial-cell-dominant ratio (e.g. 0:30:70) is characteristic of the proliferative phase.

questions.q: A maturation index ratio of roughly 0:70:30 (intermediate cells dominant) suggests:
questions.why: An intermediate-cell-dominant ratio (0:70:30) is characteristic of the secretory phase.

questions.q: A maturation index of 100:0:0 (all parabasal cells) is characteristic of:
questions.why: An all-parabasal-cell pattern (100:0:0) is characteristic of the low-oestrogen menopausal state.

questions.q: Which of these hormones/receptors is membrane-bound, unlike oestrogen (intranuclear) or progesterone (intracytoplasmic)?
questions.why: GnRH, LH, and FSH act via membrane-bound receptors, unlike the intracellular receptors of oestrogen and progesterone.

questions.q: Regarding half-life, GnRH, FSH, and oxytocin all have a short half-life of about 3–4 minutes; LH's half-life is notably longer, at about:
questions.why: LH's half-life (about 20 minutes) is notably longer than GnRH, FSH, and oxytocin (3–4 minutes each).

questions.q: Which of these is NOT typically classified as a hyperestrogenic state?
questions.why: Precocious puberty, endometriosis, fibroid, endometrial causes, and ovarian cancer are classified as hyperestrogenic states; androgen insensitivity syndrome is not.

questions.q: Common risk factors for hyperestrogenic states include nulliparity, early menarche, late menopause, and:
options: Obesity (via increased peripheral conversion of androgens to oestrogen)
questions.why: Obesity raises risk via increased peripheral aromatisation of androgens to oestrogen in adipose tissue.

questions.q: Which of these is a PROTECTIVE factor against hyperestrogenic states?
questions.why: Multiparity, along with pregnancy and physical activity, is protective against hyperestrogenic states.

questions.q: Regular physical activity and pregnancy are both considered:
questions.why: Pregnancy and physical activity are both protective against hyperestrogenic states.

questions.q: Somewhat counterintuitively, smoking is protective against hyperestrogenic states and also against:
questions.why: Smoking is also, counterintuitively, protective against pregnancy-induced hypertension — despite its many other well-established harms.

questions.q: The first-line pharmacological option for hyperestrogenic states, which downregulates oestrogen receptors, is:
questions.why: Progesterone, which downregulates oestrogen receptors, is the first-line pharmacological option.

questions.q: Letrozole manages hyperestrogenic states by acting as a(n):
options: Aromatase inhibitor, blocking conversion of androgens to oestrogens
questions.why: Letrozole is an aromatase inhibitor, blocking the conversion of androgens to oestrogens.

questions.q: Danazol has anti-oestrogenic action but is limited by androgenic side effects such as:
questions.why: Danazol's androgenic side effects include hirsutism, limiting its use despite its anti-oestrogenic action.

questions.q: Considered the BEST pharmacological options for hyperestrogenic states are:
options: Continuous GnRH agonists and GnRH antagonists
questions.why: Continuous GnRH agonists and GnRH antagonists are considered the best options among the pharmacological choices.

questions.q: Selective oestrogen receptor modulators (SERMs) act as oestrogen agonists on some tissues and:
options: Agonists on all other tissues as well
Have no effect on any other tissue
questions.why: SERMs act as oestrogen agonists on some tissues and antagonists on others — their defining mixed activity.

questions.q: Clomiphene citrate's main clinical indication is:
questions.why: Clomiphene citrate is used for ovulation induction.

questions.q: Which finding on clomiphene citrate mandates immediate discontinuation of the drug?
questions.why: Visual disturbance on clomiphene citrate is an indication for immediate drug discontinuation.

questions.q: Raloxifene's clinical indications include osteoporosis and:
questions.why: Raloxifene is indicated for osteoporosis and breast cancer, with no risk of endometrial cancer (unlike tamoxifen).

questions.q: Unlike clomiphene and raloxifene, tamoxifen (used for breast cancer) carries a notable risk of:
questions.why: Tamoxifen carries a notable endometrial cancer risk, unlike clomiphene and raloxifene, which do not.

questions.q: Because tamoxifen is teratogenic, the recommended minimum gap between stopping tamoxifen and attempting pregnancy is:
questions.why: A minimum 3-month gap is recommended between stopping tamoxifen and attempting pregnancy, given its teratogenicity.

questions.q: Ospemifene, a SERM, is specifically used to treat:
questions.why: Ospemifene is a SERM specifically used for vaginal dryness.

questions.q: Bazedoxifene combined with oestrogen (approved for managing hot flashes) has the specific advantage of:
options: Increasing endometrial cancer risk, like tamoxifen
Preventing endometrial carcinoma while treating hot flashes and osteoporosis
questions.why: This combination treats hot flashes and osteoporosis while preventing endometrial carcinoma — the opposite risk profile from tamoxifen.

questions.q: Ormeloxifene is a component of which contraceptive?
questions.why: Ormeloxifene is the active component of Centchroman (Chhaya), a non-hormonal-cycle weekly contraceptive.

questions.q: Ulipristal, a selective progesterone receptor modulator (SPRM), is used for fibroids and:
questions.why: Ulipristal is an SPRM used for fibroid treatment and as an emergency contraceptive.

questions.q: Mifepristone (RU486) acts as a progesterone antagonist and is used for medical abortion and:
questions.why: Mifepristone, a progesterone antagonist, is used for medical abortion and for fibroids.

units.title: Progestins, Sourcing, Cervical Mucus & SERM Details

questions.q: Unlike natural progesterone (a C21 steroid), synthetic progestins are classified as:
questions.why: Synthetic progestins are C19 steroids (similar to androgens), which explains their androgenic side effects.

questions.q: OCPs are classified by estrogen content into high dose (≥50 mcg), low dose (<50 mcg), and:
questions.why: OCPs are classified as high dose (≥50 mcg), low dose (<50 mcg), and very low dose (<20 mcg) based on estrogen content.

questions.q: The second-generation progestin, following first-generation norethindrone, is:
questions.why: Levonorgestrel is the second-generation progestin, preceding the third generation (desogestrel, norgestimate, gestodene).

questions.q: Fourth-generation progestins, including drospirenone (a spironolactone derivative) and dienogest, are notable for being:
options: The most androgenic of all generations
Estrogenic only, with no progestogenic action
questions.why: Fourth-generation progestins (drospirenone, dienogest) are anti-androgenic, unlike earlier generations.

questions.q: In pregnancy, progesterone is sourced from the corpus luteum in early pregnancy, with production later taken over by the:
questions.why: Early pregnancy progesterone comes from the corpus luteum, with the placenta taking over later in pregnancy.

questions.q: Regarding free (unbound, bioactive) hormone fraction, approximately what percentage of circulating progesterone is free, compared to estrogen?
questions.why: Approximately 2% of circulating progesterone is free, compared to about 1% of estrogen.

questions.q: The natural family planning method that relies on tracking cervical mucus changes to identify the fertile window is known as:
questions.why: Billing's method is the natural method of conception/contraception based on cervical mucus characteristics.

questions.q: The half-life of letrozole (an aromatase inhibitor) is notably long, at approximately:
questions.why: Letrozole's half-life is approximately 48 hours, much longer than hormones like GnRH, FSH, and oxytocin (3–4 minutes).

questions.q: Among the adverse effects of clomiphene citrate (besides hot flashes and vaginal dryness), a recognised risk is:
questions.why: Clomiphene citrate use carries an increased risk of twin pregnancy, due to multi-follicular development.

questions.q: Unlike tamoxifen (which carries an endometrial cancer risk), clomiphene citrate and raloxifene share the advantage of:
questions.why: Clomiphene citrate and raloxifene, unlike tamoxifen, carry no risk of endometrial cancer.

questions.q: The menstrual cycle comprises the ovarian cycle and the uterine cycle. The ovarian cycle refers to:
options: Cyclical growth and shedding of the endometrium
Cyclical follicular growth leading to ovulation, followed by corpus luteum growth and degeneration
Changes in basal body temperature only
questions.why: The ovarian cycle is follicular growth to ovulation, then corpus luteum growth and degeneration; the uterine cycle is the parallel endometrial growth and shedding.

questions.q: Day 1 of the menstrual cycle is defined as:
options: The day the endometrium is thickest
questions.why: Day 1 of the cycle is, by convention, the onset of menstrual bleeding.

questions.q: By current (newer) criteria, a normal menstrual cycle length is considered to be:
questions.why: Newer criteria define a normal cycle length as 24–38 days, updated from the previous 21–35-day range.

questions.q: By current criteria, the normal number of days of bleeding is:
questions.why: Newer criteria define normal bleeding duration as 4.5–8 days, updated from the previous 2–8-day range.

questions.q: Normal cycle-to-cycle variation in length is considered to be:
questions.why: A cycle-to-cycle variation of 2–20 days is considered within the normal range.

questions.q: What proportion of women actually have a 'textbook' 28-day cycle?
questions.why: Only about 15% of women actually have a 28-day cycle; considerable natural variation is normal.

questions.q: Oligomenorrhoea (old terminology) describes:
options: Fewer than 9 cycles a year, with cycle length over 38 days (previously 35)
questions.why: Oligomenorrhoea describes infrequent cycles (<9/year), with cycle length over 38 days (previously 35 days).

questions.q: Polymenorrhoea (old terminology) describes:
options: Frequent/short cycles, with length under 24 days (previously 21)
questions.why: Polymenorrhoea describes frequent, short cycles, under 24 days (previously 21 days).

questions.q: Menorrhagia (old terminology) is defined by increased blood loss (≥80 mL) together with a duration of bleeding of:
questions.why: Menorrhagia combines increased blood loss (≥80 mL) with bleeding lasting more than 8 days.

questions.q: Hypomenorrhoea (old terminology) describes scanty bleeding, defined as blood loss and duration of:
questions.why: Hypomenorrhoea describes scanty bleeding: ≤20 mL, lasting under 2 days.

questions.q: Which of these old terms describes cycles that are too INFREQUENT (long cycle length)?
questions.why: Oligomenorrhoea describes infrequent (long-interval) cycles; polymenorrhoea is the opposite (frequent/short cycles).

questions.q: The cutoff for oligomenorrhoea's cycle length has shifted with updated criteria from a previous threshold of 35 days to a current threshold of:
questions.why: The oligomenorrhoea cycle-length threshold has been updated from 35 days to 38 days.

questions.q: Metrorrhagia (old terminology) refers to:
questions.why: Metrorrhagia refers to irregular or intermenstrual bleeding.

questions.q: Amenorrhoea (old terminology, as used here) refers to absence of menstruation for:
questions.why: Amenorrhoea, in this context, refers to absence of menstruation for 3 months.

questions.q: Metrorrhagia and oligomenorrhoea are distinguished by:
options: Metrorrhagia describing infrequent cycles, oligomenorrhoea describing irregular bleeding
Metrorrhagia describing irregular cycles, oligomenorrhoea describing infrequent (but still regular) cycles
questions.why: Metrorrhagia is an irregular-cycle disorder (unpredictable timing), while oligomenorrhoea is a regular-cycle disorder (predictable, just infrequent).

questions.q: Under newer terminology, a cycle length under 24 days is termed:
questions.why: A cycle length under 24 days is now termed frequent menses (replacing ‘polymenorrhoea’).

questions.q: Under newer terminology, a cycle length over 38 days is termed:
questions.why: A cycle length over 38 days is now termed infrequent menses (replacing ‘oligomenorrhoea’).

questions.q: Under newer terminology, blood loss over 80 mL is termed:
questions.why: Blood loss over 80 mL is now termed heavy bleeding (replacing ‘menorrhagia’).

questions.q: Under newer terminology, blood loss under 5 mL is termed:
questions.why: Blood loss under 5 mL is now termed light bleeding (replacing ‘hypomenorrhoea’).

questions.q: The newer terminology system replaces older terms like 'menorrhagia' and 'polymenorrhoea' with more descriptive terms based on:
options: Specific features (cycle length, volume, duration, regularity), each described independently
questions.why: The newer system describes each feature (cycle length, volume, duration, regularity) independently, rather than bundling them into single eponymous terms.

units.title: Newer Terminology: Duration, Regularity & Special Patterns

questions.q: Under newer terminology, a bleeding duration over 8 days is termed:
questions.why: A bleeding duration over 8 days is now termed prolonged bleeding.

questions.q: Under newer terminology, a bleeding duration under 4.5 days is termed:
questions.why: A bleeding duration under 4.5 days is now termed shortened bleeding.

questions.q: Under newer terminology, cycle-to-cycle variation greater than 20 days is termed:
questions.why: Cycle-to-cycle variation over 20 days is now termed irregular cycles.

questions.q: Intermenstrual bleeding refers to:
options: Heavy bleeding during a normal period
Acyclical episodes of bleeding occurring WITH an otherwise normal menstrual pattern
Bleeding that only occurs at menopause
questions.why: Intermenstrual bleeding is acyclical bleeding occurring alongside an otherwise normal menstrual pattern.

questions.q: The modern, functional definition of heavy menstrual bleeding is based on:
options: A blood loss volume of exactly 80 mL, measured precisely every cycle
Excessive bleeding that interferes with a woman's quality of life
questions.why: Modern heavy menstrual bleeding is defined functionally — excessive bleeding that interferes with quality of life — rather than by a precise measured volume.

units.title: Average Blood Loss & Duration (Distinct from Normal Ranges)

questions.q: While the normal range of blood loss is 20–80 mL over 4.5–8 days, the AVERAGE values in a typical cycle are approximately:
questions.why: The average blood loss per cycle is approximately 30–50 mL, over an average duration of about 4.5 days — distinct from the wider normal ranges (20–80 mL, 4.5–8 days).

questions.q: AUB is classified into structural and non-structural causes using the PALM-COEIN system. Which of these is a STRUCTURAL cause?
questions.why: Adenomyosis is one of the four structural (PALM) causes, alongside polyp, leiomyoma, and malignancy/hyperplasia.

questions.q: In PALM-COEIN, which letter represents polyps?
questions.why: 'P' in PALM stands for polyp.

questions.q: The 'M' in PALM stands for:
questions.why: 'M' covers both malignancy (cervical/endometrial cancer) and hyperplasia (endometrial hyperplasia).

questions.q: In PALM-COEIN, which letter represents ovulatory dysfunction (anovulation)?
questions.why: 'O' in COEIN stands for ovulatory dysfunction.

questions.q: Iatrogenic causes of AUB (the 'I' in COEIN) include:
questions.why: Iatrogenic causes include IUCDs and OCPs.

questions.q: A specific PALM-COEIN diagnosis, such as AUB due to a polyp, is denoted as:
questions.why: Each PALM-COEIN category is denoted with the AUB prefix plus its letter, e.g. AUB-P, AUB-A.

questions.q: AUB of endometrial cause (endometritis) classically presents with cyclical heavy bleeding and:
questions.why: Endometrial-cause AUB shows a normal-sized uterus on USG, distinguishing it from structural causes.

questions.q: The pathogenesis of endometrial-cause AUB involves altered PGE:PGF2α ratio, increased fibrinolytic activity, and:
questions.why: Progesterone levels remain normal in endometrial-cause AUB; the problem lies in local prostaglandin/fibrinolytic dysregulation.

questions.q: In ovulatory dysfunction (anovulation), unopposed estrogen causes:
options: Estrogen breakthrough bleeding, giving irregular, heavy, painless cycles
questions.why: Anovulation leads to unopposed estrogen and estrogen breakthrough bleeding: irregular, heavy, and painless.

questions.q: Anovulatory AUB clinically presents with heavy bleeding and:
questions.why: Anovulatory AUB presents with heavy bleeding alongside oligomenorrhoea (infrequent cycles).

questions.q: Which of these features favours an ENDOMETRIAL cause over a structural cause of AUB?
options: An enlarged, irregular uterus on exam
A normal-sized uterus on USG with cyclical heavy bleeding
questions.why: A normal-sized uterus with cyclical heavy bleeding points toward an endometrial (rather than structural) cause.

questions.q: The most common cause of puberty menorrhagia is:
questions.why: Anovulation is the most common cause of puberty menorrhagia, more common than coagulopathy.

questions.q: In obese females, peripheral conversion of androgens to estrogen in adipose tissue leads to continuous LH stimulation, resulting in:
questions.why: Continuous (rather than cyclical) LH stimulation from persistent peripheral estrogen prevents a proper LH surge, causing anovulation.

questions.q: Androgen excess causes anovulation through which mechanism?
options: A folliculotoxic effect preventing follicle maturation
questions.why: Excess androgens have a folliculotoxic effect, preventing normal follicle maturation and thus ovulation.

questions.q: Hyperprolactinemia causes anovulation by:
options: Negative feedback on GnRH, lowering LH and FSH
questions.why: Raised prolactin negatively feeds back on GnRH, lowering LH and FSH and causing anovulation.

questions.q: Besides anovulation, hyperprolactinemia's suppression of LH/FSH also causes low progesterone, presenting as:
questions.why: Low progesterone from hyperprolactinemia-driven anovulation presents as secondary amenorrhoea, alongside infertility.

questions.q: Lactational amenorrhoea shares its mechanism with hyperprolactinemia-induced anovulation, since breastfeeding causes:
questions.why: Breastfeeding raises prolactin, which suppresses the HPO axis, similarly to pathological hyperprolactinemia.

questions.q: Key menstrual history parameters to assess in AUB include regularity, frequency, duration, and:
questions.why: Regularity, frequency, duration, and volume are the four core menstrual parameters assessed in AUB history.

questions.q: On general examination for AUB, besides vitals and pallor, it is important to check for thyroid enlargement and:
questions.why: BMI, alongside vitals, pallor, and thyroid enlargement, is part of the general examination for AUB.

questions.q: Classic examination signs of PCOS include hirsutism, acne, and:
questions.why: Hirsutism, acne, and acanthosis nigricans are classic PCOS examination signs.

questions.q: Bimanual pelvic examination assesses uterine size, contour, tenderness, fixity, and:
questions.why: Bimanual exam assesses uterine size, contour, tenderness, fixity, and adnexal mass/tenderness.

questions.q: Per vaginal and pelvic examination are generally:
options: Mandatory in every patient with AUB
NOT done in a virgin adolescent
Only done if bleeding is heavy
questions.why: PV and pelvic examination are avoided in a virgin adolescent.

questions.q: Relevant associated symptoms to ask about in AUB history include vaginal discharge, dysmenorrhoea, dyspareunia, and:
questions.why: Infertility, alongside vaginal discharge, dysmenorrhoea, and dyspareunia, is a key associated symptom to assess.

questions.q: CBC and haemoglobin level in AUB workup are used mainly to assess:
questions.why: CBC/Hb assesses the severity of blood loss.

questions.q: BT, CT, and APTT (coagulation studies) are specifically indicated in AUB when there is puberty menorrhagia, low platelet count, or:
questions.why: Coagulation studies are indicated for puberty menorrhagia, low platelets, or a coagulopathy history.

questions.q: UPT and cervical cytology are specifically recommended in AUB workup for:
questions.why: UPT and cervical cytology are recommended specifically for sexually active females.

questions.q: USG in AUB evaluation is used mainly to detect:
questions.why: USG is the main tool for detecting structural lesions in AUB workup.

questions.q: Hysteroscopy is specifically indicated in AUB when there is an intracavitary lesion on USG, intermenstrual bleeding (suggesting polyp), or a history of curettage with AUB (suggesting):
questions.why: A history of curettage with subsequent AUB raises suspicion for Asherman syndrome, an indication for hysteroscopy.

questions.q: Endometrial sampling/biopsy is the investigation of choice for endometrial pathology; in India, the instrument commonly used is:
questions.why: Worldwide, Pipelle or Vabra aspirator are commonly used; in India, Karman's cannula is the commonly used instrument.

questions.q: In a reproductive-age woman with AUB, after a negative UPT, the preferred imaging is:
questions.why: TVS is preferred over TAS in the reproductive-age AUB algorithm.

questions.q: In a reproductive-age woman, endometrial biopsy is indicated if endometrial thickness exceeds:
questions.why: Endometrial thickness over 12 mm is an indication for biopsy in reproductive-age women.

questions.q: In a reproductive-age woman with AUB, endometrial biopsy is also indicated with a normal USG plus persistent bleeding, or in the presence of high-risk factors such as:
options: PCOS, granulosa cell tumour, or obesity
questions.why: High-risk factors warranting biopsy include PCOS, granulosa cell tumour, and obesity.

questions.q: According to FOGSI (India), perimenopause is considered to begin after age:
questions.why: FOGSI (India) defines perimenopause as beginning after age 40; ACOG (worldwide) uses 45 years.

questions.q: In a perimenopausal woman with AUB, the recommended workup is a UPT (irrespective of USG) plus:
questions.why: Perimenopausal AUB workup includes UPT plus TVS and endometrial biopsy.

questions.q: In a postmenopausal woman with AUB, if endometrial thickness on TVS is under 4 mm, initial management is a trial of tranexamic acid; if thickness is 4 mm or more, the next step is:
questions.why: A thickness ≥4 mm in a postmenopausal woman warrants endometrial biopsy.

questions.q: Tranexamic acid, an antifibrinolytic, reduces AUB blood loss by approximately:
questions.why: Tranexamic acid reduces AUB blood loss by about 50%.

questions.q: Tranexamic acid is well tolerated and effective particularly in cyclical bleeding with:
questions.why: Tranexamic acid works well in cyclical bleeding with a normal-sized uterus.

questions.q: Mefenamic acid, a prostaglandin synthetase inhibitor, is particularly indicated when AUB is accompanied by:
questions.why: Mefenamic acid is specifically useful when AUB is accompanied by dysmenorrhoea.

questions.q: Mefenamic acid is typically used:
options: As the sole first-line drug for AUB
In combination with tranexamic acid, not as first-line alone
questions.why: Mefenamic acid is not used as a first-line drug alone; it is combined with tranexamic acid.

questions.q: Ethamsylate reduces capillary fragility but, despite this mechanism, is:
options: Not effective in the management of AUB
The most effective AUB drug available
questions.why: Despite reducing capillary fragility, ethamsylate is not clinically effective for managing AUB.

questions.q: Combined OCPs manage AUB by stabilising the endometrium and by negative feedback on LH and FSH, which causes:
options: Anovulation, alongside contraception and ovarian suppression
questions.why: OCPs stabilise the endometrium and, via LH/FSH suppression, cause anovulation, contraception, and ovarian suppression.

questions.q: A standard OCP pack contains how many tablets?
questions.why: A standard OCP pack contains 21 hormone tablets.

questions.q: For contraceptive benefit, OCPs are started between which days of the cycle?
options: Any day, timing does not matter
questions.why: OCPs are started between day 1 and day 5 of the cycle for contraceptive benefit.

questions.q: In AUB management, a patient with haemoglobin under 10 g/dL is generally given OCPs:
options: Only as needed for bleeding episodes
questions.why: Hb <10 g/dL warrants continuous OCP use for 3 months.

questions.q: In AUB management, a patient with haemoglobin ≥10 g/dL is generally given OCPs as:
options: 3 months continuously, same as low Hb
3 weeks of OCP followed by 1 week off, repeated for 3 cycles
questions.why: Hb ≥10 g/dL is managed with 3 weeks OCP followed by 1 week off, for 3 cycles.

questions.q: Estrogen upregulates progesterone receptors on the endometrium; progesterone, in turn:
options: Downregulates estrogen receptors, and only acts on estrogen-primed endometrium
Has no effect on estrogen receptors
Acts independently of any estrogen priming
questions.why: Progesterone downregulates estrogen receptors and requires estrogen-primed endometrium to act.

questions.q: In a patient with a THICK endometrium (estrogen having upregulated progesterone receptors), appropriate drug options include:
questions.why: With a thick, progesterone-receptor-rich endometrium, OCPs or progesterone alone are appropriate.

questions.q: In a patient with a THIN endometrium or prolonged/severe bleeding (few progesterone receptors present), the preferred approach is:
options: Estrogen followed by progesterone, or combined estrogen+progesterone (OCP)
questions.why: With few progesterone receptors, estrogen is needed first (or combined as an OCP) to prime the endometrium before progesterone can act.

questions.q: Progesterone's core action on the endometrium is to support it and:
questions.why: Progesterone supports the endometrium and reduces shedding.

questions.q: When given CONTINUOUSLY, progesterone downregulates estrogen receptors, leading to:
options: Endometrial atrophy, reduced blood loss, and amenorrhoea
questions.why: Continuous progesterone causes endometrial atrophy, reducing blood loss and inducing amenorrhoea.

questions.q: Continuous oral progesterone (without a break) for 3–6 months causes endometrial atrophy and is considered:
options: The preferred mode of oral progesterone use in AUB
questions.why: Continuous oral progesterone is the preferred mode for AUB, producing endometrial atrophy.

questions.q: Cyclical oral progesterone (day 14–25) supports the endometrium and is used in anovulatory DUB, but is less preferred mainly due to:
options: Compliance issues, and it offers no contraceptive benefit
Its high cost compared to other options
questions.why: Cyclical progesterone is less preferred due to compliance challenges and lack of contraceptive benefit.

questions.q: Mirena (a progesterone-releasing IUCD) causes endometrial atrophy and provides relief of AUB in approximately what proportion of cases?
questions.why: Mirena provides relief of AUB in approximately 30–40% of cases.

questions.q: Mirena is preferred for treating AUB in reproductive-age and perimenopausal women, and also for protecting against:
questions.why: Mirena is preferred for treating AUB and for protecting against endometrial proliferation.

questions.q: A key advantage of Mirena over continuous oral progesterone is:
options: Requiring daily dosing, improving adherence tracking
Good compliance and reduced need for hysterectomy
questions.why: Mirena offers good compliance (no daily dosing needed) and reduces the need for hysterectomy.

questions.q: The minimum duration of Mirena's presence per month required for its endometrial-protective effect is:
questions.why: Mirena needs to be in place at least 12 days a month for its endometrial-protective effect.

questions.q: GnRH analogues, used as second-line medical therapy for AUB, work by continuously lowering LH, FSH, and estrogen, which:
options: Reduces endometrial proliferation and blood loss
questions.why: Continuous GnRH analogue use lowers LH/FSH/estrogen, reducing endometrial proliferation and blood loss.

questions.q: A major disadvantage of GnRH analogue therapy for AUB is:
options: Expense and menopause-like symptoms from low estrogen
Increased fertility as a side effect
Weight gain as the only side effect
Its inability to reduce bleeding at all
questions.why: GnRH analogues are expensive and cause menopause-like symptoms from hypo-estrogenism.

questions.q: The maximum recommended duration of GnRH analogue use is:
questions.why: GnRH analogue use for AUB is limited to a maximum of 6 months.

questions.q: GnRH analogues are also used prior to which procedures, to reduce endometrial thickness beforehand?
questions.why: GnRH analogues are used pre-operatively before surgery or endometrial ablation to thin the endometrium.

questions.q: Ormeloxifene, now considered obsolete for AUB management, is a SERM that works by:
options: Antagonising estrogen's effect on the endometrium, causing atrophy
questions.why: Ormeloxifene antagonises estrogen's endometrial effect, causing atrophy, though it is now considered obsolete for this indication.

questions.q: For a STRUCTURAL cause of AUB, the general management approach is:
options: Treatment directed at the specific underlying cause
questions.why: Structural causes are managed by treating the specific underlying cause (e.g. polypectomy for a polyp).

questions.q: For a non-structural cause of AUB with bleeding controlled, management typically includes oral iron plus:
questions.why: Once bleeding is controlled, oral iron plus maintenance drugs is the typical approach.

questions.q: Indications for blood transfusion in AUB include puberty menorrhagia with haemoglobin under:
questions.why: Blood transfusion is indicated in puberty menorrhagia when Hb is under 7 g/dL.

questions.q: Before a planned surgery for AUB, blood transfusion is considered if haemoglobin is under:
questions.why: Pre-operative blood transfusion is considered if Hb is under 10 g/dL.

questions.q: Surgical management options for AUB include endometrial ablation, uterine artery embolisation (for fibroid), and hysterectomy, generally reserved for cases meeting BOTH of which conditions?
options: Young age and desire for more children
Failure of medical management AND a complete family
questions.why: Surgical options are generally reserved for cases with BOTH failed medical management AND a completed family.

questions.q: Hysterectomy for AUB is particularly considered in a perimenopausal woman with:
questions.why: Hysterectomy is particularly considered in perimenopausal women with concomitant uterine pathology.

questions.q: In a patient with severe bleeding for 15 days, normal USG, negative UPT, and a normal endometrial biopsy, one treatment option is IV oestrogen (ethinyl estradiol) 50 mg for 5 days, followed by:
questions.why: IV oestrogen for 5 days is followed by progesterone in this acute management protocol.

questions.q: Alternatively, in this scenario, tapering-dose OCPs can be used, with dosing frequency reduced over time. The FIRST 2 days are typically dosed:
questions.why: The tapering OCP regimen starts with dosing every 4–8 hours for the first 2 days.

questions.q: In the tapering OCP regimen for acute severe AUB, the middle 5 days are dosed 12-hourly, and the final 14 days are dosed:
questions.why: The tapering schedule finishes with once-daily dosing for the final 14 days.

questions.q: This tapering OCP approach for acute heavy bleeding relies on which underlying principle?
options: High-dose hormone exposure stabilising the endometrium, then gradually tapering
questions.why: High initial hormone dosing stabilises the endometrium to control bleeding, then the dose is gradually tapered.

questions.q: Endometrial ablation destroys the endometrial lining to a depth of approximately:
questions.why: Endometrial ablation destroys the lining to a depth of about 4–6 mm.

questions.q: First-generation endometrial ablation techniques (e.g. rollerball, laser, TCRE) are performed under hysteroscopic guidance, which carries:
options: An increased risk of fluid overload
A guaranteed need for hysterectomy afterward
questions.why: Hysteroscopic guidance (needed for first-generation techniques) carries an increased risk of fluid overload from distension media.

questions.q: Second-generation techniques (e.g. cryosurgery, hydrothermal ablation) are NOT performed under direct hysteroscopic view, meaning they carry:
options: A higher risk of fluid overload
The same risks as first-generation techniques
Only cryogenic risks with no other advantage
questions.why: Since second-generation techniques avoid direct hysteroscopic distension, they carry no fluid overload risk.

questions.q: Which of these is a contraindication to endometrial ablation?
options: A desire for future pregnancy/incomplete family
questions.why: A desire for future fertility (incomplete family) is a contraindication, since ablation destroys the endometrium needed for implantation.

questions.q: Endometrial ablation is also contraindicated in the presence of endometrial hyperplasia/cancer and:
questions.why: Active pelvic infection, along with pregnancy, incomplete family, endometrial hyperplasia/cancer, and IUCD presence, is a contraindication to ablation.

units.title: DUB Definition, History & Diagnostics: Missed Details

questions.q: Dysfunctional uterine bleeding (DUB) is defined as abnormal bleeding with a normal USG (no pelvic pathology), no coagulopathy, and:
questions.why: DUB is a diagnosis of exclusion: normal pelvic anatomy on USG, no coagulopathy, and no medical/endocrine pathology.

questions.q: Of all DUB cases, anovulatory DUB (AUB-D) accounts for about 80%, while ovulatory AUB (AUB-E/AUB-N) accounts for the remaining:
questions.why: Anovulatory DUB makes up about 80% of cases (AUB-D), while ovulatory AUB accounts for the remaining 20% (AUB-E/AUB-N).

questions.q: Besides coagulation and menstrual history, important history points in AUB evaluation include recent abortion and:
questions.why: A history of IUCD insertion (along with recent abortion) is relevant, as both can be iatrogenic causes of AUB.

questions.q: The gold standard investigation for endometrial pathology, combining fractional curettage with direct visualization, is:
options: Endometrial biopsy alone, done as an OPD procedure
Fractional curettage with hysteroscopy, done under general anaesthesia in the OT
questions.why: Fractional curettage combined with hysteroscopy (done under GA in the OT) is the gold standard for endometrial pathology, though endometrial sampling/biopsy is the IOC as a simpler OPD procedure.

units.title: AUB Drug Doses & Management Logic: Missed Details

questions.q: The dose of tranexamic acid used in AUB management is:
questions.why: Tranexamic acid is dosed at 1 g thrice daily for 3–4 days in AUB management.

questions.q: The dose of mefenamic acid used in AUB (with dysmenorrhoea) is:
questions.why: Mefenamic acid is dosed at 500 mg thrice daily, used alongside tranexamic acid rather than as first-line alone.

questions.q: For regularising menstrual cycles in AUB, the drug of choice (DOC) is:
questions.why: OCPs are the drug of choice for regularising cycles in AUB, in addition to controlling blood loss and providing contraceptive benefit.

questions.q: Regardless of the specific clinical scenario, blood transfusion is indicated in AUB when haemoglobin falls below:
options: 5 g/dL, or if vitals are unstable
questions.why: Blood transfusion is indicated for Hb < 5 g/dL or unstable vitals, regardless of the specific clinical context (distinct from the Hb <7 threshold in puberty menorrhagia or <10 before planned surgery).

questions.q: The dose of ormeloxifene (a SERM, now largely obsolete for this indication) in AUB management is:
questions.why: Ormeloxifene is dosed at 60 mg twice daily for 12 weeks, working by antagonising oestrogen’s effect on the endometrium (causing atrophy).

questions.q: Surgical management of AUB (e.g., endometrial ablation, hysterectomy) is indicated only when BOTH of which conditions are fulfilled?
options: Patient preference alone, regardless of family status
Age over 40 alone, regardless of medical therapy tried
Failure of medical management AND a complete family
questions.why: Surgical management requires both failure of medical management and a complete family — either alone is not sufficient.

questions.q: The HPO axis is functional in intrauterine life, then becomes:
options: Progressively more active each year of childhood
Dormant after birth, reactivating at puberty
questions.why: The HPO axis, functional in-utero, becomes dormant after birth and reactivates at puberty.

questions.q: Dormancy of the HPO axis in childhood is maintained partly by central inhibition from which neurotransmitters?
questions.why: GABA and neuropeptide Y are inhibitory neurotransmitters maintaining HPO axis dormancy.

questions.q: Before puberty, the HPO axis shows high sensitivity to circulating oestrogen, such that even very low levels (E1 <10 pg) provide:
options: Negative feedback, keeping the axis suppressed
Feedback only on the adrenal gland
questions.why: The prepubertal HPO axis is highly sensitive to oestrogen’s negative feedback, so even tiny amounts (from adrenal androgen aromatisation) keep it suppressed.

questions.q: At puberty, the HPO axis becomes functional due to release of excitatory neurotransmitters, chiefly:
questions.why: Kisspeptin (driving pulsatile GnRH release) and glutamate are the key excitatory drivers of pubertal HPO activation.

questions.q: Leptin, released from adipose tissue, has which action on puberty onset?
options: A permissive action, supporting the onset of puberty
questions.why: Leptin has a permissive role, supporting pubertal onset.

questions.q: Because leptin correlates with body fat, obese girls tend to have:
options: Only delayed menarche but normal thelarche timing
questions.why: Higher leptin from increased adipose tissue in obese girls is linked to relatively earlier puberty onset.

questions.q: As the HPO axis becomes functional, GnRH is initially released:
options: Continuously throughout the day and night, from the very start
At high pulse frequency from the outset
Nocturnally, with low pulse frequency, before day-and-night release develops over 1–3 years
questions.why: GnRH release starts nocturnally at low pulse frequency, evolving to day-and-night release over about 1–3 years.

questions.q: In early puberty, the anterior pituitary initially releases predominantly:
questions.why: FSH release predominates initially, with LH developing later.

questions.q: Because LH release lags behind FSH in early puberty, the initial menstrual cycles are typically:
options: Completely absent for the first year
questions.why: Without adequate LH surge capacity yet, early cycles are typically anovulatory.

questions.q: The functional HPO axis pathway proceeds: hypothalamus (GnRH) → pituitary (FSH/LH) → ovary, producing:
options: Estrogen and progesterone, acting on the uterus
questions.why: The activated axis drives ovarian estrogen and progesterone production, acting on the uterus.

questions.q: The growth spurt is the same for both sexes until about age 10.5, after which:
options: Girls' growth spurt is earlier and shorter; boys' is later and longer
Boys' growth spurt is earlier and shorter
There is no further sex difference
questions.why: Girls' growth spurt starts earlier and is shorter; boys' starts later and lasts longer.

questions.q: In females, puberty begins around age 10.5, with the very first sign being:
questions.why: The growth spurt (skeletal growth) is the first sign of female puberty, even before it becomes visible.

questions.q: The first VISIBLE sign of puberty in females, and the most specific marker, is:
questions.why: Thelarche (breast budding) is the first visible sign and the most specific marker of puberty onset in females.

questions.q: In females, menarche typically follows peak height velocity by about:
questions.why: Menarche typically follows peak height velocity by about 6 months.

questions.q: Average age of menarche is about:
questions.why: Average age of menarche is about 12.5 years.

questions.q: In males, puberty begins around age 11.5, with the first sign being:
questions.why: Testicular enlargement is the first sign of male puberty, followed by penile enlargement, pubarche, and peak height velocity.

questions.q: Tanner staging of breast and pubic hair development comprises how many total stages?
questions.why: Tanner staging has 5 total stages, with stages 1–2 early and stages 4–5 late (mature) development.

questions.q: Breast budding corresponds to Tanner stage:
questions.why: Breast budding corresponds to Tanner stage 2.

questions.q: Hair appearing on the mons pubis corresponds to Tanner stage:
questions.why: Hair on the mons pubis corresponds to Tanner stage 3.

questions.q: Hair appearing on the medial thigh corresponds to the LATE stage of development, Tanner stage:
questions.why: Hair on the medial thigh corresponds to the late Tanner stage 5.

questions.q: Adrenarche, the maturation of adrenal androgen secretion, is notable because it:
options: Occurs only after full HPO axis activation
Is independent of HPO axis activation and occurs under age 6
questions.why: Adrenarche is independent of HPO axis (gonadarche) activation and occurs under age 6.

questions.q: Adrenarche is biochemically indicated by DHEAS levels of:
questions.why: DHEAS ≥40 mcg/dL indicates adrenarche.

questions.q: Estrogen helps initiate the pubertal growth spurt partly by promoting anterior pituitary release of:
questions.why: Estrogen promotes anterior pituitary release of insulin-like growth factor (IGF), supporting the growth spurt.

questions.q: Besides growth spurt initiation, estrogen's roles at puberty include breast development, menarche, and:
questions.why: Bone mineralisation is one of estrogen's key roles at puberty, alongside growth spurt, breast development, and menarche.

questions.q: Estrogen causes epiphyseal closure of long bones; in precocious puberty, this leads to:
options: Short final stature, from premature epiphyseal closure
questions.why: Premature epiphyseal closure from early oestrogen exposure in precocious puberty results in short final stature.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT typically listed as a role of estrogen at puberty?
questions.why: Adrenarche is a separate, HPO-axis-independent process, not an action of oestrogen.

questions.q: Pubertal menorrhagia is defined as:
options: Abnormal uterine bleeding (AUB) occurring in a pubertal female
Bleeding limited to the first period only
questions.why: Pubertal menorrhagia is AUB occurring specifically in a pubertal female.

questions.q: The most common cause of pubertal menorrhagia is:
questions.why: Anovulation is the most common cause of pubertal menorrhagia.

questions.q: The second most common cause of pubertal menorrhagia is:
questions.why: A coagulation defect is the second most common cause, after anovulation.

questions.q: A coagulation defect should be specifically suspected in pubertal menorrhagia if there is a history of heavy bleeding at menarche, easy bruisability, profuse bleeding from wounds, or:
options: A single normal period before this episode
A family history of coagulation disorder
questions.why: A family history of coagulation disorder, along with heavy bleeding at menarche, bruisability, and profuse wound bleeding, raises suspicion for an underlying coagulopathy.

questions.q: In the workup of pubertal menorrhagia, USG is:
questions.why: USG is not mandatory in the routine workup of pubertal menorrhagia.

questions.q: Routine investigations in pubertal menorrhagia workup include haemoglobin, TSH, and a coagulation profile (bleeding time, clotting time, prothrombin time), plus UPT if the patient is:
questions.why: UPT is added to the workup specifically if the patient is sexually active.

questions.q: For MILD pubertal menorrhagia (Hb 10–12 g/dL), management is:
options: Oral iron, reassurance, and a menstrual diary/calendar
questions.why: Mild cases are managed with oral iron, reassurance, and menstrual charting.

questions.q: For MODERATE pubertal menorrhagia (Hb 8–10 g/dL), first-line management is:
options: OCPs, to reduce blood loss and regularise the cycle
questions.why: OCPs are first-line for moderate cases, reducing blood loss and regularising the cycle.

questions.q: If a patient with moderate pubertal menorrhagia refuses OCPs, tranexamic acid (500 mg three times daily for 5 days) can be used, though it:
options: Also regularises the cycle, just like OCPs
Is contraindicated in this age group
Reduces blood loss but does NOT regularise the cycle
Is the preferred first choice over OCPs
questions.why: Tranexamic acid reduces blood loss but, unlike OCPs, does not regularise the cycle.

questions.q: For SEVERE pubertal menorrhagia (Hb <8 g/dL, profuse bleeding for 15 days), initial treatment options include high-dose IV oestrogen (unavailable in India), ethinylestradiol 50 mg for 5 days, or:
questions.why: Tapering-dose OCPs are an option for initial treatment of severe pubertal menorrhagia.

questions.q: In the tapering OCP regimen for severe pubertal menorrhagia, dosing starts 8-hourly for the first 2 days, then 12-hourly, then once daily, over a total course of:
questions.why: The full tapering course runs over 21 days: 2 days 8-hourly, 5 days 12-hourly, then 2 weeks once daily.

questions.q: Maintenance therapy after severe pubertal menorrhagia is controlled includes OCP (once daily, day 5–25) for 6 cycles, or alternatively:
options: Tranexamic acid daily for a year
Progesterone for 10 days in each cycle, for 6 cycles
questions.why: Progesterone for 10 days per cycle, for 6 cycles, is the alternative maintenance option.

questions.q: Precocious puberty in females is defined as the appearance of secondary sexual characteristics before age:
questions.why: Precocious puberty in females is defined as secondary sexual characteristics appearing before age 8.

questions.q: Precocious puberty in males is defined as the appearance of secondary sexual characteristics before age:
questions.why: Precocious puberty in males is defined as secondary sexual characteristics appearing before age 9.

questions.q: Precocious puberty is more common in:
questions.why: Precocious puberty is more common in females than males.

questions.q: In isosexual precocious puberty, a female develops:
options: Female secondary sexual characteristics early, due to excess estrogen
No secondary sexual characteristics at all
questions.why: Isosexual precocious puberty means early development of characteristics matching the person’s own sex, driven by excess estrogen in females.

questions.q: In heterosexual precocious puberty, a female develops:
options: Accelerated but otherwise normal female puberty
Male secondary sexual characteristics, due to excess androgen
questions.why: Heterosexual precocious puberty means development of characteristics of the opposite sex — in females, driven by excess androgen.

questions.q: The most common overall cause of precocious puberty is:
questions.why: Idiopathic precocious puberty is the most common cause overall, though brain tumours account for about 10% of cases.

units.title: Central vs Peripheral PP: Detailed Comparison

questions.q: Central (true) precocious puberty accounts for what proportion of cases, making it the more common type?
questions.why: Central precocious puberty accounts for about 80% of cases.

questions.q: Central precocious puberty results from premature activation of the HPO axis, causing:
options: Decreased GnRH, FSH, LH, and estrogen
Isolated estrogen elevation without gonadotropin change
Increased GnRH, FSH, LH, and estrogen, in that sequence
questions.why: Premature HPO axis activation raises GnRH, then FSH/LH, then estrogen, in sequence.

questions.q: Peripheral precocious puberty is NOT related to the HPO axis; instead, the source of excess hormone is the:
questions.why: Peripheral precocious puberty arises from the ovary or adrenal gland directly, bypassing the HPO axis.

questions.q: In peripheral precocious puberty, excess peripheral estrogen/androgen causes negative feedback, resulting in:
questions.why: Excess peripheral hormone suppresses FSH/LH via negative feedback, since the axis is otherwise not driving the process.

questions.q: Premature ovulation is a feature of:
questions.why: Since central PP genuinely activates the HPO axis, it can result in premature ovulation, unlike peripheral PP.

questions.q: Central precocious puberty is always isosexual, while peripheral precocious puberty can be:
questions.why: Peripheral PP can be isosexual (excess estrogen) or heterosexual (excess androgen), unlike central PP, which is always isosexual.

questions.q: Besides idiopathic causes, central precocious puberty can result from brain tumours (e.g. hamartoma, glioma, ependymoma) or:
questions.why: CNS infection such as TB meningitis is another recognised cause of central precocious puberty.

questions.q: A granulosa cell tumour of the ovary is a recognised cause of which type of precocious puberty?
options: None; it does not cause precocious puberty
questions.why: A granulosa cell tumour secretes estrogen, causing isosexual peripheral precocious puberty.

questions.q: Chronic hypothyroidism can cause isosexual peripheral precocious puberty because:
options: The alpha subunit of TSH is similar to that of LH/FSH, allowing cross-reactivity with gonadal receptors
Hypothyroidism always causes early puberty via unrelated mechanisms
It has no real mechanistic link and is coincidental
questions.why: The shared alpha subunit between TSH and LH/FSH allows very high TSH to cross-react with gonadotropin receptors.

questions.q: McCune-Albright syndrome is a recognised cause of:
questions.why: McCune-Albright syndrome causes isosexual peripheral precocious puberty, via autonomous ovarian oestrogen production.

questions.q: Androgen-producing ovarian tumours and congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) are causes of:
questions.why: Excess androgen from these sources causes heterosexual precocious puberty.

questions.q: The most common cause of heterosexual PRECOCIOUS puberty specifically is:
questions.why: CAH is the most common cause of heterosexual precocious puberty specifically (PCOS is the most common cause of heterosexual development generally, at a later/normal age).

questions.q: The classic triad of McCune-Albright syndrome includes café-au-lait spots, polyostotic fibrous dysplasia, and:
questions.why: The McCune-Albright triad is café-au-lait spots, polyostotic fibrous dysplasia, and precocious puberty.

questions.q: The underlying pathogenesis of McCune-Albright syndrome involves:
options: A chromosomal deletion on the X chromosome
A mutation in G-protein coupled (FSH) receptors, causing constitutive activation
questions.why: A constitutively active G-protein coupled FSH receptor mutation drives the syndrome.

questions.q: This constitutively active FSH receptor mutation in McCune-Albright syndrome directly:
options: Activates the ovaries, raising oestrogen independent of pituitary FSH
Only affects bone, with no hormonal consequence
questions.why: The mutated receptor activates the ovary autonomously, raising oestrogen without needing pituitary FSH drive.

questions.q: The single best investigation to differentiate central from peripheral precocious puberty is:
questions.why: FSH and LH levels are the best investigation to distinguish gonadotropin-dependent (central) from gonadotropin-independent (peripheral) precocious puberty.

questions.q: For HETEROSEXUAL precocious puberty specifically, additional investigations include testosterone, DHEA-S (to localise the source between ovary and adrenal), and:
options: 17-OH progesterone, to rule out congenital adrenal hyperplasia
questions.why: 17-OH progesterone is checked specifically to rule out congenital adrenal hyperplasia in heterosexual PP.

questions.q: Delayed puberty in females is defined as absence of secondary sexual characteristics by age 13, or absence of menarche by age:
questions.why: Delayed puberty in females is defined by no secondary sexual characteristics by 13, or no menarche by 15.

questions.q: Delayed puberty in males is defined as absence of secondary sexual characteristics by age:
questions.why: Delayed puberty in males is defined as no secondary sexual characteristics by age 14.

questions.q: Delayed puberty is overall more common in:
questions.why: Delayed puberty is more common in males than females.

questions.q: The most common cause of delayed puberty (in both sexes) is:
questions.why: Constitutional delay is the most common cause of delayed puberty in both sexes.

questions.q: Delayed puberty from low GnRH, associated with anosmia, points to:
questions.why: Low GnRH with anosmia is characteristic of Kallmann syndrome.

questions.q: A 46,XY karyotype with delayed puberty and female external phenotype suggests:
questions.why: Androgen insensitivity syndrome presents with a 46,XY karyotype but female external phenotype, due to end-organ resistance to androgens.

sections.name: Complete Coverage: Puberty Definitions, Management & Missed Details

units.title: Definitions, Menstrual & Adrenarche Details: Missed Points

questions.q: Puberty is defined by all of the following EXCEPT:
options: The period involving transition from childhood to adulthood
Onset of development of secondary sexual characters
questions.why: Permanent cessation of menstruation defines menopause, not puberty. Puberty is defined by the childhood-to-adulthood transition, onset of secondary sexual characters, and attainment of reproductive capacity.

questions.q: The initial menstrual cycles at puberty are anovulatory, irregular, heavy, and characteristically:
questions.why: Initial pubertal menstrual cycles are anovulatory, irregular, heavy in flow, and painless.

questions.q: Menstruation occurring before the age of 10 years is specifically termed:
questions.why: Precocious menstruation refers specifically to menstruation occurring before age 10 years, distinct from the broader term precocious puberty.

questions.q: In the context of puberty, primary amenorrhoea is defined as failure of menarche within how many years of breast budding (thelarche)?
questions.why: Failure of menarche within 3 years of breast budding defines primary amenorrhoea in this context.

questions.q: The most important secondary sexual character in females is:
questions.why: Breast development is regarded as the most important secondary sexual character in females, driven by oestrogen and occurring in stages.

questions.q: Besides stimulating development of pubic and axillary hair, adrenarche in females is also associated with:
questions.why: Adrenarche (adrenal androgen release) is associated with increased libido in females, in addition to pubic/axillary hair development.

units.title: Pubertal Menorrhagia & PP Management: Missed Points

questions.q: Besides anovulation (most common) and a coagulation defect (second most common), another recognised cause of pubertal menorrhagia is:
questions.why: Thyroid dysfunction is listed as another recognised cause of pubertal menorrhagia, alongside anovulation and coagulation defects.

questions.q: In the evaluation of pubertal menorrhagia, per vaginal (PV) examination is:
options: Mandatory before any USG is done
