Only omitted if the patient is anaemic
questions.why: Per vaginal examination is contraindicated in virgin females during evaluation of pubertal menorrhagia.

questions.q: The three standard drug categories used in management of any abnormal uterine bleeding (AUB), including pubertal menorrhagia, are tranexamic acid, combined OCPs, and:
questions.why: Tranexamic acid, combined OCPs, and progesterone-only therapy are the three standard drug categories used across AUB management, including pubertal menorrhagia.

questions.q: The management of CENTRAL precocious puberty is with continuous GnRH (agonist) therapy or:
questions.why: Central precocious puberty is managed with continuous GnRH agonist therapy or GnRH antagonists, both suppressing the prematurely activated HPO axis.

questions.q: The management of PERIPHERAL precocious puberty consists primarily of:
questions.why: Since peripheral precocious puberty is not HPO-axis driven, management targets the underlying cause (e.g., ovarian/adrenal tumour, hypothyroidism) rather than suppressing GnRH.

questions.q: The drug of choice for management of delayed puberty (e.g., in Kallmann syndrome) is:
questions.why: Pulsatile GnRH is the drug of choice for delayed puberty, in contrast to the continuous GnRH used to suppress central precocious puberty.

questions.q: PCOS, via chronic anovulation, is a recognised cause of:
questions.why: PCOS (causing anovulation) is listed among the causes of delayed puberty, alongside constitutional delay, Kallmann syndrome, Turner syndrome, and androgen insensitivity syndrome.

units.title: Precocious Puberty Table & Investigation Details: Missed Points

questions.q: Recognised consequences of precocious puberty include risk related to the underlying cause, estrogen exposure at a young age, and:
questions.why: Psychological and emotional stress is a recognised consequence of precocious puberty, alongside early oestrogen exposure and risks tied to the underlying cause.

questions.q: In the central vs peripheral precocious puberty comparison table, premature menarche (<10 years) is present (+) in central PP, while in peripheral PP it is:
options: Variable (\u00b1), occurring due to oestrogen breakthrough bleeding
Always present, identical to central PP
questions.why: Peripheral PP shows variable (\u00b1) premature menarche, occurring due to oestrogen breakthrough bleeding rather than a mature ovulatory cycle.

questions.q: Since brain tumours account for about 10% of precocious puberty cases, MRI brain is indicated:
options: Only if neurological symptoms are present
Only in males with precocious puberty
In all females with precocious puberty
questions.why: MRI brain is indicated in all females with precocious puberty, given that brain tumours account for about 10% of cases.

questions.q: In the general investigation panel for precocious puberty, bone age estimation and FSH/LH are done alongside estrogen, TSH, MRI brain, and:
questions.why: USG pelvis and abdomen rounds out the general precocious puberty workup, alongside bone age, FSH/LH, oestrogen, TSH, and MRI brain.

questions.q: Menopause is defined as amenorrhoea of at least how many months, followed by permanent cessation of menstruation?
questions.why: Menopause is defined as amenorrhoea ≥ 12 months followed by permanent cessation of menstruation.

questions.q: The maximum number of ovarian follicles is present at which point in life?
questions.why: Follicle number peaks at 6–7 million in the 5th month of intrauterine life, after which apoptosis reduces the number.

questions.q: By birth, apoptosis has reduced the follicle count to approximately:
questions.why: By birth, follicle number falls to about 1–2 million, down from a peak of 6–7 million in utero.

questions.q: By puberty, the follicle count is approximately:
questions.why: By puberty, roughly 4–5 million follicles remain, further reduced from the birth count.

questions.q: At menopause, the ovaries show:
options: A rebound increase in follicle number
questions.why: Menopause corresponds to complete atresia of all ovarian follicles.

questions.q: The average age of menopause is later worldwide than in India; the correct pairing is:
questions.why: The average age of menopause is 51 years worldwide but 47 years in India.

questions.q: Premature menopause is now more accurately termed:
questions.why: Premature menopause is now termed primary ovarian insufficiency (POI).

questions.q: POI is defined as menopause occurring before age:
questions.why: POI (premature menopause) is defined as occurring before 40 years of age.

questions.q: POI classically presents with:
questions.why: POI presents with secondary amenorrhoea and secondary infertility.

questions.q: Late menopause is defined as non-occurrence of menopause in a female aged:
questions.why: Late menopause is defined as non-occurrence of menopause by ≥ 55 years of age.

questions.q: In late menopause, an endometrial biopsy is recommended because of increased risk of:
questions.why: Late menopause carries an increased risk of endometrial cancer, so endometrial biopsy is advised.

questions.q: The first sign of perimenopause (climacteric) is:
options: An increase in cycle length by ≥ 7 days
questions.why: The first sign of perimenopause is an increase in cycle length of ≥ 7 days.

questions.q: Menstrual cycles during perimenopause are typically:
questions.why: Perimenopausal cycles are anovulatory and irregular.

questions.q: STRAW staging divides the 3 phases of female adult life (reproductive age, perimenopause, menopause) into a total of:
questions.why: STRAW staging divides the 3 phases of female adult life into 7 total stages.

questions.q: Menopause is essentially diagnosed by:
options: Clinical criteria alone; no hormonal test is required
questions.why: Menopause is a clinical diagnosis; no hormonal test is required (unlike POI, where lab testing is mandatory).

questions.q: Unlike menopause, the diagnosis of POI requires:
questions.why: POI diagnosis requires a mandatory laboratory test, in contrast to menopause which is a clinical diagnosis.

questions.q: At menopause, which two ovarian hormones fall due to follicular apoptosis?
questions.why: Follicular apoptosis at menopause leads to falling estrogen and androgen levels.

questions.q: The predominant circulating estrogen after menopause is:
questions.why: After menopause, estrone (E1) becomes the most common circulating estrogen.

questions.q: AMH and inhibin levels after menopause are:
questions.why: Both AMH and inhibin fall after menopause, reflecting depleted follicular reserve.

questions.q: Loss of negative feedback from falling ovarian hormones at menopause leads to a rise in:
questions.why: Loss of negative feedback causes a compensatory rise in FSH and LH.

questions.q: Elevated FSH and LH excreted in the urine after menopause are together referred to as:
questions.why: Urinary FSH/LH after menopause are referred to as HMG (Human Menopausal Gonadotropins).

questions.q: A patient with secondary amenorrhoea and raised FSH/LH (hypergonadotropic hypogonadism) should next have which test to confirm menopause/POI?
questions.why: The next step in hypergonadotropic hypogonadism is measuring estrogen; low estrogen confirms menopause or POI.

questions.q: Pregnancy can also cause secondary amenorrhoea, but is distinguished from menopause by which hormonal pattern?
options: Decreased estrogen and progesterone, decreased FSH and LH
Decreased estrogen, increased FSH and LH (same as menopause)
Increased estrogen and progesterone, increased FSH but decreased LH
questions.why: In pregnancy, secondary amenorrhoea occurs with increased estrogen and progesterone, increased FSH, but decreased LH — unlike the menopausal pattern.

questions.q: The most common symptom of menopause is:
questions.why: Hot flushes (vasomotor symptoms) are the most common symptom of menopause.

questions.q: Hot flushes occur because falling estrogen causes:
options: Resetting of the hypothalamic thermostat with a serotonin–norepinephrine imbalance
questions.why: Falling estrogen resets the hypothalamic thermostat and causes a serotonin–norepinephrine imbalance, producing hot flushes.

questions.q: The typical presentation of a hot flush is an intense heat sensation on the face, followed by:
questions.why: A hot flush classically presents as a heat sensation on the face followed by sweating, sometimes with palpitations/tachycardia.

questions.q: Hot flushes most commonly occur at night, when they are termed:
options: Night sweats, with associated disturbed sleep
questions.why: Night-time hot flushes are termed night sweats and are associated with disturbed sleep.

questions.q: A typical hot flush episode lasts less than 5 minutes and recurs approximately:
questions.why: Each hot flush episode lasts under 5 minutes and recurs about 3–4 times.

questions.q: Hot flushes, seen in perimenopausal and menopausal women, typically begin how long before menopause and subside how long after?
options: Begin 3–4 years before, subside 5 years after
Begin only after menopause, subside within a week
Begin at menarche, subside at menopause
questions.why: Hot flushes begin 3–4 years before menopause and automatically subside about 5 years after menopause.

questions.q: Severe hot flushes causing sleep disturbance or interference with daily activities represent:
options: The only indication for post-menopausal HRT
A sign of primary ovarian insufficiency exclusively
questions.why: Severe hot flushes (with sleep disturbance or interference with daily activities) are the only indication for post-menopausal HRT.

questions.q: Menopausal osteoporosis is best described as:
options: A quantitative bone defect with reduced bone mineral density
A pure vitamin D deficiency state
questions.why: Osteoporosis is a quantitative bone defect — reduced bone mineral density (BMD).

questions.q: Menopausal osteoporosis most commonly affects which type of bone?
questions.why: Trabecular bone is most commonly affected in menopausal osteoporosis.

questions.q: The three classic fracture sites at increased risk in menopausal osteoporosis are vertebral (T12–L3), neck of femur, and:
questions.why: The three classic fracture sites are vertebral (T12–L3), neck of femur, and Colles fracture.

questions.q: The investigation of choice for menopausal osteoporosis is:
questions.why: DEXA scan is the investigation of choice for osteoporosis.

questions.q: DEXA scanning is indicated at what age?
questions.why: DEXA scan is indicated from age ≥ 65 years.

questions.q: The preferred DEXA site is the 1st–4th lumbar vertebrae, which is favoured over:
questions.why: Lumbar vertebrae (L1–L4) are the preferred DEXA site, over the neck of femur.

questions.q: On a DEXA report, comparing a patient's BMD to that of a young woman gives the:
questions.why: The T-score compares a patient’s BMD to a young woman’s BMD; the Z-score compares it to a woman of the same age.

questions.q: The drug of choice for menopausal osteoporosis is:
questions.why: Bisphosphonates are the drug of choice for menopausal osteoporosis.

questions.q: Drugs that act directly on osteoblasts (rather than osteoclasts) in osteoporosis management include teriparatide and:
questions.why: Teriparatide and strontium act on osteoblasts, unlike bisphosphonates which act on osteoclasts.

questions.q: Estrogen's cardioprotective effect includes raising HDL, lowering LDL, and increasing:
options: Nitric oxide in vascular endothelial cells
questions.why: Estrogen increases nitric oxide in vascular endothelial cells, alongside raising HDL and lowering LDL.

questions.q: At menopause, falling estrogen leads to:
options: Decreased risk of coronary artery disease (CAD)
Increased risk of coronary artery disease (CAD)
Only a change in bone density, with no vascular effect
questions.why: Falling estrogen at menopause increases the risk of coronary artery disease.

questions.q: The incidence of CAD in menopausal women particularly depends on:
questions.why: CAD incidence depends on comorbidities and smoking habits.

questions.q: Regarding HRT and cardiovascular disease, HRT is:
options: Only used to treat established CAD
questions.why: HRT is never given to prevent CAD.

questions.q: In women ≥ 60 years, HRT is associated with a slightly increased CAD risk, which is higher with:
options: Estrogen-only HRT compared to estrogen + progesterone HRT
Estrogen + progesterone HRT compared to estrogen-only HRT
questions.why: In women ≥ 60 years, E+P HRT carries a slightly higher CAD risk than estrogen-only HRT; in women <60, HRT has no effect on CAD risk.

questions.q: Senile/atrophic vaginitis is now termed:
questions.why: Senile/atrophic vaginitis is now termed genitourinary syndrome of menopause.

questions.q: The genitourinary syndrome of menopause results from falling estrogen causing reduced cervical discharge and:
questions.why: Falling estrogen reduces cervical discharge, resulting in vaginal dryness.

questions.q: Urinary symptoms of genitourinary syndrome of menopause include increased urinary frequency, dysuria, frequent UTIs, and:
questions.why: Urinary incontinence is among the urinary symptoms, along with increased frequency, dysuria, and frequent UTIs.

questions.q: Genital symptoms of this syndrome include dyspareunia and:
options: Bleeding per vaginum due to the atrophic vagina
questions.why: Bleeding per vaginum (due to the atrophic vagina) is a genital symptom, along with dyspareunia.

questions.q: On local examination, the genitourinary syndrome of menopause classically shows shiny vaginal mucosa, thin atrophied mucosa, and:
questions.why: Loss of vaginal rugosities is a classic local examination finding, along with shiny, thin, atrophied mucosa.

questions.q: Which SERMs are known to worsen vaginal dryness?
questions.why: Clomiphene, tamoxifen, and raloxifene are SERMs that can worsen vaginal dryness.

questions.q: Which SERMs are actually useful in managing senile/atrophic vaginitis?
options: Ospemifene, and bazedoxifene combined with estrogen
questions.why: Ospemifene, and bazedoxifene + estrogen, are the SERMs used to manage senile vaginitis (unlike clomiphene/tamoxifen/raloxifene, which worsen it).

questions.q: For hot flushes, first-line management is HRT; if the uterus is intact, which regimen is used?
questions.why: With an intact uterus, combined estrogen + progesterone HRT is used, since progesterone protects the endometrium.

questions.q: For hot flushes, if the uterus is absent, HRT is given as:
questions.why: With the uterus absent, estrogen-only HRT is appropriate since there is no endometrium to protect.

questions.q: Second-line therapy for hot flushes (SSRIs) includes fluoxetine, paroxetine, and:
questions.why: Venlafaxine, along with fluoxetine and paroxetine, is used as second-line SSRI therapy for hot flushes.

questions.q: The SERM combination used for hot flushes is bazedoxifene with estrogen; which SERMs are contraindicated here as they can worsen hot flushes?
questions.why: Raloxifene, tamoxifen, and clomiphene are contraindicated as they can worsen hot flushes.

questions.q: Other (non-hormonal) drugs used for hot flushes include clonidine, gabapentin, isoflavenes, and:
questions.why: Phytoestrogens (e.g. flax seed), along with isoflavenes, clonidine, and gabapentin, are non-hormonal options for hot flushes.

questions.q: For osteoporosis, first-line therapy is alendronate; HRT is second-line, along with which SERM?
questions.why: Raloxifene is the SERM option for osteoporosis management, alongside first-line alendronate and second-line HRT.

questions.q: Other drugs for osteoporosis include tibolone (an estrogen + progesterone analogue), teriparatide, strontium, and:
questions.why: Denosumab, a RANK ligand inhibitor, is another drug option for osteoporosis, along with tibolone, teriparatide, and strontium.

questions.q: For senile vaginitis, first-line management is vaginal lubricants; second-line is local estrogen therapy, given as cream/gel, ring, or:
questions.why: Local estrogen therapy for senile vaginitis can be given as cream/gel, pessary, or ring.

questions.q: The daily calcium and vitamin D requirements are higher in menopausal women than in the reproductive age group; the menopausal requirements are:
options: 1000 mg/day calcium and 600 IU vitamin D
800 mg/day calcium and 400 IU vitamin D
1200 mg/day calcium and 800 IU vitamin D
1500 mg/day calcium and 1000 IU vitamin D
questions.why: Menopausal women require 1200 mg/day calcium and 800 IU vitamin D, higher than the reproductive age group’s 1000 mg/day and 600 IU.

questions.q: Primary ovarian insufficiency is defined as exhaustion of ovarian follicles before age:
questions.why: POI is defined as exhaustion of ovarian follicles before 40 years of age (premature menopause).

questions.q: Among the causes of POI, the ovary is notable as the:
options: Organ most resistant to autoimmune damage
questions.why: The ovary is the most radiosensitive pelvic organ, making chemo/radiotherapy an important cause of POI.

questions.q: Besides chemo/radiotherapy, metabolic and infectious causes of POI include galactosemia and:
questions.why: Galactosemia and mumps are recognised metabolic/infectious causes of POI.

questions.q: Genetic syndromes associated with POI include Fragile X syndrome and:
questions.why: Fragile X syndrome and Turner mosaic are the genetic syndromes associated with POI.

questions.q: Clinical features of POI include hot flushes, vaginal dryness, dyspareunia, secondary infertility, and:
questions.why: Secondary amenorrhoea with irregular cycles is a clinical feature of POI, along with hot flushes, vaginal dryness, dyspareunia, and secondary infertility.

questions.q: Confirming POI mandates FSH testing on two occasions, one month apart; an FSH ≥ 40 IU/L is:
options: Diagnostic of menopause but not POI
questions.why: FSH ≥ 40 IU/L on two occasions one month apart is diagnostic of POI (FSH ≥ 25 IU is only suggestive, and <10 IU is normal).

questions.q: Karyotyping is indicated in POI when there is short stature, or normal stature with age:
questions.why: Karyotyping is indicated in POI for short stature, or for normal stature at age 30 years.

questions.q: For a POI patient desiring fertility, the management of choice is:
options: IVF using the patient's own eggs only
IVF with donor eggs, with the embryo implanted in the patient's uterus
questions.why: IVF with donor eggs, with the embryo implanted in the patient's own uterus, is the management of choice for infertility in POI.

questions.q: For POI patients troubled by hot flushes, HRT should be continued until:
questions.why: HRT for hot flushes in POI is continued until the age of normal menopause.

questions.q: Menopausal symptoms are due to falling estrogen and are relieved by:
questions.why: Menopausal symptoms result from falling estrogen and are relieved by post-menopausal HRT.

questions.q: HRT is indicated in postmenopausal women with severe hot flushes and in:
questions.why: HRT is indicated for post-menopausal severe hot flushes and for primary ovarian insufficiency (POI).

questions.q: HRT is also indicated in ↓estrogen states from gonadal dysgenesis, such as Turner's syndrome and:
questions.why: Turner's syndrome and Swyer's syndrome (both gonadal dysgenesis) are ↓estrogen states indicated for HRT.

questions.q: HRT is indicated following surgical oophorectomy and in ↓estrogen states from:
questions.why: Androgen insensitivity syndrome (a ↓estrogen state) and surgical oophorectomy are both indications for HRT.

questions.q: If the uterus is absent, which type of HRT is used?
questions.why: Estrogen-only HRT is used when the uterus is absent, since there is no endometrium to protect.

questions.q: If the uterus is present, which type of HRT is used, and why?
options: Estrogen-only HRT, since progesterone increases cancer risk
E+P HRT, because progesterone protects the endometrium
questions.why: With the uterus present, combined E+P HRT is used because progesterone protects the endometrium from cancer development.

questions.q: In combined HRT, estrogen reduces hot flushes while progesterone's role is to:
options: Protect the endometrium from developing cancer
questions.why: Progesterone's role in combined HRT is to protect the endometrium from developing cancer, while estrogen reduces hot flushes.

questions.q: The minimum duration of progesterone required per cycle in HRT is:
questions.why: A minimum of 12 days of progesterone per cycle is required in combined HRT.

questions.q: The ideal duration of progesterone use in a woman on combined HRT is:
options: As long as estrogen is given
Not needed if BMI is normal
questions.why: Ideally, progesterone should be given for as long as estrogen is given, to continuously protect the endometrium.

questions.q: Giving unopposed estrogen (without adequate progesterone) in a woman with an intact uterus mainly risks:
questions.why: Unopposed estrogen in a woman with an intact uterus increases the risk of endometrial cancer, which is why progesterone is co-administered.

questions.q: Benefits of estrogen-only HRT include reduced hot flushes, reduced osteoporosis, and reduced chances of:
questions.why: Estrogen-only HRT reduces hot flushes, osteoporosis, and chances of colorectal cancer.

questions.q: A key disadvantage of estrogen-only HRT is increased risk of:
questions.why: Estrogen-only HRT carries an increased risk of venous thromboembolism.

questions.q: The increased VTE risk with estrogen-only HRT is lower with which route of administration?
questions.why: The transdermal route carries a lower VTE risk compared to oral estrogen.

questions.q: Estrogen-only HRT increases the risk of endometrial cancer specifically when:
options: The patient has had a prior hysterectomy
questions.why: Estrogen-only HRT increases endometrial cancer risk only if the uterus is present (unopposed estrogen effect).

questions.q: Estrogen-only HRT carries a variably increased (±) risk of:
questions.why: Estrogen-only HRT is associated with a variably increased (±) risk of ovarian cancer.

questions.q: Like estrogen-only HRT, combined E+P HRT reduces hot flushes, osteoporosis, and chances of colorectal cancer; unlike estrogen-only HRT, it also:
options: Has no effect on endometrial cancer risk
questions.why: Unlike estrogen-only HRT, combined E+P HRT reduces the chances of endometrial cancer, because progesterone protects the endometrium.

questions.q: A disadvantage shared between combined and estrogen-only HRT is increased risk of:
questions.why: Both combined and estrogen-only HRT carry an increased risk of venous thromboembolism.

questions.q: Combined E+P HRT carries a variably increased (±) risk of:
questions.why: Like estrogen-only HRT, combined E+P HRT carries a variably increased (±) risk of ovarian cancer.

questions.q: A disadvantage specific to combined E+P HRT (not listed for estrogen-only) is increased risk of:
questions.why: Increased breast cancer risk is a disadvantage specific to combined E+P HRT.

questions.q: Which statement correctly contrasts endometrial cancer risk between the two HRT types?
options: Both types increase endometrial cancer risk equally
Both types reduce endometrial cancer risk equally
E+P HRT reduces endometrial cancer risk, while estrogen-only HRT (with uterus present) increases it
Neither type affects endometrial cancer risk
questions.why: E+P HRT reduces endometrial cancer risk (progesterone protects the endometrium), while unopposed estrogen-only HRT in a woman with a uterus increases it.

questions.q: Regarding coronary artery disease, HRT:
options: Fully protects against CAD in all age groups
Is specifically prescribed to prevent CAD
Does not protect against CAD in females ≥ 60 years; risk is actually increased
questions.why: HRT does not protect against CAD in females ≥ 60 years — risk is actually increased in this group.

questions.q: HRT does NOT increase the risk of:
questions.why: HRT does not increase the risk of cervical cancer, unlike the other listed risks.

questions.q: The maximum duration of HRT in a postmenopausal woman is:
questions.why: The maximum duration of HRT in a postmenopausal woman is 5 years.

questions.q: In women with POI, Turner's syndrome, or Swyer's syndrome, HRT duration extends:
options: Up to the age of normal menopause
questions.why: In POI, Turner's syndrome, or Swyer's syndrome, HRT is continued up to the age of normal menopause (rather than the fixed 5-year postmenopausal limit).

questions.q: General indications for continuing HRT include age less than 60 years and time since menopause onset less than:
questions.why: HRT indication generally requires age <60 years and <10 years since the onset of menopause.

questions.q: In a woman with hot flushes who has a contraindication to HRT, the drug of choice is:
questions.why: Fluoxetine is the drug of choice for hot flushes when HRT is contraindicated.

questions.q: The drug of choice for the estrogen component of HRT is:
questions.why: 17β-estradiol is the drug of choice for the estrogen component of HRT.

questions.q: For estrogen administration in HRT, which route is preferred over oral?
questions.why: The transdermal route is preferred over oral for estrogen administration in HRT.

questions.q: The oral dose of 17β-estradiol is 1 mg/day, typically started at:
questions.why: Oral 17β-estradiol is dosed at 1 mg/day, typically started at 0.5 mg/day.

questions.q: The transdermal dose of 17β-estradiol is 0.05 mg/day, typically started at:
questions.why: Transdermal 17β-estradiol is dosed at 0.05 mg/day, typically started at 0.025 mg/day.

questions.q: Conjugated equine estrogen (CEE), once commonly used, is now considered:
questions.why: Conjugated equine estrogen (CEE) is now considered obsolete.

questions.q: The drug of choice for the progesterone component of HRT is:
options: Micronized oral progesterone, at a dose of 100–200 mg/day
questions.why: Micronized oral progesterone (100–200 mg/day) is the drug of choice for the progesterone component of HRT.

questions.q: Besides micronized oral progesterone, another drug of choice for the progesterone component of HRT is:
questions.why: Dydrogesterone is also listed as a drug of choice for the progesterone component of HRT.

questions.q: Absolute contraindications to HRT include a past history of DVT, stroke, and:
questions.why: A past history of DVT, stroke, and coronary artery disease are contraindications to HRT.

questions.q: HRT is contraindicated in women with a past history of:
questions.why: A past history of breast cancer is a contraindication to HRT.

questions.q: Undiagnosed vaginal bleeding is a contraindication to HRT because it may indicate:
questions.why: Undiagnosed vaginal bleeding is a contraindication as it may indicate underlying endometrial cancer.

questions.q: A history relevant to hepatic function that contraindicates HRT is:
questions.why: A history of acute liver disease/biopsy is a contraindication to HRT.

questions.q: Which lipid abnormality is an absolute contraindication to HRT?
questions.why: Hypertriglyceridemia is an absolute contraindication to HRT.

questions.q: HRT is contraindicated in women with:
questions.why: Severe uncontrolled hypertension is a contraindication to HRT.

units.title: Practical Points & E+P HRT with Absent Uterus

questions.q: Standard HRT does not provide:
questions.why: Standard HRT does not provide any contraceptive benefit.

questions.q: In perimenopausal women with hot flushes who also need contraception, which combination provides contraceptive benefit?
questions.why: Estrogen combined with the Mirena (levonorgestrel IUS) provides contraceptive benefit in perimenopausal women with hot flushes.

questions.q: Even in women with an absent uterus, E+P HRT (rather than estrogen-only) is indicated if there is a history of hysterectomy due to:
questions.why: A history of hysterectomy due to endometrial cancer is an indication for E+P HRT even with an absent uterus.

questions.q: E+P HRT is also indicated (despite an absent uterus) in women with a history of:
questions.why: A history of endometriosis is an indication for E+P HRT even with an absent uterus, since endometriotic implants can still respond to unopposed estrogen.

questions.q: Another indication for E+P HRT with an absent uterus is a history of:
questions.why: A history of endometrioid tumor of the ovary is an indication for E+P HRT even with an absent uterus.

questions.q: E+P HRT (despite the uterus being technically absent) is also used after:
options: Total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy for benign disease
questions.why: After supracervical/subtotal hysterectomy, residual endometrial tissue may remain, so E+P HRT is used.

questions.q: In intrauterine life, adrenal androgens are converted to estrogen via which enzyme?
questions.why: Adrenal androgens are converted to estrogen via aromatase in intrauterine life.

questions.q: At puberty, androgens in females are produced by the ovary (theca interna cells) and:
questions.why: At puberty, androgens are produced by the ovarian theca interna cells and the adrenal glands.

questions.q: Androgens produced by the ovary include androstenedione, testosterone, and:
questions.why: The ovary produces androstenedione, testosterone, and DHEA.

questions.q: Which androgen is produced exclusively by the adrenal glands (not the ovary)?
questions.why: DHEA-Sulphate is produced exclusively by the adrenal glands, unlike androstenedione, testosterone, and DHEA, which the ovary also produces.

questions.q: Testosterone is converted to the more potent DHT by which enzyme?
questions.why: Testosterone is converted to dihydrotestosterone (DHT) by 5α-reductase.

questions.q: A key feature distinguishing androgen metabolism in females is that:
options: Females cannot produce testosterone at all
questions.why: 5α-reductase is absent in females, so testosterone is not converted to DHT as it is in males.

questions.q: The normal level of androgen (testosterone) in females is:
questions.why: The normal androgen (testosterone) level in females is < 70 ng/dL.

questions.q: Androgens are classified structurally as:
questions.why: Androgens are C19 steroids.

questions.q: Androgen receptors are located in the cytoplasm and act on:
questions.why: Androgen receptors are intracytoplasmic and act on intranuclear receptors.

questions.q: Circulating androgens bind predominantly to which protein, more than albumin?
questions.why: Androgens bind predominantly to SHBG, more than to albumin.

questions.q: Androgens have which effect on SHBG levels, in contrast to estrogen?
options: Both androgens and estrogen increase SHBG
Androgens decrease SHBG, while estrogen increases it
Both androgens and estrogen decrease SHBG
Androgens increase SHBG, while estrogen decreases it
questions.why: Androgens decrease SHBG, while estrogen increases SHBG.

questions.q: Functions of androgens in females include pubarche (growth of pubic and axillary hair) and:
questions.why: Androgens contribute to pubarche and increased libido in females.

questions.q: Androgen produced in the theca cell is converted to estrogen in the granulosa cell via:
questions.why: Theca cell androgen is converted to estrogen in the granulosa cell via aromatase.

questions.q: Estrogen produced in the granulosa cell promotes:
questions.why: Granulosa cell estrogen promotes growth of follicles.

questions.q: Excessive androgen within granulosa cells has which effect?
questions.why: Excessive androgen in granulosa cells is folliculotoxic.

questions.q: Excess androgen arrests follicular growth, inhibiting maturation into:
questions.why: Excess androgen arrests growth and inhibits maturation into Graafian follicles, leading to anovulation.

questions.q: Besides anovulation, excessive androgens in females can cause hirsutism and:
questions.why: Excessive androgens can cause anovulation, hirsutism, and virilization.

questions.q: Hirsutism is defined as growth of thick, coarse, terminal hair in a male pattern, commonly at the lips, chin, chest, and:
questions.why: Common sites of hirsutism include lips, chin, periareolar area, and chest.

questions.q: Virilization is defined as:
options: A female acquiring male secondary sexual characteristics
questions.why: Virilization is defined as a female acquiring male secondary sexual characteristics.

questions.q: Features of hirsutism (without virilization) include scarring acne and:
questions.why: Hirsutism features include alopecia (male pattern baldness) and scarring acne.

questions.q: Features specific to virilization (beyond hirsutism itself) include deepening of voice, breast atrophy, increased muscle mass, and:
questions.why: Virilization features include hirsutism, deepening of voice, breast atrophy, increased muscle mass, and clitoromegaly.

questions.q: Clitoromegaly, a feature of virilization, is defined as clitoral size:
questions.why: Clitoromegaly is defined as clitoral size ≥ 1 cm.

questions.q: Compared to hirsutism, virilization reflects:
options: A milder degree of the same testosterone elevation as hirsutism
questions.why: Virilization reflects markedly increased testosterone, compared to only mildly increased levels in hirsutism.

questions.q: Conditions associated with hirsutism (not virilization) include PCOS, idiopathic hirsutism, and:
options: Some cases of late-onset congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH)
questions.why: Hirsutism is associated with PCOS, idiopathic hirsutism, and some cases of late-onset CAH.

questions.q: In idiopathic hirsutism, androgen levels are:
questions.why: In idiopathic hirsutism, androgen levels are normal.

questions.q: Conditions associated with virilization include androgen-producing ovarian tumor and:
questions.why: Virilization is associated with androgen-producing ovarian tumor and most cases of CAH.

questions.q: The scoring system used for hirsutism is the modified Ferriman-Gallwey score, which assesses:
questions.why: The modified Ferriman-Gallwey score assesses 9 sites, each scored 0–4.

questions.q: A modified Ferriman-Gallwey score of what value or above is diagnostic of hirsutism?
questions.why: A modified Ferriman-Gallwey score ≥ 8 is diagnostic of hirsutism.

questions.q: The scoring system used specifically for virilization is the:
questions.why: Virilization is scored using the Prader score, distinct from the Ferriman-Gallwey score used for hirsutism.

questions.q: A serum testosterone level under 70 ng/dL indicates:
questions.why: A serum testosterone < 70 ng/dL indicates normal androgen levels, as in idiopathic hirsutism.

questions.q: A serum testosterone level of 70–200 ng/dL (mildly elevated) is seen in PCOS and:
questions.why: A mildly elevated testosterone (70–200 ng/dL) is seen in PCOS and some cases of late-onset CAH.

questions.q: A serum testosterone level above 200 ng/dL suggests an androgen-secreting ovarian tumor or CAH, associated with:
questions.why: Testosterone > 200 ng/dL suggests an androgen-secreting ovarian tumor or CAH, with associated virilization.

questions.q: The most common cause of hirsutism in a young female is:
questions.why: PCOS is the most common cause of hirsutism in a young female.

questions.q: The most common cause of rapid-onset hirsutism in a young female is:
questions.why: An androgen-secreting ovarian tumor is the most common cause of rapid-onset hirsutism in a young female.

questions.q: To differentiate PCOS from late-onset CAH, the screening test used is:
questions.why: 17-OH progesterone level is used to screen for CAH and differentiate it from PCOS.

questions.q: A 17-OH progesterone level below 200 ng effectively:
questions.why: A 17-OH progesterone level < 200 ng rules out CAH.

questions.q: A 17-OH progesterone level between 200–800 ng, suspicious for CAH, is confirmed by:
questions.why: A 17-OH progesterone level of 200–800 ng is suspicious for CAH and confirmed by ACTH stimulation test.

questions.q: A 17-OH progesterone level above 800 ng:
questions.why: A 17-OH progesterone level > 800 ng confirms CAH.

questions.q: The drug of choice for management of hirsutism is:
questions.why: OCPs (low-dose pills with 3rd/4th generation progesterone) are the drug of choice for hirsutism.

questions.q: The typical duration of OCP therapy for hirsutism before reassessment is:
questions.why: OCP therapy for hirsutism is typically given for 6 months before reassessment.

questions.q: One mechanism of OCPs in hirsutism is estrogen + progesterone suppressing LH and FSH, thereby reducing:
questions.why: Estrogen + progesterone suppress LH and FSH, reducing androgen production.

questions.q: A second mechanism of OCPs in hirsutism is estrogen increasing SHBG, which in turn:
questions.why: Estrogen increases SHBG, which decreases free (bioavailable) testosterone.

questions.q: If OCPs fail to control hirsutism, the next drug added is:
questions.why: If OCPs fail, spironolactone is added.

units.title: Second-line Drugs, Contraindicated Drug & Other Modalities

questions.q: Spironolactone, used as add-on therapy for hirsutism, works by which mechanism?
questions.why: Spironolactone works via an anti-androgenic mechanism.

questions.q: Spironolactone is contraindicated in pregnancy because it can cause:
options: Ambiguous genitalia in a male fetus
questions.why: Spironolactone is contraindicated in pregnancy as it can cause ambiguous genitalia in a male fetus.

questions.q: Other drugs used in the management of hirsutism include cyproterone acetate, flutamide, finasteride, and:
questions.why: Other drugs used for hirsutism include cyproterone acetate, flutamide, finasteride, and ketoconazole.

questions.q: Among adjunct drugs for hirsutism, which is described as only slightly effective?
questions.why: Metformin is noted as only slightly effective for hirsutism.

questions.q: Eflornithine, used in hirsutism management, is administered as a:
questions.why: Eflornithine is a topical drug used in hirsutism management.

questions.q: The last resort in refractory hirsutism management is continuous GnRH therapy, which works by:
options: ↓FSH only, with no effect on LH
questions.why: Continuous GnRH therapy (last resort) works by decreasing LH, which decreases androgen production.

questions.q: Which drug is specifically contraindicated in hirsutism because it can itself cause hirsutism as a side effect?
questions.why: Danazol is contraindicated as it can itself cause hirsutism as a side effect.

questions.q: Besides pharmacological therapy, an additional modality used for hirsutism management is:
questions.why: Laser hair removal is an additional (non-pharmacological) modality for hirsutism management.

questions.q: PCOS is best characterized as:
options: A single uniform disease with one defined cause
A group of symptoms with various presentations and different underlying pathophysiology
A purely genetic disorder with no environmental influence
A disease exclusive to obese women
questions.why: PCOS is a group of symptoms with various presentations and different underlying pathophysiology.

questions.q: The older/previous term for PCOS was:
questions.why: PCOS was previously termed Stein-Leventhal syndrome.

questions.q: Etiological factors in PCOS include environmental factors, lifestyle factors, and:
questions.why: Genetic factors (a complex genetic trait), along with environmental and lifestyle factors, contribute to PCOS.

questions.q: Genetic factors implicated in PCOS as a complex genetic trait involve chromosome 2 and:
questions.why: Chromosomes 2 and 9 are implicated as complex genetic traits in PCOS.

questions.q: The etiological factors of PCOS lead to excessive androgen production, defective folliculogenesis, insulin resistance, obesity, and:
options: Defect in gonadotropin secretion and action
questions.why: These factors lead to excess androgen production, defective folliculogenesis, insulin resistance, defective gonadotropin secretion/action, and obesity.

questions.q: In PCOS, the main source of excessive androgen production is:
questions.why: The ovaries are the main source of excessive androgen production in PCOS.

questions.q: In PCOS, the adrenal glands make only a minor contribution to androgen excess, reflected by an increase in:
questions.why: The adrenal glands contribute a minor amount to androgen excess in PCOS, reflected by increased DHEA-S.

questions.q: In PCOS, serum androgen (testosterone) levels are typically:
questions.why: PCOS androgen levels are typically ≥ 70 ng/dL but < 200 ng/dL.

questions.q: This degree of androgen elevation in PCOS (70–200 ng/dL) clinically leads to:
questions.why: This mild-to-moderate androgen elevation in PCOS leads to hirsutism (not virilization, which needs markedly higher levels).

questions.q: Folliculotoxicity of androgens in PCOS arrests follicular growth, preventing maturation into:
questions.why: Folliculotoxic androgens arrest follicular growth, preventing maturation into Graafian follicles.

questions.q: Complications of the androgen excess/dyslipidemia pathway in PCOS include increased risk of:
questions.why: PCOS pathophysiology contributes to dyslipidemia and increased risk of coronary heart disease.

questions.q: The dyslipidemia pattern associated with PCOS pathophysiology includes:
questions.why: PCOS-associated dyslipidemia shows ↑LDL and ↓HDL.

questions.q: On ultrasound, PCOS shows small unruptured follicles (not true cysts) arranged along the ovarian periphery, giving a:
questions.why: The peripherally arranged small follicles create a classic necklace appearance on USG.

questions.q: Per the Rotterdam criteria, the number of follicles required per ovary to define polycystic morphology is:
questions.why: The Rotterdam criteria require ≥ 12 follicles per ovary.

questions.q: The Rotterdam criteria specify a follicle size of:
questions.why: Follicles are 2–9 mm in size per the Rotterdam criteria.

questions.q: Per the Rotterdam criteria, polycystic morphology can also be defined by ovarian volume of:
questions.why: Ovarian volume ≥ 10 cc also satisfies the polycystic morphology criterion.

questions.q: The American and European Societies use a stricter follicle count criterion of:
questions.why: The American and European Societies use a stricter cutoff of ≥ 20 follicles, 2–9 mm size.

questions.q: Anovulation in PCOS directly causes:
questions.why: Anovulation is a direct cause of infertility in PCOS.

questions.q: Anovulation means no corpus luteum forms, resulting in:
questions.why: Without a corpus luteum, progesterone is decreased.

questions.q: Due to low progesterone from anovulation, PCOS patients classically present with secondary amenorrhea or:
questions.why: Secondary amenorrhea or oligomenorrhea (< 9 cycles/year) are classic presentations.

questions.q: If pregnancy does occur in a woman with PCOS, low progesterone increases the risk of:
questions.why: Low progesterone in PCOS increases the risk of abortion during pregnancy.

questions.q: Oligomenorrhea in PCOS is defined as fewer than how many cycles per year?
questions.why: Oligomenorrhea is defined as fewer than 9 cycles per year.

questions.q: Anovulation in PCOS occurs due to folliculotoxicity of androgens and:
questions.why: Anovulation results from both folliculotoxic androgens and absence of the LH surge.

questions.q: Lab findings in PCOS include increased serum testosterone, increased DHEA-S, and a lipid pattern of:
questions.why: PCOS lab findings show ↑LDL and ↓HDL, alongside increased testosterone and DHEA-S.

questions.q: Progesterone levels in PCOS lab findings are typically:
questions.why: Progesterone is decreased in PCOS due to anovulation.

questions.q: AMH levels in PCOS are typically:
questions.why: AMH is increased in PCOS, reflecting increased small antral follicles.

questions.q: An AMH level of what value or above supports the diagnosis of PCOS (reflecting increased small follicles)?
questions.why: An AMH ≥ 7.3 ng/mL supports the diagnosis, reflecting the increased number of small follicles.

questions.q: The elevated AMH in PCOS reflects:
options: An increased number of small follicles
A decreased number of small follicles
questions.why: Elevated AMH reflects the increased number of small antral follicles characteristic of PCOS.

questions.q: Insulin resistance in PCOS contributes to dyslipidemia and leads to:
questions.why: Insulin resistance contributes to dyslipidemia and leads to theca cell hyperplasia.

questions.q: Theca cell hyperplasia from insulin resistance causes oversensitivity to LH stimulation, due to loss of the normal:
questions.why: Loss of the normal cut-off (threshold) causes theca cell oversensitivity to LH stimulation.

questions.q: The end result of theca cell oversensitivity to LH is:
questions.why: Theca cell oversensitivity to LH results in increased androgen production.

questions.q: Insulin resistance in PCOS is:
options: Directly proportional to BMI in all cases
questions.why: Insulin resistance in PCOS is independent of obesity — it occurs in both obese and non-obese patients.

questions.q: Among PCOS patients, approximately what proportion are obese versus not obese?
questions.why: Approximately 70% of PCOS patients are obese and 30% are not obese.

questions.q: In all patients diagnosed with PCOS, OGTT (oral glucose tolerance test) should be performed every:
questions.why: All PCOS patients should have OGTT performed every 2 years.

questions.q: If insulin resistance is confirmed (positive) in a PCOS patient, OGTT should be repeated every:
questions.why: If insulin resistance is present, OGTT is repeated yearly instead of every 2 years.

questions.q: Acanthosis nigricans is a clinical manifestation of:
questions.why: Acanthosis nigricans is a clinical manifestation of insulin resistance.

questions.q: Acanthosis nigricans presents with skin that is:
questions.why: Acanthosis nigricans presents as dark, velvety, and thick skin.

questions.q: Common sites for acanthosis nigricans include the nape of the neck, axillary region, groin, and:
questions.why: Common sites include the nape of the neck, axillary region, groin, and under the breast tissue.

questions.q: The HAIRAN syndrome mnemonic in PCOS stands for hyperandrogenism, insulin resistance, and:
questions.why: HAIRAN stands for Hyper-Androgenism, Insulin Resistance, and Acanthosis Nigricans.

questions.q: HAIRAN syndrome is best understood as a triad reflecting:
options: The interconnection of hyperandrogenism, insulin resistance, and its skin manifestation
A distinct disease separate from PCOS
A diagnostic criterion of the Rotterdam criteria
questions.why: HAIRAN reflects the interconnected pathophysiology of hyperandrogenism, insulin resistance, and its cutaneous manifestation (acanthosis nigricans).

questions.q: Obesity is present in what proportion of PCOS patients?
questions.why: Obesity is present in 40–80% of PCOS patients.

questions.q: Obesity is:
options: Not a defining feature of PCOS; PCOS can occur in thin individuals
A mandatory diagnostic criterion for PCOS
The primary cause of PCOS in all cases
questions.why: Obesity is not a defining feature of PCOS — PCOS can occur in thin individuals too.

questions.q: In adipose tissue, androgens are converted to estrogen via aromatase, leading to increased levels of:
questions.why: Adipose tissue aromatization of androgens leads to increased estrone (E1).

questions.q: This increase in estrone in obese PCOS patients causes estrogen breakthrough bleeding, presenting as:
questions.why: Increased estrone causes estrogen breakthrough bleeding, presenting as menometrorrhagia.

questions.q: The normal E2:E1 ratio is 2:1, but in an obese PCOS female this ratio shifts to approximately:
questions.why: In an obese PCOS female, the E2:E1 ratio shifts to approximately 1:2 (favouring E1).

questions.q: A thin PCOS patient, with normal estrogen levels, most commonly presents with:
questions.why: A thin PCOS patient with normal estrogen levels most commonly presents with secondary amenorrhea.

questions.q: An obese PCOS patient, with increased estrone, may present with secondary amenorrhea or:
questions.why: An obese PCOS patient may present with secondary amenorrhea or menometrorrhagia (due to increased E1).

questions.q: In PCOS, the underlying gonadotropin defect begins with an increased pulse frequency of:
questions.why: The gonadotropin defect in PCOS begins with an increased pulse frequency of GnRH.

questions.q: Increased GnRH pulse frequency in PCOS leads to increased secretion of which pituitary hormone?
questions.why: Increased GnRH pulse frequency leads to increased LH secretion by the pituitary.

questions.q: Persistently elevated LH throughout the cycle in PCOS results in:
questions.why: Persistently elevated LH results in absence of the normal mid-cycle LH surge.

questions.q: In PCOS, the typical FSH:LH ratio is:
questions.why: The typical FSH:LH ratio in PCOS is 1:2 or 1:3 (versus normal 1:1).

questions.q: In PCOS, FSH is typically normal while LH is:
questions.why: FSH remains normal while LH is increased in PCOS.

questions.q: The best time in the menstrual cycle to evaluate LH and FSH levels is:
options: Any day — timing does not matter
questions.why: Day 2/day 3 of the cycle is the best time to evaluate LH and FSH.

questions.q: In PCOS, which of the following hormones is typically increased?
questions.why: Serum testosterone is increased in PCOS, while FSH, prolactin, and TSH remain unchanged.

questions.q: Along with testosterone, PCOS shows increased levels of DHEA-S, LDL, AMH, LH, and (in obese females):
questions.why: In obese PCOS females, estrone (E1) is also increased, along with testosterone, DHEA-S, LDL, AMH, and LH.

questions.q: Which set of hormone levels remain unchanged in PCOS?
questions.why: FSH, estradiol (E2), prolactin, and TSH remain unchanged in PCOS.

questions.q: Which of the following is decreased in PCOS?
questions.why: HDL, serum progesterone, and SHBG are all decreased in PCOS.

questions.q: The decrease in SHBG seen in PCOS is due to the effect of:
questions.why: Decreased SHBG in PCOS is due to the combined effect of androgens and insulin.

questions.q: Given this hormonal profile, PCOS is best characterized by an elevated:
options: Both LH and FSH equally elevated
questions.why: PCOS is characterized by elevated LH with normal FSH, giving the classic increased LH:FSH ratio.

questions.q: The Rotterdam criteria for PCOS diagnosis include hyperandrogenism, ovulatory dysfunction, and:
options: Polycystic appearance of ovaries on USG
questions.why: The three Rotterdam criteria are hyperandrogenism, ovulatory dysfunction, and polycystic ovarian appearance on USG.

questions.q: Hyperandrogenism in the Rotterdam criteria can be defined biochemically (elevated serum testosterone) or:
questions.why: Hyperandrogenism can be defined biochemically or clinically (hirsutism).

questions.q: Ovulatory dysfunction in the Rotterdam criteria manifests as:
questions.why: Ovulatory dysfunction manifests as secondary amenorrhea or oligomenorrhea.

questions.q: How many of the three Rotterdam criteria must be present for a provisional diagnosis of PCOS?
questions.why: Any 2 of the 3 Rotterdam criteria give a provisional diagnosis of PCOS.

questions.q: After a provisional diagnosis of PCOS (2 Rotterdam criteria positive), the essential next step is to check:
options: 17-OH progesterone levels, to rule out late-onset CAH
questions.why: 17-OH progesterone levels are checked next, to rule out late-onset CAH before confirming PCOS.

questions.q: A 17-OH progesterone level below 200 ng in this workup:
questions.why: A 17-OH progesterone level < 200 ng rules out CAH.

questions.q: A 17-OH progesterone level above 800 ng in this workup:
questions.why: A 17-OH progesterone level > 800 ng confirms late-onset CAH.

questions.q: Which of the following is explicitly NOT a diagnostic criterion for PCOS?
questions.why: Obesity is explicitly excluded from the diagnostic criteria for PCOS.

questions.q: The LH:FSH ratio, though classically associated with PCOS, is:
questions.why: The LH:FSH ratio, despite its classic association, is not a diagnostic criterion for PCOS.

questions.q: Which of these is also NOT a diagnostic criterion for PCOS?
questions.why: Insulin resistance, though central to PCOS pathophysiology, is not a diagnostic criterion.

questions.q: Which of the following, though a common clinical feature of PCOS, is NOT part of the diagnostic criteria?
questions.why: Menometrorrhagia, a common clinical feature, is not part of the diagnostic criteria.

questions.q: The "necklace appearance" seen on USG in PCOS is:
options: Not itself a separate diagnostic criterion, but included within polycystic appearance
Diagnostic on its own without follicle counting
Only seen in POI, not PCOS
questions.why: The necklace appearance is included within the polycystic appearance criterion, not a separate criterion.

units.title: Workup of PCOS with Secondary Amenorrhea

questions.q: In the workup of PCOS with secondary amenorrhea, the urine pregnancy test (UPT) is typically:
questions.why: UPT is typically negative in this workup, ruling out pregnancy as the cause of amenorrhea.

questions.q: In this workup, LH is typically:
questions.why: LH is typically increased in this workup.

questions.q: In this workup, FSH is typically:
questions.why: FSH is typically normal in this workup.

questions.q: TSH is checked and expected to be normal, because thyroid dysfunction causing amenorrhea would act via:
questions.why: Thyroid dysfunction causes amenorrhea via negative feedback on GnRH, so TSH is checked to exclude this.

questions.q: Serum prolactin is checked and expected to be normal, because hyperprolactinemia causing amenorrhea would act via:
questions.why: Hyperprolactinemia causes amenorrhea via negative feedback on GnRH, so prolactin is checked to exclude this.

questions.q: In additional workup, a progesterone challenge test is performed by giving progesterone for 5 days and stopping; a positive test shows:
questions.why: A positive progesterone challenge test shows withdrawal bleeding after stopping the 5-day course.

questions.q: A positive progesterone challenge test with increased LH, normal FSH, and secondary amenorrhea suggests:
questions.why: This combination (positive test, ↑LH, normal FSH, secondary amenorrhea) suggests PCOS.

questions.q: A positive progesterone challenge test with increased LH, normal FSH, but primary amenorrhea instead suggests:
questions.why: The same hormonal pattern but with primary (not secondary) amenorrhea suggests androgen insensitivity syndrome.

questions.q: Comparing PCOS to primary ovarian insufficiency (POI), both ovarian causes of secondary amenorrhea, the number of follicles is:
options: Increased in PCOS, decreased in POI
Decreased in PCOS, increased in POI
questions.why: Follicle number is increased in PCOS but decreased in POI.

questions.q: FSH levels differ between PCOS and POI as follows:
options: Increased in PCOS, normal in POI
Normal in PCOS, increased in POI
questions.why: FSH is normal in PCOS but increased in POI.

questions.q: LH levels in PCOS versus POI are:
questions.why: LH is increased in both PCOS and POI, though the mechanisms differ.

questions.q: Estrogen levels differ as follows:
options: Increased in PCOS, decreased in POI
Normal/decreased in PCOS, decreased in POI
Decreased in PCOS, increased in POI
questions.why: Estrogen is normal or decreased in PCOS, but decreased in POI.

questions.q: AMH levels differ as follows:
options: Increased in PCOS, decreased in POI
Decreased in PCOS, increased in POI
questions.why: AMH is increased in PCOS (reflecting excess small follicles) but decreased in POI (reflecting depleted reserve).

questions.q: The associated symptom typically seen with PCOS is hirsutism, whereas with POI it is:
questions.why: PCOS is associated with hirsutism, while POI is associated with hot flashes/osteoporosis (menopausal-type symptoms).

questions.q: Short-term complications of PCOS include menstrual irregularities, hirsutism, alopecia, infertility, and:
questions.why: Insulin resistance is a short-term complication, along with menstrual irregularities, hirsutism, alopecia, and infertility.

questions.q: Long-term consequences of PCOS include dyslipidemia, diabetes, and:
questions.why: Coronary artery disease is a long-term consequence, along with dyslipidemia and diabetes.

questions.q: Due to increased estrogen in obese PCOS females, long-term risks include endometrial cancer, NASH, and:
questions.why: Increased estrogen in obese PCOS females raises risk of endometrial cancer, NASH, and variably ovarian cancer.

questions.q: Due to obesity, long-term consequences of PCOS include sleep apnea syndrome and:
questions.why: Obesity-related consequences include sleep apnea syndrome and anxiety/depression.

questions.q: PCOS is also associated with a cluster of cardiometabolic abnormalities known as:
questions.why: PCOS is associated with metabolic X (metabolic) syndrome.

questions.q: Obstetric complications of PCOS include infertility (which is reversible) and abortion, the latter due to:
questions.why: Decreased progesterone in PCOS contributes to increased abortion risk during pregnancy.

questions.q: Due to underlying insulin resistance, pregnant PCOS patients are at increased risk of:
questions.why: Insulin resistance in PCOS increases the risk of gestational diabetes during pregnancy.

questions.q: Obstetric complications of PCOS also include pregnancy-induced hypertension (PIH) and:
questions.why: PIH and stillbirth are recognised obstetric complications of PCOS.

questions.q: In a patient presenting with hirsutism, acne, and irregular cycles, the appropriate next investigation is:
questions.why: Serum testosterone levels are the appropriate next step in a patient with hirsutism, acne, and irregular cycles.

questions.q: In a confirmed case of PCOS, baseline workup includes lipid profile, OGTT, and ultrasound to assess:
questions.why: Baseline workup in confirmed PCOS includes lipid profile, OGTT, and USG to assess endometrial thickness.

questions.q: In a reproductive-age PCOS patient, an endometrial thickness of what value or greater is an indication for endometrial biopsy?
questions.why: An endometrial thickness ≥ 12 mm in a reproductive-age PCOS patient is an indication for endometrial biopsy.

questions.q: Full-blown/classical PCOS (Phenotype A) is defined as a case where:
options: Only 1 of the 3 Rotterdam criteria is positive
Only 2 of the 3 Rotterdam criteria are positive
No Rotterdam criteria are met, but symptoms are present
questions.why: Phenotype A (full-blown/classical PCOS) is defined by all 3 Rotterdam criteria being positive.

questions.q: The 3 Rotterdam criteria that are all positive in classical PCOS (Phenotype A) are high testosterone levels, ovulatory dysfunction, and:
options: Polycystic appearance of ovary on USG
questions.why: The third criterion is a polycystic appearance of the ovary on ultrasound, along with high testosterone and ovulatory dysfunction.

questions.q: Management of PCOS is fundamentally based on:
options: The primary presenting feature of the patient
questions.why: PCOS management is tailored to the patient\u2019s primary presenting feature (menstrual irregularity, infertility, hirsutism, or insulin resistance).

questions.q: The four primary presenting features that guide PCOS management are menstrual irregularity (most common), infertility, hirsutism, and:
questions.why: The four presenting features guiding management are menstrual irregularity (m/c), infertility, hirsutism, and insulin resistance.

questions.q: The FIRST line management for PCOS, regardless of presenting complaint, is:
questions.why: Lifestyle modification and weight loss is the universal first-line management step in PCOS.

questions.q: Lifestyle modification and weight loss alone leads to spontaneous ovulation in what proportion of PCOS cases?
questions.why: Lifestyle modification and weight loss alone leads to spontaneous ovulation in 5\u201310% of cases.

questions.q: In all cases of PCOS, which condition must specifically be ruled out?
questions.why: Hyperprolactinemia must be ruled out in all cases of PCOS.

questions.q: If prolactin is elevated in a PCOS workup, the proposed mechanism is that prolactin acts on the adrenal glands, leading to:
questions.why: Elevated prolactin acts on the adrenal glands to increase androgen production, a mechanism relevant to PCOS-like presentations.

questions.q: In pubertal/young females, irregular menstrual cycles due to anovulation may normally persist for up to:
questions.why: Irregular anovulatory cycles may persist for up to 3 years after menarche as a normal physiological phase.

questions.q: A normal cycle length in this context is defined as:
questions.why: A cycle length of 21\u201345 days is considered within the normal range.

questions.q: Evaluation for menstrual irregularity is indicated if cycle length is \u226590 days, OR if irregularity persists beyond:
questions.why: Evaluation is indicated for a cycle length \u226590 days, or if the irregularity continues beyond 3 years after menarche.

questions.q: The first-line management (drug of choice) for menstrual irregularity in PCOS is:
questions.why: Very low dose OCPs are the DOC for first-line management of menstrual irregularity in PCOS.

questions.q: In the very low dose OCPs used for PCOS menstrual irregularity, the ethinyl estradiol component is dosed at:
questions.why: Ethinyl estradiol is used at \u226420 mcg (very low dose) in this regimen.

questions.q: The progesterone component of the very low dose OCP used for PCOS menstrual irregularity is a:
options: 3rd/4th generation progesterone (e.g., MALA-D/MALA-N may be used)
questions.why: 3rd/4th generation progesterone is used (MALA-D/MALA-N may be used as options).

questions.q: OCPs (estrogen + progesterone) act in PCOS by suppressing LH and FSH, leading to ovarian suppression, which in turn causes anovulation, decreased androgens, and:
options: Decreased natural estrogen, leading to endometrial thinning
questions.why: Ovarian suppression from OCPs decreases natural estrogen, leading to endometrial thinning, alongside anovulation and decreased androgens.

questions.q: The standard OCP regimen duration is:
questions.why: The standard OCP regimen is 21 days (3 weeks on, 1 week off).

questions.q: Advantages of OCPs in PCOS include regularising cycles, treatment of hirsutism, contraceptive benefit, and:
questions.why: OCPs protect against endometrial cancer, in addition to regularising cycles, treating hirsutism, and providing contraception.

questions.q: In PCOS-related hirsutism, OCPs act partly by decreasing LH/FSH (hence decreasing androgens), and partly through estrogen increasing:
questions.why: OCP-derived estrogen increases SHBG, which binds testosterone and decreases the free (active) testosterone fraction.

questions.q: Per this chapter\u2019s summary note, the overall drug of choice for PCOS is:
questions.why: OCPs are noted as the overall DOC for PCOS.

questions.q: As a 2nd line/alternative to OCPs for menstrual irregularity, progesterone is given cyclically every 12-14 days in the:
options: Only on day 1 of the cycle
questions.why: Cyclical progesterone is given every 12\u201314 days in the 2nd half of the cycle.

questions.q: The specific progesterone used in this regimen is medroxyprogesterone acetate (MPA), dosed at:
questions.why: MPA is dosed at 10\u201320 mg for 5 days in this regimen, facilitating withdrawal bleeding.

questions.q: Advantages of cyclical progesterone therapy include regularising cycles and a protective effect on the endometrium, specifically:
options: Decreased risk of hyperplasia and cancer, with a minimum duration of 12 days
questions.why: Progesterone protects the endometrium (decreasing hyperplasia/cancer risk) when given for a minimum duration of 12 days.

questions.q: Disadvantages of the progesterone-only regimen (compared to OCPs) include that it does not regularise cycles as reliably, and it provides no protective effect on the endometrium if given for:
questions.why: If given for less than 12 days, progesterone provides no protective effect on the endometrium.

questions.q: The very first step in managing infertility in PCOS is:
options: Advice weight loss, followed by a trial of natural conception with folic acid supplementation
questions.why: The first step is advising weight loss, followed by a trial of natural conception with folic acid supplementation.

questions.q: The 1st line management for PCOS infertility (after the initial step) is:
questions.why: Pharmacological therapy with ovulation-inducing drugs is the 1st line management for PCOS infertility.

questions.q: Among 1st line ovulation-inducing drugs, the overall drug of choice is letrozole, while the 2nd drug of choice is:
questions.why: Letrozole is the DOC, with clomiphene citrate (CC) as the 2nd DOC among 1st line ovulation-inducing drugs.

questions.q: 2nd line drugs for PCOS infertility include CC+metformin, CC+dexamethasone, OCPs followed by CC, HMG, and:
questions.why: Recombinant gonadotropins round out the list of 2nd line drugs, alongside CC+metformin, CC+dexamethasone, OCPs f/b CC, and HMG.

questions.q: The 2nd line MANAGEMENT (procedure, not drug) for PCOS infertility is:
questions.why: Laparoscopic ovarian drilling is the 2nd line management approach (as a procedure) for PCOS infertility.

questions.q: The 3rd line management for PCOS infertility is pulsatile GnRH or:
questions.why: IVF is the 3rd line management option, alongside pulsatile GnRH.

questions.q: Clomiphene citrate (CC) belongs to which drug class?
questions.why: Clomiphene citrate is a SERM (Selective Estrogen Receptor Modulator).

questions.q: Clomiphene citrate is a non-steroidal drug that is:
options: Centrally acting, anti-estrogenic, causing ovulation induction
Peripherally acting only, with no central effect
questions.why: CC is a non-steroidal, centrally acting anti-estrogenic drug that causes ovulation induction.

questions.q: CC's central mechanism of action involves blocking estrogen receptors in the hypothalamus and pituitary because:
options: CC's half-life is longer than estrogen's (T1/2 CC > T1/2 E)
CC\u2019s half-life is shorter than estrogen\u2019s
CC has no relation to estrogen half-life
questions.why: Because CC\u2019s half-life exceeds that of estrogen, it occupies estrogen receptors longer, sustaining the false low-estrogen signal.

questions.q: By blocking hypothalamic/pituitary estrogen receptors, CC causes the pituitary to falsely interpret this as low estrogen, leading to:
questions.why: The false low-estrogen signal leads to increased LH and FSH release.

questions.q: The rise in LH and FSH from CC\u2019s central action results in:
options: Maturation of multiple follicles and ovulation
questions.why: Increased LH and FSH drive maturation of multiple follicles and ovulation.

questions.q: CC's PERIPHERAL action involves binding to peripheral estrogen receptors in the endometrium and cervix, resulting in endometrial thinning and:
questions.why: Peripheral anti-estrogenic action produces endometrial thinning and thick cervical mucus.

questions.q: The endometrial thinning and thick cervical mucus from CC's peripheral action together make the environment:
options: Favourable only for implantation, not fertilization
questions.why: CC's peripheral anti-estrogenic effects make the endometrium and cervix unfavourable for achieving pregnancy, despite inducing ovulation centrally.

questions.q: With CC, the reported rate of ovulation is about 80%, while the pregnancy rate is only about:
questions.why: Despite an 80% ovulation rate, the pregnancy rate with CC is only about 5\u201310%, reflecting its peripheral anti-estrogenic effects on endometrium/cervix.

units.title: Clomiphene Citrate: Prerequisites, Dosing & Adverse Effects

questions.q: The prerequisites for using clomiphene citrate are an intact HPO axis and:
questions.why: An intact HPO axis and normal FSH levels are the two prerequisites for CC use.

questions.q: The two components of clomiphene citrate are zuclomiphene and:
options: Enclomiphene, which potentiates the anti-estrogenic action
questions.why: Enclomiphene (potentiating the anti-estrogenic action) and zuclomiphene are the two components of CC.

questions.q: The half-life (T1/2) of clomiphene citrate is approximately:
questions.why: CC has a half-life of about 2 weeks.

questions.q: The starting and maximum doses of clomiphene citrate are:
options: 2.5 mg OD starting, up to 7.5 mg OD maximum
500 mg OD starting, up to 1000 mg OD maximum
50 mg OD starting, up to 150 mg OD maximum
5 mg OD starting, up to 20 mg OD maximum
questions.why: CC is started at 50 mg OD and can be increased up to a maximum of 150 mg OD.

questions.q: Clomiphene citrate is administered for 5 days, specifically on cycle days:
questions.why: CC is given for 5 days, on cycle days 5\u20139.

questions.q: Follicular monitoring with CC begins from day 10 onwards, via TVS, performed:
questions.why: Follicular monitoring is done daily or on alternate days via TVS starting day 10.

questions.q: When follicles reach a size of 18-20 mm on CC, ovulation occurs naturally OR is triggered with:
questions.why: At 18\u201320 mm follicle size, natural ovulation may occur, or hCG (acting like LH) is given as a trigger.

questions.q: After the hCG trigger injection with CC, ovulation occurs after:
questions.why: Ovulation occurs 32\u201336 hours after the hCG trigger injection.

questions.q: After ovulation with CC (natural or triggered), the next step in management is typically:
questions.why: Intrauterine insemination (IUI) commonly follows ovulation in the CC protocol.

questions.q: The most common adverse effect of clomiphene citrate is:
options: Hot flushes, due to decreased estrogen
questions.why: Hot flushes (due to decreased estrogen effect) are the most common adverse effect of CC.

questions.q: The second most common adverse effect of clomiphene citrate is:
options: Ovarian cysts, due to increased LH and FSH
questions.why: Ovarian cysts (due to increased LH and FSH) are the second most common adverse effect.

questions.q: Besides hot flushes and ovarian cysts, other adverse effects of CC include headache, vaginal dryness, breast tenderness, and multiple pregnancies in what proportion of cases?
questions.why: Multiple pregnancies occur in about 7\u201310% of CC cycles.

questions.q: Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS) with clomiphene citrate is:
questions.why: OHSS is the least common adverse effect associated with CC use.

questions.q: Visual disturbances (diplopia, blurring of vision, scotoma) with clomiphene citrate are significant because they are:
options: An indication for immediate stoppage of the drug
Only seen with letrozole, not CC
Treated by increasing the CC dose
questions.why: Visual disturbances with CC are an indication for immediate stoppage of the drug.

questions.q: Advantages of clomiphene citrate over gonadotropin therapy include no risk of:
questions.why: CC carries no risk of teratogenicity or ectopic pregnancy, unlike some other therapies.

units.title: Clomiphene Citrate vs Letrozole: Detailed Comparison

questions.q: In the CC vs letrozole comparison, clomiphene citrate is categorised as a SERM, while letrozole is categorised as:
questions.why: Letrozole is an aromatase inhibitor, in contrast to CC, which is a SERM.

questions.q: Letrozole's peripheral mechanism of action works by blocking aromatization of androgen to estrogen, which decreases estrogen and causes:
options: Increased negative feedback, decreasing LH and FSH
Loss of negative feedback, increasing LH and FSH
questions.why: Reduced peripheral estrogen removes negative feedback, raising LH and FSH.

questions.q: Letrozole's starting and maximum doses are:
options: 50 mg OD starting, up to 150 mg OD maximum
2.5 mg OD starting, up to 7.5 mg OD maximum
500 mg OD starting, up to 1000 mg OD maximum
0.5 mg OD starting, up to 2 mg OD maximum
questions.why: Letrozole is started at 2.5 mg OD, up to a maximum of 7.5 mg OD.

questions.q: Letrozole's half-life, in contrast to CC's 2 weeks, is approximately:
questions.why: Letrozole's half-life is about 48 hours, much shorter than CC's 2 weeks.

questions.q: Regarding follicular development, CC typically produces multifollicular development, while letrozole produces:
options: Purely monofollicular development only, with no exceptions
questions.why: Letrozole produces monofollicular plus multifollicular development, differing from CC\u2019s purely multifollicular pattern.

questions.q: The risk of multiple pregnancies is lower with letrozole (3-7%) compared to CC, which carries a risk of:
questions.why: CC carries a 7\u201310% risk of multiple pregnancies, higher than letrozole\u2019s 3\u20137%.

questions.q: Regarding effect on endometrium and cervix, CC blocks estrogen receptors (thinning effect), while letrozole has:
options: No effect, hence increased chances of pregnancy
A thickening effect on the endometrium only
questions.why: Letrozole has no adverse effect on endometrium/cervix, hence better pregnancy chances compared to CC.

questions.q: Because letrozole doesn't have CC's adverse peripheral anti-estrogenic effects, its live birth rate is:
options: Markedly increased, making it the DOC
questions.why: Letrozole's live birth rate is markedly increased compared to CC, making it the drug of choice.

questions.q: Side effects of CC (hot flushes m/c, vaginal dryness) contrast with letrozole, which is:
options: Associated with more severe hot flushes
Never associated with any side effects
Well tolerated with no anti-estrogenic side effects, and rare headache
questions.why: Letrozole is well tolerated, without anti-estrogenic side effects, with headache being rare.

questions.q: Regarding teratogenicity, both CC and letrozole are reported as:
questions.why: Both drugs are reported as not teratogenic in this comparison.

questions.q: Regarding uses, CC is DOC for ovulation induction AND DOC for PCOS historically, while letrozole is specifically:
options: The DOC for PCOS (superseding CC for this indication)
Only used for infertility unrelated to PCOS
questions.why: Letrozole has become the DOC for PCOS, given its superior live birth rate and tolerability.

questions.q: The prerequisite shared by both CC and letrozole is:
options: Intact HPO axis and normal FSH level
questions.why: Both drugs require an intact HPO axis and normal FSH level as prerequisites.

questions.q: Contraindications shared by CC and letrozole include Sheehan syndrome, pituitary ablation, hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, and:
questions.why: Kallmann syndrome is a shared contraindication, along with Sheehan syndrome, pituitary ablation, and hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (all reflecting a non-intact HPO axis).

questions.q: CC combined with glucocorticoids (dexamethasone) is indicated in clomiphene-resistant PCOS with:
questions.why: CC + glucocorticoids is used in clomiphene-resistant PCOS specifically with raised androgen (DHEAS) levels.

questions.q: The principle behind CC + glucocorticoids is that glucocorticoids suppress the adrenal glands, leading to:
questions.why: Glucocorticoids suppress the adrenal glands, decreasing androgen output.

questions.q: CC combined with metformin is indicated in clomiphene-resistant PCOS with:
questions.why: CC + metformin is used specifically in clomiphene-resistant PCOS with insulin resistance.

questions.q: When OCPs are used with CC, the duration of OCP pretreatment is 2 months, followed by CC, working on the principle:
options: Increased LH leads to increased androgen
Decreased LH leads to decreased androgen
questions.why: OCPs are given for 2 months (decreasing LH and androgen) before starting CC.

questions.q: HMG (human menopausal gonadotropin) is sourced from:
questions.why: HMG is sourced from the urine of postmenopausal women.

questions.q: The composition of HMG is:
questions.why: HMG contains 75 IU LH + 75 IU FSH, along with impurities.

questions.q: HMG is indicated in hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (as the DOC for ovulation induction in that setting), as a 2nd line drug for PCOS, and in:
questions.why: HMG is used in hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (DOC there), as a 2nd line PCOS drug, and in all cases of IVF.

questions.q: Adverse effects of HMG include multiple pregnancies (15-30%), OHSS (5-15%), and:
questions.why: Increased risk of spontaneous abortion is an adverse effect of HMG, along with multiple pregnancies and OHSS.

questions.q: An advantage of HMG, despite its adverse effect profile, is:
questions.why: HMG carries no teratogenicity risk, despite its risks of multiple pregnancy and OHSS.

questions.q: Recombinant injectable FSH is described as a purified form of FSH, with the main disadvantage being:
questions.why: Recombinant FSH is purified, but its main disadvantage is that it is expensive.

questions.q: The principle of laparoscopic ovarian drilling is to burn the ovarian stroma, destroying theca cells, thereby:
questions.why: Burning the ovarian stroma destroys theca cells, decreasing androgen production.

questions.q: Advantages of laparoscopic ovarian drilling include no risk of multiple pregnancies and:
questions.why: Laparoscopic ovarian drilling carries no risk of OHSS, in addition to no risk of multiple pregnancies.

questions.q: The disadvantage of laparoscopic ovarian drilling is the risk of premature menopause/POI, occurring due to:
questions.why: Follicular destruction from the drilling procedure risks causing premature menopause or POI.

questions.q: The 'Rule of 4' for laparoscopic ovarian drilling specifies 4 sites, for 4 seconds, and:
questions.why: The 'Rule of 4' specifies 4 sites, 4 seconds duration, and 40 watts power.

questions.q: IVF is indicated in PCOS-related infertility when the patient is \u226535 years old AND has:
questions.why: IVF is indicated when the patient is \u226535 years old and has additional factors contributing to infertility.

questions.q: Spironolactone is contraindicated in PCOS patients seeking pregnancy because, being anti-androgenic, it can cause:
options: Ambiguous genitalia in a female baby
Ambiguous genitalia in a male baby
questions.why: Spironolactone\u2019s anti-androgenic action can cause ambiguous genitalia in a male fetus, so it is avoided when pregnancy is being pursued.

questions.q: OCPs are generally contraindicated when trying to conceive in PCOS, except in which scenario?
options: Clomiphene-resistant cases (used as pretreatment before CC)
questions.why: OCPs may still be used in clomiphene-resistant cases as pretreatment before CC, despite being generally avoided when actively trying to conceive.

questions.q: SERMs capable of causing ovulation induction include clomiphene citrate, tamoxifen, and:
questions.why: Raloxifene, along with clomiphene citrate and tamoxifen, is a SERM capable of ovulation induction.

questions.q: Ormeloxifene is a SERM that specifically:
options: Is the most potent ovulation inducer
Is identical in action to clomiphene citrate
questions.why: Unlike clomiphene, tamoxifen, and raloxifene, ormeloxifene does not cause ovulation induction.

questions.q: Ormeloxifene is a component of which contraceptive, marketed under the name \u2018Chaya\u2019?
questions.why: Ormeloxifene is the active component of centchroman, marketed as \u2018Chaya\u2019.

questions.q: The drug of choice for managing insulin resistance in PCOS is:
questions.why: Metformin, an insulin sensitizer, is the DOC for managing insulin resistance in PCOS.

questions.q: Indications for metformin in PCOS include insulin resistance, inability to lose weight, and:
